" CAPITAL " CHAT.
Mr. Gladstone is going to Florence,towards the end of October, and he will remain in Italy until the meeting of Patliament. Sir James Lacaita has placed his villa at Mr. Gladstone's disposal,

Mr. Justin McCarthy had a consultation on Wednesday with Mr. _Parnell on the subject of political expenditure incurred in Ireland before the spa in the Irish party. The public disagreement between the two members has not interrupted their personal friendship, and after their conversa- tion they drove to the House of Commons together.

It is now settled that the Czar and the Czarina with their children will arrive towards the end of this month on a visit co the Danish Court, but it is not certain whether-they will remain there as long as on former occasions. In any case, our Berlin correspondent telegraphs, the silver wedding of the Russian Imperial couple on the 28th of October, will not be celebrated at the Danish Court, but at St. Petersburg, and then only privately.

For some time past Mr. Henry Irving has been suffering from an affection of the throat which, as threatening to deprive him of the use of his voice, has caused considerable anxiety. Mr. Irving has been under the care of Sir Morrell McKenzie, who the other day successfully performed an operation on him. Since then he has made rapid progress to- wards recovery, and has left town for Malvern, where he intends to.remain till the beginning of the autumn play season.

Mr. Brand, M.P., has received a letter from Mr. Gladstone congratulating him heartily upon the striking success in the recent election contest in the Wisbech Division of Cambridgeshire, express- ing satisfaction that the son of the late Speaker has been the means of winning such a victory for the Liberal cause, and adding that, to judge from their recent utterances, even the Unionists and Conservatives now recognised the fact that in its present form their "game is up."

The Archbishop of Treves and the Archbishop of Versailles, our Paris correspondent says, have agreed to submit a dispute of very long standing to arbitration. The Pope is naturally to be umpire, and the question at issue is whether the seamless garment at Treves or the one at the- Church of Ar- genteuil has the best claims to genuiness. The Ar- genteuil relic; is of camel's hair, and is handwoven, and has faint traces of purple. It was given by the Empress Irene to Charlemagne in the year 800.

It is narrated in a Chinese native paper that the natives of Soochow baying made every effort to get rain, but all in vain, at last heard that the small town of Kuang-Fuching had an idol that was very propitious. The chief magistrate was instructed to go and bring the image to Soochow. When the goddess had completed only half the journey, the skies became clouded, and the moment she entered the gates a tremendous shower descended, accom- panied by thunder and lightning. The image of the goddess was placed in a temple to receive the thanks and incense of the officials and the people, who rejoiced exceedingly.

Your remarks the other day, writes a correspond- ent, on Bjornstjerna Bjornsson, the famous Nor- wegian writer, reminds me of an incident of his visit to Helsingfors a year or two ago. He was in- vited to a wealthy merchant in the city, and every- thing was done to make his stay an agreeable one. The morning after his arrival the hostess got up early to arrange about breakfast, when, to her astonishment, she met Mr, Bjornsson in the garden. "What, are you already up?" she asked. "Up! why, my dear lady, I have been up since six, and had my breakfast." The lady afterwards heard that he had had his breakfast with the servants.

The proceedings of the Wesleyan Conference in its annual sessions at Nottingham have naturally attracted attention, and Nonconformists generally are struck with tie changed attitude of Metho- dism in its relation to the Church and the out- spoken utterances of the newly-elected President, with others of the Forward party who represent the future of Methodism. The serious proposal made by one of the foremost ministers in the North of England that the Conference should, on high religious grounds, commit itself to the principle of Disestablishment is, to say the least, a remarkable sign of the times. It is said that in the event of a general election there are several prominent Wes- leyan laymen who are prepared to come forward as candidates in the Liberal cause.

The gathering at Birmingham to honour the memory of Dr. Priestley recalls an anecdote of that eminent man. One Sunday, whilst the doctor was in his pulpit, and in the middle of his sermon, a terrific thunderstorm broke over the chapel so as greatly to alarm the congregation. and they were visibly affected. Thereupon the preacher stopped, and at once began to explain the nature of light- ning with a view to allay the fright of the congre- gation. "Be not alarmed," he said, " the heavy showers which you now observe are removing the cause of danger—the electric fluid israpidly coming down in this torrent of rain." Having calmed the fears of his audience, and delighted them with a brief scientific lecture, he returned, with perfect ease, to the subject of his sermon, and then pro- ceeded as if nothing had happened to interrupt it.

"There is a man who knew Sir Walter Scott " any traveller in Melrose might be told any day al- most, until Wednesday of last week. This old friend of Scott's, Mr. John Bell of Abbey-st., Mel- rose, died lagt Wednesday afternoon at the age of 92. With Mr. Bell's death, says a correspondent, "the last living link with the days of Scott has been broken." Mr. Bell's house used to be greatly frequented by American tourists during the holiday season. Mr. Bell was born in beautiful Melrose, lived in it all his life—wag-miserable if he lost sight of it for a day. It appears that Berwick-on-Tweed marked the utmost limits of Mr. Bell's travels from his birthplace. Among his friend were (besides Sir Walter Scott) Sir David Brewster, Sir David Erskine, Thomas Aird, the poet and the late Duke of Buceleuch.

The Glasgow lasses take, it appears, something more than kindly to their school lessons in cookery. Nearly a third of the total number of school girls in Scotland examined on this subject belong to that vast city were eagerness for instruction in this in- sinuating art is said to be almost universal. Clearly the haggis of the future promises to be a far more scientific dainty than that savoury but homely concoction which caused the poet Burns to sweep to ecstasy the living lyre. The board, we are officially assured, have been encouraging their ordinary teachers to qualify themselves to receive cookery diplomas, 30 that they may be able to take the cookery lessons in the schools in which they are engaged, and the results have been "in every way satisfactory." It is gratifying to learn that the expense of teaching this important subject is pretty nearly covered b 3 the grant and the profits on articles sold.

There has been so much lying by both parties to the sanguinary struggle in Chili that it has been difficult from the published accounts to get more than a general idea of the terrible character of the internecine quarrel. Bit by bit, however, as British ships.and seamen arrive home, details of the fierce fighting at the seaport towns are becoming known. The captain of a merchant steamer, who has just arrived in England,via Antwerp, where his vessel lies, tells me that he accommodated nearly 1,000 re- fugees for the time being outside Iquique. The strange thing is that, notwithstanding the upset of all commerce and the chaotic state of the country generally, the belligerents seems to experience zio lack of money. They are prepared to pay the most extravagant sums for officers and sailors to man their war vessels and for the purpose of arms, am- munition, and coals, and there is no doubt, my in- formant adds, that the financial obligations would be duly met.

It is, it seems, the practice of the medical pro- fession in Edinburgh to beguile the scanty leisure that falls to their lot by recording cases in rhyme after the fashion of a well-known legal volume. Here is a sample, cited by Dr. John Chiene : Cam Second. An unhealthy lad To Duncan's Ward came in, sir, And showed to him a shocking bad Affair upon his shin, sir. Says Duncan, twirling of his probe, I fear that this won't cobble; 'Twill never make a decent job, And all your life you'll hobble. He gave the ether. Off the leg Was snipped before their noses; Chap woke and found a wooden peg Where there had been necrosis.
The author of this remarkable effort in rhyming is stated to have been Sir Douglas Alaclagan, "the Nester of Medicine in the capital of the INorth."

div.head: TnE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 8, 1891.
div.p: TnE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 8, 1891.

Letters received from Robert Louis. Stevenson by friends in San Francisco, report that his health is improving, though the lungs are still delicate. He gives as his reasons for selecting Samoa as a resi- dence, that it is an easy place to buy land; that communication is prompt with the outer world, enabling him to read his proofs with despatch; and that the island is not afflicted with "red-tapeism and petty arrogance," as is the case, according to Mr. Stevenson, with so many that are under European government. He has just finished build- ing himself a house on the plantation he has pur- chased. The site is a plateau at the base of a mountain with a flne view of the ocean.

One of the most interesting questions with which the end of thdsession is greeted is of course, "How many more under this Government?" Rumour is busy with the answer, and next July is the date confidentially spoken of for a dissolution. As Lord Salisbury took occasion to remind us the other day, the Governmental lease does not necessarily expire until August of 1893, but opinion grows that to go to the very end and then to cap Parliamentary labours with the exertions of a general, election would be more than the most untiring politicians could bear. A short and sharp session, with 'a fight at the end of it, for next year is held to be a more inspiriting programme.
AMERICAN FUNERALS.

It is perhaps appropriate that I should here say a word as to American Funerals. It is no unusual thing in passing down the streets to see a funeral procession of twelve or fifteen coaches and teams making for the cemetery at a good trot. The numer- ous carriages are not obtained as a display of wealth,but in conformity with an American custom which would bear transplanting in England. The memorial service is held at the house of the de- ceased, and then the friends are conveyed in separ- ate coaches to witness the interment at the ceme- tery. This over the friends are immediately driven to their own houses, and the bereaved are left to mourn their loved and lost ones in the qaiet of their homes. There is no feasting and jollification such as distinguish too many English funerals,and which for days keep the bereaved from fully realising their loss The outward sign of mourning at American houses is not in blinds or shutters, as every house has to resort to these to keep out the sun, but it consists of a wreath of crape hung on the front door, with different-coloured ribbon streamers to denote the particular disease that caused the death. in win- ter the ground is frozen so very hard that it is quite impossible to dig graves,and those who die in the winter months are deposited in the .cemetery conservatory and buried when the weather is more genial. In the early months of the year when the earth was held in the solid grip of King Frost friends of mine lost their little son, who was there deposited, and as the interment was to take place during my visit, I went as a witness. Americans bury their dead in their best attire, and often with much jewellery. The bodies are first placed in beautiful caskets with glass tops, and afterwards in wooden boxes in which they are in- terred. The undertakers inject embalming fluids into the bodies which make most lifelike corpses, and make it hard for relatives to realise that death has visited them. The little fellow 1 went to see buried died very suddenly—a victim to physic, and it will be sometime before I forget the anguish of the mother, who blamed herself for having adminis- tered the deadly dose. He was buried in his first suit of clothes—poor little dear—and was said to make what I have heard women describe as " a beautiful corpse:" Winter had relapsed its hold on the ground, but it was still bitterly cold as we as- cended the hill to the cemetery, and saw the little box containing the body and casket at the grave side. The box lid was unscrewed,and even the glass lid of the casket removed so that we might have a last look at the remains of the dear boy, but the earthly tenement had then already begun to dis- solve, and it was not a pretty bight. We turned away from the spectacle preferring to have pleasanter recollections of the last appearance of our departed ones,and meanwhile the lids were replaced and the casket lowered to its last resting place amid the deepest silence. The poor parents had their own sad thoughts, and having seen thedast of their little one, they turned to other scenes; but what was uppermost in their minds was evidenced by the father's remark sometimeafter—" What a mystery death is'!"

div.head: ACROSS THE ATLANTI C. By 4, Tow NEIMAN.° VIII—AMONG TILE AMERICANS.
div.p: ACROSS THE ATLANTI C. By 4, Tow NEIMAN.° VIII—AMONG TILE AMERICANS.
ARBOUR DAY. - DECORATION DAY.-AMERICAN

div.head: FUNERALS.
div.p: FUNERALS.

From a cloudless blue sky the sun, gleaming like a fiery orb, sent forth its scorching rays, which were daily gaining greater power, until the earth became quite hot, and everything seemed eager to seek shelter and repose. Birds ceased their songs and hid themselves in the thick foliage of the trees, cattle sought the shade of weather stalls erected by considerate owners, or lay within the cool shadow of umbrageous trees, and every person that could manage it sought relief from the mid-day heat by indulging in a siesta on the shady side of the house, or in a hammock suspended beneath the garden elms. Not a breath of wind came wafting across the meadows or down the broad avenues to relieve the almost stifling atmosphere, and the few people who were forced to bestir themselves did so in a listless sort of way, stopping every now and then to fan themselves, or to stretch out their arms to give the air a chance of penetrating beneath the garments that stuck to them with the adhesiveness of glue. The poor horses in the streets had a very melanckoly appearance as they gently jogged along beneath the blazing sun, and even they scarce had energy enough to resist the onslaughts of the per- sistent flies, which alone appeared to find life worth 'living. Such was the condition of things the last Friday in May when I proceeded, in company with relatives and friends,to assist in what is to the peo- ple ot the United States a very necessary and impor- tant function. Were it not for the trees which are planted everywhere in the cities, life would be un- bearable, and it is not therefore surprising to learn "Arbour Day has becomea legalised institution in 38 states of the Union. Within the last ten• years the state of New York, through her department of Public Instruction, has encouraged its observance by the public schools, until it has become an established school holiday, to be celebrated by the planting of trees on school grounds and in public parks, and dedicating them to authors, statesmen, and distinguished citizens. This has engendered a widespread sentiment leading to the study of trees and their uses in beautifying the landscape; and the sentiment is fostered in the native youth at a very early period. At every school in the city in which I found myself that day, a set programme was gone through by children of all ages, and a general invitation was issued to the citizens to wit- ness the ceremony. The school I visited was devoted to elementary instruction, and conse- quently the benches were occupied by very young children. It was just on the border of the city limits, and was not so well attended as the schools in the city itself. The visitors, however, were made very welcome, and were very pleased with the man- ner in which the young folk acquitted themselves. One by one boys and girls arose in their places,made their way to the platform, bowed to the whole school, and then proceeded to give a solo, a recita- tion, or an address, appropriate to the day. Then the mistress asked questions relative to the institu- tion of Arbour Day, and one reply was to the effect that 78 million acres had been planted with trees in one state alone since the custom of tree planting was inaugurated. A vote was then taken as to which should be the state flower for the year—the Golden Rod or the Rose—and at our school the lat- ter was declared to have the preference. This was followed by chorus singing, special for the occasion and the hearty rendering of the "Star-Spangled Banner," brought the indoor proceedings to a close. An adjournment was afterwards made to the school grounds where the young trees selected were, planted, and thus the institution of Arbour Day was once more duly observed. •

div.head: DECORATION DAY.
div.p: DECORATION DAY.

A ceremony of a totally different character was that of Decoration Day, which I witnessed about the same time. On this day the cemeteries through- out, the land are visited by thousands of people who make a point of decorating with flags and flower s the graves of departed warriors. Every year on this day a new, neat little banner of the national stars and stripes is placed on the grave of every known deceased member of the Grand Army of the Republic ; and some portions of the burial grounds, where the dead heroes lie almost shoulder to shoul- der in their last trenches are quite gay with the tiny banners as they flutter bravely in the breeze. At the graves of the leaders of tho Union troops in the anti-slavery war, grand orations are delivered to the assembled crowds, and the newspapers are tilled with glowing tributes to the nation's dead. The cemetery I attended is delightfully situated on a hill top in the centre of New York State, and commands an extensive view of the lovely Mohawk valley. About two o'clock on the Saturday after- noon, the citizens began to flock to the burial ground, and presently the strains of a fife band heralded the approach of the veterans of the G.A.R. who were coming to do honour to the memory of their late comrades. The old warriors were pre- ceded by the sons of veterans, nearly all of whom wore military dress. The veterans themselves were of all ranks of life, and of all shades of colour, and not a few of them showed reminiscences of the war in the shape of maimed or miss- ing limbs. The ceremony on this occasion was unusal, inasmuch as a plot of land had been purchased for the interment of soldiers who had no relatives to care for them, and a huge granite boulder in its natural state was dedicated to their honour and to mark the site. Immediately on entering the cemetery grounds the attention of the visitors was attracted by a splendid floral design suggestively inscribed To the unknown,' and D as- ing round to the south of the necropolis, past noble monuments to the memory of the city's great and good, they came to the plot reserved for the soldiers who have neither kith nor kin. Here the veterans formed a circle round the boulder,by which a platform had been erected, and near which stood• the widows and women-kind of the old soldiers. A quartette of male voices occupied a position near the platform,and after they had sung,and the Post chaplain had read prayer, a gentleman mounted the platform and gave an oration in commemoration of the deeds of the G.A.R. The rough unhewn boulder, said he, was a fit memorial to the brave men to whose heroic deeds their descendants owed so much, and he made a passing reference to the bronze in- scription it bore :

FRATERNITY, CHARITY, LOYALTY. They sleep so calm and stately, Each in his graveyard bed, It scarcely seems that lately They trod the fields blood red, With fearless tread. They marched and never halted ; They scaled the parapet ; The treble lines assaulted, And paid without regret, The final debt. The oration over, the quartette sang." The vacant chair," and brought tears to the eyes of many women within the circle. At the conclusion ot the ceremony the veterans re-formed ranks, and cast- ing a lingering look at the graves of half-a-dozen ' of their comrades who had already found a resting- place within the sacred reservation, they des- cended the hill and proceeded to headquarters in the city. The ceremony throughout was very touching, and many of the spectators were affected to tear,s during its progress. The Americans have not much history,and it is only natural they should make the most of it." Do you have Decoration Day in England ?" said a young lads' who stood near me, and was most anxious I should see everything because I was an Englishman. "Oh, dear, no," I responded; "we are such a blooduhirsty lot that if we began such a ceremony it would last from New Year's Day to Ckristmas.'

div.head: BATHING FATALITIES.
div.p: BATHING FATALITIES.

Sarah Russell, a shipbuilder's wife from Liverpool, was drowned on Wednesday in the Solway Firth, off Mary- port, while bathing. A similar fate overtook William Wilkinson, a .bugler in the Worcester Artillery Volun- teer Corps, who went to bathe in the river Conway.

div.head: BREACH OF PROMISE.
div.p: BREACH OF PROMISE.

At the Sheriff's Court at Oakham on Wednesday, Emma Lacey, a shopkeeper's daughter., now living at Leicester, obtained a verdict with £4OO damages against John Haynes, a man of independent means, residing at Market Deeping, in Lincolnshire, for a breach of pro- mise of marriage. Some extraordinary letters were read during the hearing of the case.

div.head: ANOTHER SALFORD GAS SCANDAL.
div.p: ANOTHER SALFORD GAS SCANDAL.

The Gas Committee of the Salford Town Council, act- ing on the fiat of the Attorney-General, have determined to prosecute a coal contractor who is alleged to have offered the Gas Engineer (Mr. Shoubridge), by way of bribe, an envelope containing money. It is possible, ap- parently, that we may not yet have heard the last of the previous gas scandal. The whole question will come up again for discussion a month hence.

div.head: ALDERSHOT CASE.
div.p: THE ALDERSHOT CASE.

The trial of police-officers arising out of the case of Alice Millard, of Aldershot, was concluded At the Win- chester Assizes, on Wednesday. Constable Bradbury was found not guilty of perjury, but the jury added a rider to their verdict expressing their opinion that the police had greatly neglected their duty in not making fuller inquiries into the character of the girl between the time of her arrest and the Police Court proceedings. No evidence was offered against Sergeant Cottle, who was accordingly found "Not guilty."
EXTRA.ORDINARY ADVENTURES AMONGST THE MANIPURIS.

Among the later stories of the Manipur affair that of the adventures of Signaller Williams is certainly not lacking in thrilling interest. He was in charge of the Chief Commissioner's telegraph camp and was left for political reasons at Sengraai when Mr. Quin- ton went on to Manipur. When the revolt broke out he and his ten Sepoys were attacked by a hun- dred Manipuris armed with rifles, spears, and bows and arrows. He e-caped to the jungle, and this was set on fire by his pursuers. His Sepoys were shot down as they fled from the smoke and flame. Mr. Williams managed to remain in hiding, and made his escape at nightfall,only to fall into an am- bush in the morning. Here he was under fire for a time, but the Manipuris were bad marksmen. They misSed him and he succeeded in finding refuge in a tree. The tree was struck by lightning, but the signaller was unharmed. After all these hair- breadtk escapes and incidents one hears almost as a inatter of course that, though he was taken pri- soner, confined in a modern black-hole and ordered to be shot, he came triqmphantly through his trials. The Manipuri chiefs; indeed, made much of him, hoping to better their chances of lenient treatment by their behaviour to him, and he came back to camp with honour.

div.head: "TILE QUEEN'S CLOSET OPENED."
div.p: "TILE QUEEN'S CLOSET OPENED."

Some curious ancient recipes are given in an article in "The Atlantic Monthly" called "The Queen's Closet Opened," this being the title of a volume printed in 1656, which contained a number of receipts, both chirurgical and housewifely, col- lected for the benefit of Queen Henrietta Maria. Pearls, red coral, and white amber are frequent in- gredients in the medical prescriptions. A pretious water " for reviving the spirits has half a dram of each of these, and an equal quantity of leaf gold to be put in a linen bag and suspended in four quarts of ale, with many herbs added. Sir Edward Spen- cer's eye-salve was costly with powdered pearls. Minute directions are given for powdering the pearls. A prescription" to ease the passion of the heart" is made of the juice of damask roses boiled with sugar to a syrup and thickened with powders of amber, pearl and rubies. A little of this mixture was to betaken on a knife's point morning and evening. Charles I.'s queen suffered from insomnia, an odd cure for which consisted of " annis-seeds " bruised and steeped in red rose water, then made up in little bags, one of which was bound to either nostril. Hard-boiled eggs applied to the nape of neck was another means adopted for inducing sleep. The remedy for toothache is a strange one. "The tooth of a dead man carried about a man pre- sently suppresses the pains of the teeth." An ail- ment of which one never hears nowadays was then known under the title of "cold stomach." The pre- scribed cure for it was the application of a sod of turf, the green side next to the skin. The Countess of Mounteagle's remedy seems much more comfort- able, consisting as it did of periwinkle and rosemary tops made hot.

div.head: SELECTED READINGS.
div.p: SELECTED READINGS.

CUSTOMS OF THE ANCIENT ROMAN PRIESTESSES. —A lecture was delivered lately in the Lowell Institute, Boston, by Professor Lanciani. His sub- ject was "The Discovery of the House of the Ves- tals." The discovery, said the lecturer, was made in September. 1883, and the excavations have been carried on until the ruins are almost entirely unearthed. The house, or courtyard, as it was more properly called, was situated at the foot of the Palatine Hill, and immediately adjoined the wing of the Palace of the Cresars. The discovery furnished a most fascinating subject for investiga- tions, but the splendid results achieved were unexpected. In all the experience which Professor Lanciana has had in these matters never before was a more delightful and interesting subject for exca- vation entered upon. This dwelling, which was the sacred and unapproachable shelter of the Vestala, and in which were kept secrets inviolate, presented a field for the imagina- tion rarely encountered by the archaeologist. Let us revivify these halls with the maidens clad in snow white garments, emblematic of their purity of character. Imagine the punishments there undergone for trivial or more serious offence; and the holy rites peaformed through many centuries. The origin of the order is simple. In prehistoric times each village kept a fire burning night and day for the benefit of the villagers, who there obtained coals by which to kindle their own house- hold fires. These fires were tended by maidens, who were less likely to be called away, and were .chosen on this account. Finally, this constant tending of fires grew to be a sacred custom, and worked its way into Rome. The requirements for admission as a vestal were very strict. The girl .must be between the ages of 6 and 10 years. Her 'character must be above reproach, and she must be physically perfect, the slightest fault in this respect making admission impossible. The parents must be alive and free and of irreproachable character. When elected, and these candidates were .selected from the noblest families of Rome, the inau- .guration or rites of admission were performed. First the hair was cut, then theraimantwas changedto the simple white garb of the priestesses, and the young girl was shown her duties. At the age of 36 years she was free to return to the world and her family, but this privilege was rarely, if ever, taken advan- tage of, as the position of a vestal was certainly an enviable one in many ways. The life was divided into 10 year periods. During the first the virgin was under instruction, during the second she prac- tised what had been taught her, and then for ten years became an instructor herself. The advan- tages of the order were many and varied. Wealth was one characteristic. The Emperor Tiberius gave in the year 24 A.D., a sum corresponding to ,18,000 of our money, to a vestal named 'Cornelia, and a large income was realised in other ways. The vestals were exempt from the autho- rity of the law. Being liable to be sum- moned as witnesses in a Court of law was their only annoyance. Seats were set apart for them at the theatre and at the circus, although these were, with some few exceptions, rarely used. The noble women of Rome usually travelled in sedan chairs, but the vestals were accorded two kinds of carriages, and every one, even a consul, was obliged to make room for their passage. Their horses were exempt from the seizure in time of need which threatened nearly every Roman's equine possessions. At solemn religious meetings or at State ceremonies the vestals had important duties, and important documents were intrusted to their keeping. Several months before his death, Augustus left his will and many important docu- merits of State in charge of the abbess of Vesta. In a diplomatic line, the virgins were often called upon to act as ainha.ssadresses, making treaties of peace and performing important duties. Any offence against vestals was punished immediately by death. Their wishes had but to be expressed and they were granted. A privilege which was doubt- less highly estemed was that of being buried within the city walls; yet among the 80,000 tombs un- earthed, but one grave of a vestal was found. This Is, perhaps, explained by the fact that the name was not allowed to go on the tombstone- of a vestal virgin. The least offence against chastity by a, vestal virgin was punished with death by starva- tion, and several graphic accounts of this frightful punishment and the way it was inflicted have been banded down to us. If such an offence were com- mitted, the offender was immediately tried and deprived of the snow white raiment of the order. If convicted, the vestal was carried through the streets in a long procession, just beyond the city gates, where a tomb had been prepared. The tomb was reached by a ladder, and the descent of one of these fallen maidens into this dark, damp hole, must have been a most horrible sight. The tomb was supplied with a bed, a small lamp, and a few provisions, this last being a cruelty, prolonging the life of the miserable occupant. When the procession had arrived ,at the tomb, surrounded by a weeping but silent throng, the high priest opened the hearse and led the maiden to the ladder, raising his hands in prayer and turning the head from the heart-rending sight. The ladder was withdrawn aftßr the descent, and the tomb carefully closed and sealed and many tons weight of earth piled upon it, until every trace of the grave was obliterated. Every precaution was taken to keep the vestals entirely excluded, and free from temptation. Spies were present among the servants, and one case is reported where a spy informed against a virgin, the charge being that the maiden in question paid too much attention to her personal attire. No physician was ever allowed to enter the sacred walls; but if a priestess was ill she was immediately removed to the home of her parents or put in charge of a matron, in each ease being carefully watched and guarded.

A GHASTLY CQLLECTION.—" Baron Henickstein was a banker in Vienna to whom I had a letter of ' introduction " said a lady to a correspondent of the Cleveland Leader. "With some friends I called upon him. He received us cordially. When our business was completed, the Baron invited us to visit his private museum, which filled an upper floor of the bank building. It had taken the noble banker some 50 yeas to form this collection of rare and valuable antiquities. After making the tow' of the long hall the baron drew from his pocket • massive iron key, and, unlocking a door at one end, beckoned us to follow him into a dimly-lighted room. On entering we saw ranged about it a series of tall and narrow mahogany wardrobes, the doors of which our host rapidly threw open, disclosing to our astonished gaze a grim and ghastly human skeleton in each. Ladies,' said this extra- ordinary man, 'let me introduce you to this select circle of my intimate friends—friends, ladies, in whom I confide all, and. who reveal nothing. Here is my beautiful Etalka, the love of my youth, who cast aside her flesh half a century ago, and is still true to me. This is all that remains to me of old Heinrich, the faithful cashier of 40 years of my father and myself. Enter and fear nothing!' and as much afraid of refusing as to obey we passed the box and found ourselves standing in a close, cell- like apartment, hung with heavy black draperies, and lavishly ornamented with armorial bearings and numerous death's heads and cross-bones. Nearly filling the pace was a huge casket or coffin of ebony, lined with black velvet, and arranged to receive a body; and on the silver plate attached to the lid was inset ibed the Baron's name and title, with a blank space left for his age and date of death. To the foot of the coffin was attached a parchment scroll, containing instructions for the Baron's funeral, in whi,ilr, among other stipulations, he directed that the horses attached to the hearse should be driven on a fast trot to a tune which he had his music box play for us."

SOMEBODY has compared the world to a beehive, The empty comb represents the possibilities of life, which may be tilled with honey or stuffed with bee bread; and as in gathering honey the bee uses the sting as a spatula, and mingles a portion of its sting poison with the sweet for the sake of preserving it, so the wealth which the human bee accumulates last all the better when deposited little at a time at an expense of much care and labour. .

ONE very hot day a case was being tried in a court of law. The counsel for the plaintiff had been speaking at greF.t. length, and after referring to numerous autitm 'ties, was about to produce an imposing volume, when the judge inquired what was the amount in dispute. On being informed that it was two pounds," Well," said he," the weather is very hot, I am very old, and also feeble— I'll pay the amount myself."

A Cherbourg telegram on Monday describes the ,fes- tivities in honour of the Russian cruiser Admiral Korni- loff, from which it would appear that the enthusiasm on both sides was unbounded. Crowds lined the route of the procession, and shouts of " Vive la Russe, vive la Greece," continuously rent the air.

div.head: LETITIA THORNTON.
div.p: LETITIA THORNTON.
BY LOUISA BIGG. AUTHOR OF "CLARE WELSHAN," ETO.
CHAPTER XII.

The weeks and months passed on, and from time to time Robert wrote. There were his letters in the Chronicle, too, with news of the political crisis, which had been the occasion of his sudden dismissal to America, so that he never seemed very far off. Letitia kept her secret closely to herself, for there was no acknowledged engagement as yet between her and her cousin, and she was glad that it was so, and that the first fragrance of their love was sate from the breath of idle gossip and formal con- gratulations. And one afternoon in the autumn when she did not in the least expect it, Mr. Dela- field asked her to be his wife and she gently but firmly refused him.

It happened in this way. She an Miss Priscy had been covering some new books for the Institute and not having a catalogue at hand, had decided that Laetitia should follow the messenger who carried them, and number and enter them in the room. She was accordingly seated at a deal table with the volumes in their shining brown paper covers spread round her and a catalogue open before her, when Mr. Delafield suddenly entered. He did not know that she was there, and had no further object in coming than to take a general survey and see that all was going to his mind, but as soon as he beheld Miss Thornton he was seized with an uncontrollable desire to end all doubt and delay at once.

In- a few words he asked her to marry him, not professing any ardent passion, for which she liked him all the better, but simply telling her that he loved her, and would make her as good a husband as he could if she would accept; him. "It is impossible," answered Ltitia quietly; "it is an honour for me that you should have thought of it, bat please forget that all this has passed and let us be just as we were before." As she was speaking someone passed the window, and in a moment Jessie Grayson entered. "Jessie," said Miss Thornton, readily, "I wish you would finish these books for me ; there are such a number of them, and I am in a hurry to go on."

"I do not think I can wait," said Jessie, with a blush. "I came to look for a book for Lizzie, and I did not know you were here." "There is only this heap to be done, and it will not take long." "Well, I will do them if you like." Ltetitia bade them both good-by, but Mr. Dela- -field did not offer to follow her and further press his suit. Jessie went on numbering the books with deft thuogh trembling fingers, and a gentle deference in her manner towards him that did much to soothe his wounded self-esteem. She liked working for him, and if he had lost everyone of those accessories that had, fascinated her at first, she would have liked it even better, so far had things gone with her now. After a little while he left her there to finish her work, and she neatly stacked the books on their deal shelves, and made the room tidy with a tender devotion that left nothing prosaic in the labour. She was suffering all the while a far keener heartache than the man who had been denied his love ; her history was a blank like Viola's, but that is what so many women's histories are that she had no right to complain of it. When she got home she found two of the children crying, a damp-looking cold shoulder of mutton for dinner, and her sister out of spirits and irritable, and she bent all her energies to set these various discomforts right, as was her habit. "After all it is quite as well that I should be an old maid." she soliloquised, as she showed the in- experienced cook how to fry potatoes in the French way so as to make the cold mutton more palatable; "I do not know what they would do without some- body to see after things." LEetitia went on to Mary Preston's, feeling greatly relieved that the dreaded moment had passed so quickly, and that she was so entirely sure of her own mind at last; she was amused, too, at her own diplomacy in immediatly introduc- ing Jessie as her successor. She found Mary with her boy in her lap, look- ing, in her black dress, like a sweet-faced, homely madonna, and the child stretched out its little arms to L..Ttitia,, who bent down and kissed him. She often came to see Mary, and of late it was strange how much they talked of America. To- day she read aloud part of Dillon's last letter, while the baby played with the envelope, greatly to his own satisfaction, and Mary, as she shyly watched the reader's glowing face, divined the secret that she had long suspected. But it was known to none except those two.

div.head: CHAPTER XIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XIII.
"What a night for a walk—l am tired to death of this life."

"Well you will not hurt much more of it if we have good weather for two days longer, and the captain says he never saw a better chance of it." The first speaker was Robert Dillon, and the second a young Londoner who had been varying his duties on the Stock Exchange with a view of the United States, and was somewhat unwilling to get back into harness. They were smoking their evening cigars together on the deck of the Anda- lusia bound for London and most of the other passengers had gone below, for the air was chilly since the sunset.

"Young fellow, you ought not to be on deck," said Dillon, pausing in his walk by a figure muffled in a rug and half lying on one of the seats. "I am going down now," answered a feeble voice. "I wanted to see so'me of the stars come out." He rose from his place and Dillon supported him to the ladder, down which he obediently tottered.
"Who is that lad ?" asked Dillon's companion, carelessly. "I don't remember to have noticed him before."

"His name's Simpson, he's only nineteen, and all by himself; he was not at all fit to start, but he has got on better than I expected. I ran against him somehow, the first day we came on board, and he told me all about himself. He suffers with his lungs, and is going bank to live with his mother in England." "Poor chap! he does'nt look like living with anybody much; horrid complaint, consumption." And he blew a long cloud of smoke into the air and watched it float fragrantly away, with a placid satisfaction in being the possessor of exceptionally good lungs. Robert did not answer, for he stood lookinc, out moss the darkening waters and thinking of home. Just now the Firs was lighted up, and he could almost see the glowing windows and a light shadow now and then flitting across the blind in the draw- ing-room, as he had seen it from the garden on bygone evenings. In three short days they were to Teach port, and his heart beat quicker with gladness as he thought of La3titia's waiting face. Somehow this evening those he loved were especially present with him, and more real to his consciousness than the men and women round him. " See that craft out there?" asked the other, unconscious of his compvion's abstraction, " it looks only like a dark patch now in the twilight. The captain told me half-an-hour ago that he thought it was a New York trading vessel." "I see,' answered Didon, laconically. "Suppose we go below; I can hear that the music has begun." "No music for me, thank you—l shall see you again presently ; I'll finish this cigar before I come down. Dillon left him and went down into the saloon, where the grand piano was, a gaily i,ecorated room with mirrors and velvet cushions and elaborate panels. A little impromptu ball was going on, and on the seats at the sides were groups of passe, gers working or reading. Yount, Simpson was watcaing the scene with feverishly bright eyes, and made room for Dillon at his side.

"I wish I could sit hero all night," he said, "I cannot bear the berths; they make me feel as if I was going to be smothered; won't it be jolly to sleep in a bed again ? " "I shall be glad enough to be on land again," answered Dillon, "but the berths do not trouble me much now. I remember years ago I was very nervous on the water, but I have quite got over it, and you must try to be bold. It will never do for you to go into port looking thin and seedy." "I do not feel quite so well to-day, and I sup- pose that makes me cowardly," said the lad, raising his thin face and looking wistfully into Dillon's eyes, "it must be so dreadful to be drowned." "Ron t forget, old fellow, that Heaven is as near at sea as on land ; ' that was a brave speech ot the old sea-captain as true as brave. Come, you must turn in, and I'll sit by you till you feel like sleeping,' as the Yankees say."
It was a clear, moonlight night, and the sea gently rocked the vessel as she sped on rapidly to- wards home. Dillon lay sleeping in his berth and along ray of moonlight streatning across the ca,b4o,

floor reached his pillow and lit up his clear profile. He Might well have been the Crusader, to whom Jessie Grayson had likened him, resting on his tomb in stone, so still and noble he looked in the dim, silvery light. Every object in the tiny cabin was distinctly visible, from the trunk on which its owner's clothes lay in a confused heap to a leather case with Ltetitia's likeness inside. It was just two bells, and the ripple and plash of the water against the timbers of the ship was the only sound audible. Quarter of an hour passed, and Dillon. moved restlessly aside, oppressed by an uneasy dream. He thought that he was in his own rooms. at home, and Miss Priscy suddenly appeared;' he, knew that she had some ill news for him, buti before she could speak a cloud of smoke came between them and he could not find her. There- was a strange odour in the cabin, and the moon— light had grown pale, but he did not awake. Foot- steps hurried across deck, and there was a rushing. of water unlike the sound of the waves. Then. instead of moonbeams there was a dull red light and the sleeper woke with a start, and leapt up seized with a horror that turned his brain giddy. He huddled on some clothes and opened the door. The great saloon was full of smoke, and he could not find the ladder, but his unavailing efforts brought him back to his own cabin door. A sudden thought struck him, and he rushed in again and seized his life-belt, and Ltitia's likeness and made for the ladder once more. The smoke had cleared a, trifle, and this time he found it, and in three bounds was on deck.

A column of smoke was rising from the vessel's side and the sailors were pouring in water with desperate haste. "Fire ! fire! the storeroom's in a blaze !" it was the stewardess who ran shrieking on deck after him.

"Good God, we're lost!" cried Dillon, as a great cloud of smoke came sweeping up the stairs and another tongue of flame stole up into the open air from the engine-room. "Stop that and lower the boats I" shouted the captain to the sailors, and one passenger after another staggered on deck half clad and frantic with fear. The fire had begun in some hidden nook below and spread stealthily from side to side,, till now it crept into sight a full grown resistless giant. The engineers, faithful to their post,, stopped the engines; the man at the wheel did not stir from his place; the sailors lowered the boats; there was a young bride, fainting in her husband's• arms, and a crowd of women clinging together— some on their knees wildly praying, and others shrieking for help, while a few stood in the face: of a dreadful death calm and collected and tried to soothe the rest. Every moment the power of: the fire grew and there was imminent danger of a leak. The fierce red columns flared up into the, calm sky and the sea all round was red as blood and there was a fearful roar and crackle of wood- work and tackling were swallowed up in the rapid: flame. They filled a boat with the women, and the men in the struggle for life were pushing and crowding for places in the other, Dillon with the rest. His turn had nearly come to scramble down the side into the boat, when turning to look. back at the deck, he saw, lying near the funnel distinct in the glare of the fire, the figure of young Simpson.
Dillon grasped the arm of the maa standing next him—
"Help me to get that boy off," shouted. "Let the poor devil al one—he's booked to die any- how ; save yourself !" said the other roughly, swinging himself over the side and down to the boat.

Dillon was young and life was sweet; he was beloved and hopeful and in the flush of manly strength and health, and deliverance was at his feet —deliverance not only from death, but from a death of torture. The instinct of self-preservation triumphed for a moment and he clung to the rail in front of him; then he suddenly loosed his hold— slipped aside, and hurried over to Simpson—the dense crowd filling up his place and one by one hurrying over the side of the fated ship. He shook the lad and Simpson opened his eyes and tried to get up. "Come along! there's another boat ?" shouted Dillon, dragging his charge across the deck. A crash— a dull rushing sound, and the Anda- lusiayeeled from stein to stern.

"Over the side ! jump over!" roared the cap- tain, and those who dared leapt one by one into the awful sea. It was but a choice of deaths, for not a quarter of them could swim, and hardly one had a lifebelt. In the few minui es of waiting for the boats, Dillon had fastened his belt on, but now he hastily took it off and fastened it on Simpson's body. _ _ -

"-I won't have it," cried he, feebly resisting, "you have none yourself." "I'm all right," said Dillon, seizing him, and dragging him to the edge, "I can swim. Over with you ! " and without more ado he threw him down into the sea, and leapt after him. In two minutes more the ship heeled heavily over, swamp- ing the nearest boat, the water hissing as the flames touched it. An hour later, and the moon looked serenely down on blackened timbers, and floating debris, all that wiz left of the splendid steamship of yester- day. And here and there some perishing human, being clung to plank or spar, hopelessly drifting with the tide to his eternal haven.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF COMMONS. —Sierran/a. Mocermmous.—The House of Commons had a sitt- ing on Saturday, the Speaker taking the chair at a quarter past twelve,when the consideration of the Lords' amendments to the London and North-Western Railway Company (Rates and Charges) Provisional Order Bill was proceeded with. Mr. Lloyd George complained of the terminal charges which the iill sanctioned, particularly With regard to some small branch lines in Wales. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach said the matter was thoroughly thrashed out before the Committee. The amendments Were agreed to. The Intoxicating Liquors (Ireland) Bill and the Assistant County Surveyors (Ireland) Bill were withdrawn. SUPPLY.—The report of Supply was brought up, and on the Post Office vote a discussion took place on Post Office administration, Mr. Raikes being urged to effect further reductions in telegraph charges, and to make further reinstatements of postmen who had been dis- missed or degraded in consequence of participation in the recent strike. Mr. Lloyd George availed himself of the transport vote to bring forward a complaint of the military forces being brought in to assist the police in the collection of tithes in Wales. He moved to reduce the vote by £lOO. Mr. Byrn Roberts and others sup- ported the reduction, but it was negatived without a division. Other subjects touched on in the report were the magazine rifle, the armament of field artillery, the employment of discharged soldiers and reservists, the regimental organisation of the Royal Artillery,gambling in the army, the visit of the French fleet, and education in England and Wales. The report of Supply was ultim- ately agreed to, and the Appropriation Bill brought in amid general cheers and read a first time. BILLS ADVANCED.—The Coinage Bill passed through Committee, and a number of Bills were read a third time. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes to eight 'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at half-past four. The Bill was read a second time. THE WESTERN HIGHLANDS BILL.—The Marquis of Lcerawf, in moving the second reading of this measure, said it was purely a rating Bill enabling the County Councils to borrow money for the construction and maintenance of local harbours. The Bill was read a second time, and the standing order being suspended, it passed through all its stages and was read a third time. MISCELLANEOBS.—The Public Works Loan Bill was read a second time. The Redemption of Rents (Ireland) Bill passed through Committee. The London County Council (Money) Bill also passed through its Committee stage, and was read a third time. IMPRISONMENT UNDER THE VACCINATION ACT.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY asked whether the Secretary of State had the power,under section 38 of the Prisons Act (1877), to mitigate the treatment in prison of persons impri- soned for non-payment of fines under the Vaccination Acts. Lord De RAMSEY replied that, as had been legally decided, a person imprisoned for non-payment of fines Under the Vaccination Acts was a criminal prisoner. At half-past five the sitting was suspended during pleasure.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-MONDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. NEw Win.—On the motion of Mr. CYRIL FLOWER, a new writ was issued for Walsall, to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Sir C. Forster. MR. ATKINSON'S RETURN.—Two motions stood on the paper in the name of Mr. Atkinson, one asking the House to express its disapproval of the Speaker's discourtesy in not replying to a constitutional inquiry; the other re- questing a return of the number of times that a demand for a division had been entered upon the journal of the House as being frivolous, and the circumstances of each case.—Mr. GOSCHEN, in answer to Mr. Atkinson, whose Period of expulsion had expired, declined to give a day for the discussion of the motions, whereupon the mem- ber for Boston said he would either have the matter con- firmed or have the record struck out of the journals. THE LEEDS MURDER.—MT. MATTHEWS, replying to MT. Pickersgill, said he had only seen the newspaper reports regarding the sentence passed on the woman Turner for being concerned in the Leeds murder. He had not had time to make inquiries into the case. THE APPROPRIATION BILL.—Mr. J. REDMOND, On the Second reading of the Appropriation Bill, moved that the cases for treason-felony should be reconsidered, with a view to recommending the extens on towards the pri- soners of the clemency of the Crown.—Mr. MATTHEWS upheld the verdict come to in the case of the dynamit- ards, and said no one reading the evidence of the trial could come to any other conclusion than that the sen- tence was right.—The amendment received the support, amongst others, of Mr. Atkinson and Mr. Parnell, but was rejected by 96 to 39.—After same discussion as to the amount of Ireland's share of the educational grant, the Appropriation Bill was read a second time. FACTORIES AND WORKSHOPS BILLS.—The House pro- ceeded with the consideration of the Lords' amendments to the Factories and Workshops Bill.—The HOME SECRE- TARY moved that the House disagree with the Lords' amendment as to the County Councils providing for the inspection of workshops.—The House disagreed with the Lords' amendment by 66 to 45.—Sir HENRY Dams moved an amendment providing for the punishment by fine of any person bribing an operative to.disclose an employer's trade secret in the processes of manufacture. This was agreed to, and a Committee was appointed to draw up reasons for disagreeing with the Lords' amendments. I kThe House was counted out at a quarter to one. HOUSE OF LORDS—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. ADJUSTING DIFFERENCES .—The Commons' reasons for disagreeing with some of the Lords' amendments to the Elementary .Education Bill were considered, and Lord Cranbrook and Lord Salisbury protested against the at- titude taken by the House of Commons, but at the same time made no objection to the variation of the clause re- garding the grouping of schools. The alterations of the other Plouse were accordingly agreed to. The Commons amendments regarding the Land Purchase Bill were agreed to with a slight alteration. The Labourers' (Ire- land) Acts Amendment Bill was read a second time, and passed through its remaining stages. On consideration of the Factories and Workshops Bill, their lordships de- cided not to insist on their own amendments. On the motion of Lord Kimberley, the Law of Property Act, 1881, Amendment Bill was read a second time, and after- Wards considered in Committee. OTHER Brus.—The Marquis of SALISBURY protested against rushing a bill of that description through on the day before the prorogation, and moVed that progress Should be reported, the motion, being agreed to. The Coinage Bill went through its remaining stages, and was Passed. The Commons' amendments to the Statute Law Revision Bill were considered and agreed to. The House adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock till I half-past ten o'clock next day. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. The end of the Session was conspicuously marked by the scanty attendance of members. QUESTIONS.—Mr. GOSCHEN, replying to Mr. Cobb, said he did not propose to issue any orders, as suggested, removing exceptional restrictions on the political action of Government officials out of official hours. The Attorney-General for Ireland, replying to Mr. W. A. Macdonald,expressed regret,on behalf of the Chief Secre- tary, that it had not been found possible during the pre- sent session to complete a measure dealing with free education in Ireland. Sir M. HICKS-BEACH, replying to Mr. Atkinson, regarding the fourth section of the Load- line Act, 1890, said he was not aware that any country had adopted the provisions of that section .—Mr. GOSCHEN informed Mr. E. Robertson that the Government were very anxious to pass the Betting and Loans (Infants) Bill, and Mr. Robertson complained strongly that Mr. Goschen had allowed private bills to be taken in defiance of the pledge given to the House. INDIAN FACTORY ACTS.—The Consolidated Fund Appro- priation Bill passed through Committee, and on the order of the day for going into Committee on the East India Revenue Accounts,Mr. FROTAND expressed a hope that the recent Indian Factory Act would not be regarded as final. Mr. S. Smith expressed a strong conviction that simply on the ground of justice and humanity a reasonable degree of factory restraint was called for. The House adjourned at ten minutes past twelve o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—WEDNESDAY. The Earl of Limerick took his seat on the woolsack at eleven o'clock, when there were present the Earl of Wemyss, Earl Waldegrave, Lord Churchill, Lord Den- man, Lord Balfour, of Burleigh, and the Bishop of Manchester. THE APPROPRIATION BILL.—The Appropriation Bill was brought up for the House of Copmons, and passed all its stages. The sitting was then suspended, at five minutes past eleven o'clock. The House reassembled at half-past six o'clock, when the Lord Chancellor, the Earl of Limerick, the Marquis of Lothian, Viscount Cross, and Lord Knutsford took their seats as Royal Commissioners, on a bench in front of the throne. THE ROYAL ASSENT.—The Lord Chancellor directed the Usher of the Black Rod to summon the House of Com- mons, and shortly after the Speaker appeared at the bar. accompanied by about fifty members of the Lower House The Royal assent was then given in the usual form to the following bills :—Consolidated Fund (Appropriation), Mortmain and Charitable Uses Act Amendment (Scot- land), Forged Transfers No. 2, Returning officers (Scot- land), Commissioners for Oaths Act (1889) Amendment,

Slander of Women,Turbary (Ireland) ,Metalliferous Mines (Isle of Man), Post Office Acts Amendment, Public Health (Scotland) Acts Amendment. Ranges, Local Registra- tion of Title (Inland), Judicature Acts Amendment, Western Highlands and Islands (Scotland) Works, Ex- piring Laws Continuance, Public Works Loans,Redernp- don of Rent (Ireland), London County Council (Money), Highways and Bridges,Land Registry (Middlesex Deeds), Lunacy, County Councils (Etections), Penal Servitude, Markets and Fairs (Weighing of Cattle), Schools for Science and Art, Purchase of Land and Congested Dis- tricts (Ireland), Labourers (Ireland) Acts Amendment, Factories and Workshops, Coinage, Foreign Marriages, Statute Law Revision, the Railway Rates and Charges Bills, the Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Rail- way Bill, several Provisional Orders Bills, and a number of private bills_ THE QUEEN'S SPEECH.

The Lord Chancellor then read the Royal Speech as follows : MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN,— I am glad to be able to release you from the labours of a protracted session. My relations with all other Powers continue to be those of peace and amity. A convention has been concluded with the King of Portugal, and has been ratified, defining the boundaries which separate the dominions and the spheres of influence of the two Crowns in Eastern Africa. I have also entered into an agreement with the King of Italy, by which the one has been fixed which separates the Protectorate of Italy in the north-east of Africa from the British sphere of influence and from the territory of Egypt. I have made proposals to the President of tke United States for submission to arbitration of the difference be- tween us as to the seal fishery in the Behring Sea. The negotiations are far advanced, but they are not yet con- cluded. A suspension of the seal fishery in these waters for the present year has intermediately been agreed to between the two Governments, in order to prevent an excessive destruction of the species, which there is reason to apprehend. The French Chambers have not yet approved of an agreement between myself and the French Republic for reference to arbitration of certain differences with respect to Newfoundland, which was signed during the present year. The ratification of the final act of the Brussels Confer- ence for the repression of the slave trade has also been postponed, and also the ratification of the North Sea Con- vention for the prevention of the sale of spirits at sea. GENTLEMEN OF THE HOI7SE OF COMMONS,7-

I thank you for the provision you have made for the charge of the public services. lam glad to be able to devote a considerable sum to the mitigation of the bur- den which the law of compulsory education has im- posed upon the poorer portion of my people. MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN, .

The various measures which you have adopted in recent years for securing the observance of the law in Ireland and improving the general condition of that country have resulted in a marked abatement of agra- rian offences and a considerable advance in prosperity. The steps which have been taken to cope with the distress threatened by the serious failure of the potato crop in the poorest districts of the West of Ireland have proved effectual in averting the great calamity of a famine. You have also passed a beneficial measure for dealing permanently with the congested districts- of Ireland, which it may be hoped will, by fostering agriculture and stimulating the fishing industry, contribute largely to the prevention of similar dangers in the future. The provisions for enabling occupying tenants to pur- chase their holdings, and the measure for facilitating the transfer of real property in Ireland, will furnish the best guarantee for public security and order, by increasing the class of small proprietors of land. The Act which you have passed for imposing on the owners of laud a direct liability for the payment of the tithe rent-charge will remove a frequent cause of con- flict between the occupiers and the titheowners, and will also afford relief to the tithepayers in those cases in which it is most urgently required. • In response to the growing demands of commerce and agriculture, you have completed an important part of the work of simplifying and adjusting railway rates, the results of which will doubtless Justify the heavy labour which it has involved.

The measures which you have passed for improving the laws with respect to factories and workshops, savings banks, and public health, will, I am confident, conduce to the comfort and well-being of my people. I trust that in a future session you may be able to examine several questions of interest to which I have drawn your attention, but which the time at your dis- posal has not permitted you to approach. I pray that in the discharge of your various duties throughout my kingdom you may be attended by the guidance and protection of Almighty God. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY.

MISCELLANEOUS.—The House of Commons, in order to complete its business, met at 10 o'clock yesterday morn- ing. Among the notices of motion for next session was one by Mr. CREMER to the effect that the power of veto now possessed by the House of Lords should be limited to one session of Parliament, and it was received with both cheers and laughter. Mr. ATKINSON appealed to the House to expunge the resolution with regard to his sus- pension from its records, but Mr. Gosehen said such a course was impossible without notice. The Appropria- tion Bill was read a third time, and some discussion fol- lowed with regard to the Indian Councils Bill. The House went into Committee on the Mairiage of None= - formists Bill, which Mr. Atkinson refused to withdraw; but Mr. M'Laren's motion to report progress was carried by 40 votes to 2. and the sitting was suspended at half- past eleven o'clock. The House resumed at twenty minutes past six o'clock, when Mr. krittrisoN gave notice that next ses- sion he should move that the Home Secretary resign or be dismissed because of his conduct towards the Salva- tion Army at Eastbourne, and the feebleness of his ad- ministration generally. At half-past six o'clock the Speaker, in response to the usual summons, proceeded to the House of Lords accompanied by most of the mem- bers present. On his return, standing at the clerk's table, he read a copy of the Queen's Speech proroguing Parliament. Members then filed past the chair, and cordially took leave of the right hon. gentleman.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held in the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Sutton, Burgess, Greenall, Wright, Holmes; Councillors Pierpoint, Cannel!, Muir, Plumpton, Heaton, Shaw Green, Garner, Blackhurst, Monks, Dixon,Hill. Hutch inson, Bolton, J. Fairclough ; Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (Town Clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor). THE NEW MAGISTRATES. The Mayor reported that Alderman Greenall, Mr. .1. Geddes, Alderman J. E. Wright, and Councillor James Fairclough had been placed on the commis- sion of the Bench, and had taken the oath and qualified. STREET lAIPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that the house recently purchased from the trustees of the will of Joseph Chrimes, deceased, be let to Mr. R. W. Marsh, at the rent of £3O per annum, subject to three months' notice to terminate the tenancy. The plans of the following buildings, &c., had been approved :—Ten cottages in Chorley-st., for Mr. John Platt; three houses in Liver- pool-road, for Mr. J. Simmonett ; " give-and-take " line behind premises at Bridge foot. On the motion of Alderman Surrox seconded by Coun- cillor Mum, the minutes were confirmed.

THE SANITARY COMMITTEE. This Committee's minutes contained the following resolutions :—That the tender of Mr. John Lunt to supply brown vitriol at 425. ed. per ton for the next six months be accepted; that the tender of Mr. Jacob San- key to purchase the manure made at the Corporation stables during the next 12 months at ss. per ton be accepted; that the tender of Mr. Thomas E. Pickton to repair two vans for the sum of £39 be accepted ; that the tender of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Limited, to supply 190 furnace bars at £l9 13s. 3d. be accepted; that the tender of Messrs. Thos. Bradford & Co. to supply complete laundry apparatus at the Hospi- tal of Infectious Disease; at £54 be accepted; that Mr. Councillor Henry Roberts and the Medical Officer of Health be appointed to attend the International Congress of Hygiene and Demography to be held in London in August next. Cn the motion of Alderman BURGESS, seconded by Alderman SUTTON, the minutes were confirmed.
PAVING AND SEWER. AGE COMMITTEE. -THE COST OF STREET
MAKING.
