Alderman WRIGHT moved the confirmation and re- marked that the Committee were making progress with street making as rapidly as was consistent with the supply of material. They had that month apportioned the expenses of, street making to the extent of over £2,000. Councillor HEATON seconded the:confirmation of the minutes, which was agreed to.

MUSEUM, LIBRARY AND ARTS COMMITTEE. - Return for the month of June: Visitors to the Museum 1,703, decrease 17 per cent. compared with June, 1890; books issued in reading-room 662, no change; books issued lending department 1,910, increase 5 per cent. Report of the following gifts, for which the thanks of the Committee were ordered to be sent to the donors : " Comte's General View of Positivism," from Mr. W. F. Blake; Proceedings of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society, 1890-1, from the Society; parcel of pamphlets from Mr. T. Robinson. The minutes also contained the amended rules for the Museum and library. Councillor PIERPOINT, in moving the adoption of the minutes, referred to the freeing of the library, and said he had special pleasure in moving the adoption of the minutes because to some considerable extent he took a rather active part in freeing the library. Councillor MONKS seconded, and the minutes were adopted. THE CEMETERY COMMITTEE.

* The report of the registrar to this Committee showed that the interments during the past four weeks were : Adults, 63; minors, 50; stillborn and premature, 10; corresponding period last year, adults, 23; minors, 38; stillborn and premature. 10. The receipts for the past four weeks were :—L93 15s. 6d.; corresponding period last year, £57 6s. Councillor Jenkins was appointed deputy-chairman, in place of Councillor Heaton, who had resigned . Minutes confirmed on the motion of Councillor HEA- TON, seconded by Councillor JENKINS. TOWN HALL, PARK, & BATHS COMMITTEE. From the report of the Bathkeeper to this Committee it appeared that theincome from the baths for the past four weeks was £44 15s. 6d.' corresponding perio i last year £2l 14s; increase, £23 is. 6d. It was resolved that the thanks of this Committee be given to the following donors :—Mr. John Wainwright, for aquatic plants; Mr. Blinston, for aquatic plants; Mr. Porter, for two thrushes.
Adopted on the motion of Alderman SUTTON. MARKETS COMMITTEE.

This Committee reported that the total income from all sources for the past four weeks was £343 17s. 4d., corresponding period last year £298 19s. 9d. Alderman GREENALL moved, and Councillor BLACK- HURST seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor Mum asked if the Committee had taken in- to consideration the case of Simpson. The MAYOR said that subject was not on the minutes. The minutes were then adopted. GAS COMMITTEE.

The Gas Committe-e-rePOrted that the average illumi- nating power of the gas for the past six weeks was equal to 18.31 candles at both works. A resolution had been passed that £3,190 10s. 6d. be paid for annuities and interest. The Committee had passed the following resolution :—That the following resolutions be accepted : Cross, Tetley, and Co. 8,000 tons of coal; J. and R. Stone, 3,500 ; Newton. Chambers, and Co., 2,500 ; Wigan Coal and Iron Co., 4,000 ;. Padesvrood, 2,000 tons of can-

nel ; J. and W. Wood, 1,000; Cross, Tetley, and Co., 100. Also that the following tenders be accepted :—Tangyes, Limited, to supply 16 retort mouthpieces at £4.0; Kirk- ham, Hulett. and Chandler, Limited, to supply a patent washer scrubber and engine at the sum of £345 ; Bryan, Donkin, and Co., Limited, to supply engine and ex- hauster at £345' ; Mr. Samuel White, to supply Livesey's Patent Washer at £B9. Alderman HOLMES moved, and Alcierman WRIGHT seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor H. ROBERTS asked what was the reason why the prices at which large tenders of coal and cannel were accepted,were not published.lt was perfectly well-known that there was a resolution on the books of the Council requiring that to be done. He had asked that question before and he had been told that it was not the interests of the Council, or of the colliery owners to publish those prices, but he said at once that he had not the slightest sympathy with that reason. (Rear, hear.) He knew there were larger Corporations than that who bought larger quantities of coal for the same purpose and yet the prices were published. While he did not for a moment, or in the faintest degree possible suggest that there was anything improper, it would be much more satisfactory if these prices were published. It could not possibly be an injury to the Corporation to publish them, and it was not their interest to protect in any degree the interests of the colliery owners. Let the prices be pub- lished and let the whole town know what they were paying for their coal and cannel, and if any firms who tendered to the Corporation declined to do se on the ground that they did not wish their prices to be made public let the Corporation do without their tenders. (Hear, bear.) Councillor JENKINS quite agreed with Councillor Roberts that not only those contracts but all other mat- ters dealt with by Committees should be freely exposed to the light of day. There was a great inclination on the part of chairmen of some Committees to get up and say,in faint imitation of the foreign secretary in another house, that it was not desirable, from very high motives, that they should disclose %Ant was going on. The burgesses did not want that sort of thing; they were getting heartily sick of it. There were matters in another Committee which had gone on for some time tut it would be all the better if they saw the light of day. It would be infinitely better for the intprest of the borough and the comfort of chairmen of committees if there was no hesit- ation in disclosing freely everything that took place in committee, and every inquiry contemplated or beingbe- ing made, and the result of such inquiry. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HOLMES said he always made a point of bringing the prices of contracts with him in his pocket so that anybody could see them. The reason why the Gas Committee did not publish those prices was that it was in the interest of the Corporation not to do so. Several persons to whom they had sent their specifica- tions had told them that they would. not tender if the prices were published. The tenders that had been accepted were rather lower than at this time last year, with the exception of cannel. The minutes were then passed. TIRE ENGINE COMMITTEE.

The above Committee had resolved that Mr. Thomas Fletcher be appointed engineer to the brigade, and that the tender of Mr. W. Fletcher for thepainting and white- washing required at the fire engine station house' at £l7 55. be accepted. The MAYOR moved, and Councillor HEATON seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor PLERpontx asked if the Committee had not advertised for a fitter, and if they did advertise for a fit- ter he should like to know if .Thomas Ratcliffe who had been appointed engineer was a fitter. The MAYOR having obtained a copy of the advertise- ment, said it read that the Committee were prepared to receive applications for "practical engineers "to "work and keep in repair the steam and manualfire engines." Councillor PIERPOINT said the Committee had acted rather unfairly to other applicants. They had gone out- side the terms of their advertisement as Thomas Ratcliffe was not a Dractical engineer in any sense of the word; he was nothing more than an intelligent labourer. Councillor DixoN said it was often the case that one , kind of man was advertised for and another appointed. , Alderman SUTTON said Ratcliffe had had the manage- , ment of the engines for a large number of years and un- derstood all about them, and as far as his knowledge of those engines went he would be fully entitled to call him- self an engineer. Councillor ROBERTS said that was the first time he had heard the man who drove an engine called an engineer. The MAYOR: They are often called engineers. Councillor H. ROBERTS said that perhaps the Committee had got the sort of man they wanted, but they had un- doubtedly deceived a number of people by tke terms of their advertisement. The man appointed did not comply with the terms of the advertisement, for he was not a fitter and was not an engineer. Councillor Mum said the man who was appointed was the only one who could do the work that was required of him. He had never seen such a rubbishy lot of engi- neers in all his life as those who came before the Com- mittee. Councillor CANNELL, speaking as one of the Committee, said the best man had not been appointed. Councillor HEATON said the other candidates were asked if they knew anything about fire engines, and the Com- mittee were assured by every one of them that they had never seen one. The MAYOR said there were some good applicants before the Committee, but there was not one of them who had anything to do with fire engines. He was afraid the advertisement had conveyed a wrong idea to the public of the kind of man that was wanted.(Hear, hear.) The minutes were then confirmed. OAS ACCOUNTS DEPOSITS..

Councillor Thu, had on the agenda the following mction :—" That when a deposit is charged to any per- son about to consume gas it be insered on the Deposit Form the amount of deposit paid the Gas Committee, the rate of interest of such deposit, and the date such in- terest is due." _ _ _ _ _ - - - -
- Alderman Homos said the Committee had already adopted this resolution. LONGFORD AND THE INTERCEPTING DEPOTS. ANOTHER IMPEACHIViENT. A LIVELY SCENE.

Councillor DIXON was about to propose the following motion which stood in his name :—" That the members of the Sanitary Committee be required to resign forth- with in consequence of their mismanagement of Long- ford and the Intercepting Depots," when Alderman Suwon' said before Councillor Dixon made any remark on it, he thought that it would be better for him (the Alderman) as an interested party to withdraw from the room, and take no part as a member of the Committee in the debate. All he would ask the Mayor and the Council was that they should take the matter fully into consideration. If they thought fit to adopt the resolution well and good ; he should be prepared to accept it, but he should hope that the Council would finally dispose of it. They had it on the agenda paper, and notice had been given for it many successive months. Councillor Fl. ROBERTS objected that Alderman Sut- ton's remarks were not in order, and said he was sur- prised that any member of the Sanitary Committee , should make them. Alderman SUTTON : You may be surprised. We are often surprised at many things, but I was going to ex- plain why I should retire. The MAYOR ruled Alderman Sutton out of order, and he having left the room, Councillor Dixon proceeded to move his resolution. In doing so, he said he stood in a very curious position. (Laughter.) Out of 36 members of the Council 8 or 9 years ago, he was the only one debarred from going to the Longford works. There was one thing that had I been very prominent to him during the last 10 years. There had been more managers for Longford works than any other works he knew of. Nine or ten years ago a manager was appointed at some £2OO a year. How long he stopped he had no idea.
The MAYOR: The Council would do that, not, the Committee. _

...... Councillor DIXON said the members of the Committee had done it. The Council might have done it. But here was the result that for some cause or other the managers appointed during the last 10 years had never stopped I very long. Now, why? If the Committee wanted to have success in the works they could not go on changing their managers every two or three years as they- had done. The structure of the works was the most un- reason Ole of any in existence. The structure was so disgraceful and badly ventilated that, as far as he was concerned, he would not allow a workman ever to be employed in it. Then again, the process adopted had not been adopted in any town save Warrington. At Birmingham it was partly adopted some years ago, but there it was found, as he had found, that it was not only the most expensive process. but that it produced the most inferior manure that was manufactured in any such works. There was a time when the best quality was produced at Longford, taking into account the material they had to deal with, but they were not doing that now. He would tell the Council why. As he pointed out to the Commissioner when he sat in that Chamber, the system was faulty, font had been found during the last ten or fifteen years that the moment sulphuric acid was put into the excreta, agitation must be commenced. The process was checked half-way, the consequence being that money was wasted. He protested against the employment of workmen in such an ill-ventilated place as Longford Works. He knew of no works which were so defectively arranged and where workmen had to work in such an atmosphere. He never saw any which were so disgraceful. There was not a man in that room who could tell the Council the condition of the plant at Long- ford. It was in a deplorable state, and when the Chair- man of the Committee said the other night that the works were complete, he was ignorant of their condition, or he would not have made such an assertion. If the members of the Council knew more about the process employed and had been to the works as he had been during the last day or t wo, they would agree that the time had come for a change to be made in the Commit- tee. It was very necessary that the Committee should resign, and that other persons having some practical , experiace should take their places. Alderman WRIGHT : Would you be kind enough to give us till next November? - - - -

Councillor PIERPOINT seconded the motion. Alderman &mons : I want to know by what authority Mr. William Pierpoint rises in this room to second any motion. Councillor PIERPOINT I rise to a point of order. My name in this room is Mr. Councillor Pierpoint, not Mr. William Pierpoint. lam sorry to call any member of the Council to order, but he must certainly be taught etiquette. (Lau 7,hter.) Alderman BURGESS: I Will receive no lesson in etiquette from Mr. William Pierpoint. I say he has neither part nor lot in anything appertaining to this municipal corpor- ation, and that he ought not to take part; but your Town Clerk will tell you. Councillor PIRRPOINT : I rose to a point of order. and I shall insist upon it being settled. Alderman Burgess says I have no right or authority to say anything with reference to the borough of Warrington. Councillor BOLTON: Let him finish. Councillor PIERPOINT : Don't you interfere with me, I should like to have that point settled, whether Alder man Burgess is in order or is not. Councillor MUIR : Sit down. Councillor BOLTON: He is not in (vier. Councillor PIERPOIN'T : lam not speaking to Coun- cillor Bolton. Am lin order sitting here in this way and taking part in any discussion? The MAYOR: That is the question. Let the Town Clerk answer. Alderman BURGESS: If I am correctly informed Mr. Wm. Pierpoint is not a ratepayer within the limits of the municipal borough of Warrington. The Towx CLERK: I can only say that the point raised can only be settled in a court. I cannot do anything in the matter; I cannot give an opinion up(an it. Councillor JENKINS : If there is any difficulty as to Councillor Pierpoint seconding this motion, as a matter of form I will second it if lam allowed. Councillor H. ROBERTS i I hope Councillor Pierpoint will not withdraw. He is here by election,and so long as his name remains on the burgess roll I contend that he is qualified to act. This is not the place to settle a question of registration law. I am:sorry the question has been raised in that form. The MAYOR: We cannot discuss it now ,neither can we settle it here. Councillor PIERPOINT : You can settle a point of order. The MAYOR: Ob. yes! But not a point of law. Councillor HENRY ROBERTS: We have nothing to do with the question at all. The MAYOR: The resolution,as now proposed, is moved by Councillor Dixon, and seconded by Councillor Pier- point. Councillor MUIR said he should certainly support the motion, and he suggested that the Council go at once to a division, and so settle the matter for ever. Councillor PrumProx said hehad not had very much ex= perience with respect to the sanitary matters of Warring- ton, but he had had some experience with the electors, and knew something of their opinion respecting these matters.' There was one particular point that he should like to refer to, and he did it with all due respect to Alderman Burgess, the Chairman of the Sanitary Com- mittee. He did wish that he would not be quite so sar- castic towards every one who might happen to differ from him. (Hear, hear.) Surely ratepayers had a right to send a representative to that Council, and that repre- sentative had a right to ask a question without being treated with contempt. (Hear, hear.) There had been gentlemen on the Sanitary Committee who, he felt sure, had left it in disgust on account of the contempt they had received from the Chairman. He (Mr. Plumpton) had been down to the Longford Dept, and spent an hour and a half or two hours there. It was not a very pleasant experience, he could tell them; and he wanted something to refresh him when he came out. (A laugh.) He wanted to satisfy himself with respect to the rumours that were circulating about the town as to the machinery being so much out of order, and the bad ven- ,tilation of the works, and he could assure the Council it was not a fit place for any man to work or live in. (Hear, hear.) The thing altogether,in his opinion,was too com- plicated. (Hear. hear.) In his opinion, he was sorry-to say, it would ultimately end in failure. (Hear, hear. Councillor H. ROBERTS: "Nonsense.") He did not blame the whole of the Sanitary Committee. Many of the members, when they came before the electors, said, "We are not responsible for this state of things : it has been a legacy left to you by previous members of the CoMmittee." He wished those members would speak out openly that day, and admit what the present state of affairs at Longford was. He was sure any gentleman who went through the works would agree that the employment of men there under the present circumstances was simply dis- gusting. Mr. Councillor Greenall had been down that day, and hecould not stay in the place five minutes; and he might say the same as to Councillor Blackhurst, and if the Council kept up a place of this sort it ought to be made fit to work in. They were bringing fresh plant there, and there was no room to place it ; and there were thick walls where there ought to be open spaces. (Hear, hear.) The excreta went on to the ironwork and it was most destructive to all ironwork it came in contact with. The pans were being put into corners, and there was no room to get round the pans to clean them, however many men there might be on the premises. He did not know whether the Committee had been down of late or not. He was told that cab fares were paid for the Chairman to go three times a week; he must have had something tied over his eyes or he would have seen before now how things were going on. The members of the Committee who had been down from time to time ought to have seen what:was going on before things got

div.head: WIFE.
div.p: WIFE.

On Tuesday a man and a woman, the former seriously wounded,and the latter actually dead, were taken to the London Hospital. It Is alleged the woman's husband surprised them drinking together in a Limehouse tavern, stabbed them both, ,and decamped, The man has ndt yet been arrested.
MURDER OF A WOMAN NEAR EPSOM.

A brutal murder was committed at Leatherhead. near Epsom, on Tuesday, the victim being a woman named Ellen Cox, a field worker. The woman was found :early fin the morning in a field with her throat cut and both eyes blackened. She stated that as she was going along the road towards Dorking three or four young men demanded money, and on her refusal to give them any attempted to throttle her. Afterwards they cut her throat and ran away. Close by where the woman was lying a shilling was afterwards found by the polite, and is supposed to have dropped from her pocket. Unfortu- nately no medical aid could be obtained, but the police carried the woman to the Epsom Infirmary, where she died shortly after her admission.
'SAD ACCIDENT NEAR DOUGLAS. PLEASURE BOAT RUN DOWN AND THREE VISITORS DROWNED.

On Tuesday afternoon an accident of a frightful nature occurred off Santon Head, by which three visitors lost their lives. The Manx Queen, belonging to the Barrow Company, went round the Isle of Man on Tuesday morn- ing, with a large complement of visitors. In return- ing in the afternoon, when near Santon Head, a small boat was seen heading off from the shorein the direction of Port Soderiek. The boat contained two gentlemen and two ladies, who had been on a visit to Port 'Soderick, and had gone out for a sail. They were pulling across the course of the Manx Queen. Captain Myerscough, on observing them on the port bow, star- boarded his helm to let' them go astern, but the occu- pants of the boats stopped rowing, and fouled the paddle of the steamer. The boat was smashed in two, and the occupants were drawn under the water. The two men were not seedigain. The two women were picked up by •the steamer's boat, which was lowered immediately. One of them kvas dead, but the other, Miss Davis,of Birming- ham, was resuscitated. The three persons who have lost their lives are :—Miss Smith, 61, Montgomery-st., Birmingham; Mr. Shaw, of Sheffield; and Mr. Richard Turner, gilder, Sheffield. News of the sad disaster was telegraphed to the relatives, and boats started a search for the bodies of the two missing gentlemen. Miss Davis, the sole survivor, has been removed to the hospi- tal, as she is suffering from a broken forearm and bruises. _ _

Miss Davis made a statement on Wednesday describ- ing how she and her companions went out in the boat and became frightened as the steamer bore down upon them. She says they were paralysed, and those in charge of the oars must have lost all presence of mind. One of the men exclaimed, "Oh, God, I am sure she will run us down." In a minute after the boat was run down and all were thrown into the water. Miss Davis, cling- ing to the boat, saw Miss Smith floating in the water, and heard one of the men shout, but saw no more of them.
'The " Birmingham Daily Post" says :—The ladies were both of them teachers under the Birmingham School Board, having served their apprenticdhip in the Dixon- road Board School.

to such a pitch. Ile cad not say-that he altogether liked the resolution. He thought some members of the Sanitary Committee were good men. He had no doubt that the Chairman would be very glad to be relieved from his post. Alderman BURGESS: Pardon me. I assure you that is a great Mistake. (Laughter and "Hear, hear.") Councillor PLIMPTON said at any rate he should have liked the resolution much better if it had been for an inquiry. He did not think the Committee ought to put themselves up as infallible. COUGelliOr HENRY ROBERTS.—They don't. Councillor PLIMPTON thought the Coirtinittee would be wise to consult with other members of the Council, to see whether some better arrangement could not be brought about. He did not expect the resolution would be, carried, but the matter would have to come up again in the form of an inquiry. If Alderman Burgess could see his way to retire, it would be a great relief to him and the town, and to everyone concerned. (Laughter.). Alderman GREENALL expressed his intention of sup- porting the Committee. Comacillor BLACICHURST said he had been to the works and the depots that day, and though not at all satisfied with what was going on, he was not prepared to go the length that Mr. Dixon did. It would be rather too drastic a measure to sweep away the whole Committee unless they had got men ready to take up the dirty work,, and he did not think the Council could get a committee of men who would like to take it off their hands. So far as he was concerned, a more abominable stench he never smelt. What Couinillor Plumpton said, that you would not stay in the place five minutes, was quite true. Bow the men stood it he did not know. They must get used to it. Anyway, it was certainly not fit for anyone who was not accustomed to it to go there. The intercepting depots he regarded as a huge blunder. It was a very cruel and wicked act to put depOts creating such a stench among a lot of cottagers, who were poor people and could not help themselves. He was in favour of doing away with the depots, even if they could not do so without loss of money. Alderman HOLMES said he was not prepared to take upon himself the responsibility of dismissing the mem- bers of the Sanitary Committee. They had done the best they could. (Hear, hear.) There was, however, a very easy way of getting rid of the difficulty. The 9th of November was not far off, and on that day, if necessary, fresh names could be substituted for those of members objected to. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BOLTON wanted to know why there should be any, particular reason for such a drastic resolution, as if the Council had some very good reasons why the whole committee should resign they might perhaps be able to consider the matter. The ratepayers were not satisfied with either Longford works or the Sanitary Committee as to the way business was done. They wanted a little more ventilation as to how their money was spent. Cer- tain great mistakes had occurred, and they had occurred in this case through things being kept in the dark. As to changing the committee, November he thought was the time for that, and he did not think Councillor Dixon at present could have better men on it. He had no doubt many members would be very pleased to see Alderman Burgess resign, as he said he we s the Sanitary Committee and the members were his ciphers. Alderman BURGESS : Permit me to say that that is not the kind of language which I think ought to be used in this room. The last time I was here:a great outrage was perpetrated in this room, and I was the victim of it. It seems as if it must come again to-night. They will none of them drive me out,and they might as well give up the policy of attempting it. I mean to see this thing finished. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BOLTON said that they did not wish to drive Alderman Burgess away. They simply wished to be taken into his confidence.

Councillor JEERING said the "worthy alderman who presided over the destinies of the Sanitary Committee had just told them that a gross outrage was committed in that Council Chamber at the last meeting. Well, he (Councillor Jenkins) only wished that that worthy alder- man could see himself as others saw him, and ho wished he would remember that they lowly beings, members of the Corporation, had to bear his bitter sarcasms and his kindly jests. (Hear, hears and laughter.) He did not forget them and he should not. With regard to the Sanitary Committee, Alderman Burgess had himself, during the last 12 months, shown amnle grounds why. something serious should be done with regard to an in- quiry into the working of the Sanitary Committee. He (Councillor Jenkins) regretted very much that the courteous way in which he approached the Sanitary Committeea short time since was treated by Alderman Burgess with scant respect, although it was obvious to any reasonable man that an inquiry then in the terms upon which he sought it would not only have benefitted the town, but would probably have strengthened the hands of the Sanitary Committee and taken away from them the odium which undoubtedly now rested upon that committee. He, for one, deeply regretted that the public mind might possibly be at fault with regard to the working of the Longford depot, but if an inquiry of the kind be had referred to had been granted the public mind would have been set at rest. If true disclosures had been made, and no effort made to throw dust in the eyes of the public and the members of that Council, then he ventured to say that the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee and its members would have gone on with their work cheerfully and with a feeling that they carried with them the approbation of the Council and the burgesses. When the chairman proposed an increase in the salary of the late manager at Longford, they might have thought from what he said that no such man had ever existed before, but what was the result? A discovery was made ()Rho loss of about 200 tons of manufactured manure, and from that day to this neither the loss of that manure, nor the value of it had been accounted for in any way; not a syllable had been vouchsafed to that Corporation by way of explanation as to that very seri- ous loss. Was that the way in which any committee should treat that Council? Further than that was it the 'way in which the ratepayers of the borough should be treated who had to find the money? Shortly after that the accounts of the manager at Longford were found in a most abominable condition, and those accounts were placed in the hands of Messrs. Tunstall for the purpose of being audited,a,nd they had heard froth sources which were perfectly reliable that those accounts were in such a 'condition that they were a disgrace to the Sanitary Committee and to the oversight which should have been used either by the chairman of the Committee or to whoever was responsible. From that day to this not a syllable had they heard about those accounts—no report as to the result of the audit had been vouchsafed to that Corporation. Again, was that the way in which that Council and the burgesses should be treated? He said not. (Hear,hear.) A little later on they found the worthy alderman placed in a most contemptible position, as he had to come into that Council and declare that at Longford Depot there had been "criminal neglect." Were they a lot of chil- dren that they had to be treated in t hat manner? He did not intend to vote for the resolution, because he did not think it was couched in proper terms, and for that reason only. He had the greatest respect for all the members of the Sanitary Committee and for Alderman Burgess, although he took great pleasure in condemning him--(laughter)—but he thought the time had passed when the Sanitary Committee should bare taken the Council into their confidence and consented to an in- quiry. If they had called to their assistance men of un- doubted intelligence in sanitary matters, he was sure they would never have been placed in that dilemma. Councillor HEATON did not think he could vote for the resolution, because during the last two or three years a lot of new and very good members had been put upon the Committee, and he must confess that, although every one tried to throw a bit of dirt at Alderman Bur- gess, he thought him a good man in agood place. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) What they wanted at Longford was an intelligent, hard-working man, who would do his work and make others do their work. His men would not work unless he was there himself or somebody nearly as good as himself. Councillor DIXON: They are a bad lot then. Councillor HEATON concluded by &tying that Alder- man Burgess was a little bit pig-headed and stupid. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: Do you object to that language, Alder- man Burgess? Alderman BURGESS.: Not at all. (Laughter.) Councillor HEATON: I don't think he will; he knows what I mean by it. Councillor H. ROBERTS said that, whatever the pecu- liarities of Alderman Burgess might be, there was no man in or out of that room who had served the people of Warrington so faithfully, so continuously, and so honestly and well for 40 years. He might well quote scripture and say "For 40 years long have I served this generation, and said it is a people that do err in their hearts," as far as some of them were cOncerned who had spoken that night. (Hear, hear.) If half the things which were said about Alderman Burgess's sarcastic and overbearing manner were correct, some members of the Committee would not remain as such. They had too much self-respect to allow their own feelings and opinions to be overborne even by Alderman Burgess. They did find this: that not one member of the Commit- tee did a tithe of the work which the Chairman did. In season and out of season and on every possible occasion, he gave his time, ability, • and energy, without fee or reward, in carrying out what was the most unpleasant work in connection with any department of the Corpora- tion. A good deal had been said that night which would have been more properly said when Councillor Jenkins's motion for inquiry was before the Council. Councillor Jenkins had his opportunity a short time ago and he contended that a more favourable opportunity he could not have had. He said with all respect- to Councillor Jenkins that he never saw an important motion more mismanaged on the part of the proposer than was the motion of Councillor Jenkins— Councillor JENKINS said Councillor Roberts knew the circumstances under which he laboured. He was seri- ously ill at the time, and it was quite impossible to deal with the motion as he should otherwise have done. Councillor H. ROBERTS, continuing, said the accusa- tion which had been brought in support of Councillor Dixon's motion referred to the condition of things at Longford. They had been told the Committee were not infallible. Most decidedly. He admitted that the Com- mittee were not infallible, and one of the great blunders made was the appointment of the man who had lately

left-- thrir - service. Itthtrnnimittee were" fo-rt^tmate-- enough at the present time to select the right man for the position of manager, the Council would hear very little of the difficulties which beset the Committee with regard to the works at Longford. The Committee were asked by the resolution to resign; but he was pleased to find that few members of the Council were prepared, even in jest, to go to the extent of supporting such a motion. The Sanitary Committee was only appointed last November, and if the members of the Council had any serious fault tcifind with it, let them wait till the next election. They could then remove Alderman Bur- gess if they chose, but he contended that if they did so it would be a great mistake. The work which had to be Ae done was too big for one Committee to msnage. They required the Sanitary Committee to do for a town of 50,000 inhabitants a great deal more than a Sanitary Committee had to do for a town of half the size. Th time had, indeed, come when a sub-division of work was imperative. The work of cleansing the streets, the management of the Infectious Diseases Hospital, the notification of infectious disease, was quite sufficient work for one Committee, and the management of the Longford and the intercepting depots was enough for another Committee to undertake. (Hear, hear.) He admitted that there was a reasonable cause of complaint with regard to the management of Longford. It was a disgrace to them, and there was not a member of the Committee who would not admit that the state of things. was different from what they wished to see. But they remember that they had to devolve the responsibi- lity of the management upon a paid official. (Hear, hear.) _

CoUncillor PIER.POINT said the only object he had in seconding the motion of Councillor Dixon was to have it debated. He would not complain of the treatment of Alderman Burgess, but from the tone adopted by that gentleman, it seemed to him that he anticipated with pleasure his (the speaker's) departure from among the members of the Council in November. He had been with them nine years, and had done what he could for the town, but he was one of those men who was determined to look after his own business first. Much that Councillor Roberts had said described his opinions with regard to Longford. Alderman Burgess had never heard him say a disrespectful word of the work at Longford. He had seen the temper of the Council with reference to it, and knew that it would be labour in vain to do so, and he joined with the remainder of the Council and did what he could to help the Committee. He quite agreed with Councillor Roberts that it would be the best thing in the interests of the Corporation to establish a Comnittee to take into consideration the manufacturing department of the Sanitary Committee. The plant at Longford was most expensive and valuable' and required special treat- ment. A Committee should be appointed who could de. vote the whole of its time to it. (Hear, hear.) He could not vote for Councillor Dixon's motion, as he did not agree with it: _ _

-Alderman BURGESS said it had been represented that the work at Longford was of such an offensive and abom- inable character that men ought not to work there, but he could say that a complaint from anybody in the neigh- bourhood of Longford had been unknown for months and months. The Rural Sanitary Authority would, if they were committing a nuisance, very soon point it out and prevent it being done,
Councillor HEATO-N said that for three meetings past the Rural Sanitary Authority had had complaints before them.

Alderman BURGESS said they had had applications from the Sanitary . Authority to collect their pails and treats the contents7at Longford. Ccuncillor HEATON said they had not had any official application from the Sanitary Authority. , Alderman BURGESS said the books of the Rural Sanitary Authority would show what he had represented was a fact. They had had deputations more than once on those premises. With regard to the accounts being in a de- plorable condition, all he could say was that no accounts had been sent by the :Sanitary Committee to Messrs. Tunstall to be auditeck Councillor JENKINS : Who were:they sent by? Alderman BURGESS: No such things were sent; it is an error that has crept into your heads. Councillor JENKINS : The accounts of the manager at Longford were submitted, either by you or your'Com- mittee, or some authority to Messrs. Tunstall.
Alderman BURGESS : Not accounts, but weekly reports of the manager, which he has sent to me, and which I have reserved week by week.
Counciller ,TENgiz.Ts Are not sucll reports in the] char- acter also of accounts?

Alderman BURGESS said they were riot, tie added that he thought the Committee could get through their difficulty without going beyond the limits of the esti- mates. The rates would have been 3d. in the £ more this year but for the money contributed by the Longford works. (Laughter.) Mr..Chorley had nearly £1,500 last year, which was an unfortunate year. He ought to have had nearly twice that amount, and would have had it if the management had been better. (Oh, oh and laughter.) Councillor DfxoN briefly replied. The voting was proceeded with, and resulted as follows :--
For the motion. Councillor Dixon Dr. Cannell,
Against it. Alderman Holmes „ Burgess ~ Wright Greenall Councillor Bolton „ Blackhurst „ Heaton „ Garner . Roberts „ Green „ Monks „ Hill J. Fairclough And the:Mayor
, . .., - —2j —l4 The MAYOR said the *lotion was therefore Ina carried.

METER RENTS. Councillor HILL moved—" rnat the :Gas Committee be requested as soon as possible to abolish all meter rents; and all meters in the possession of the gas consumer and their property be purchashed :by the Gas Com- mittee."
There was no seconder, however, and the motion fell to the ground. This was all the business.

div.head: TRA.GEDY AT HIGH WYCOMBE.
div.p: TRA.GEDY AT HIGH WYCOMBE.

A tragic occurrence took place at Downley, sigh Wycombe, on Tuesday night. Joseph Sharpe, aged SEI, a general dealer, was at home with his wife, the rest of the family being at the West Wycombe Flower Show. About half-past eight a man, who was passing the house, heard the report of a gun, and on going inside found that Mrs. Sharpe had been shot. She expired in a few moments. Sharpe, who has been arrested, had only a short time before borrowed a gun from a neighbour.
MURDER AND SUICIDE AT RAMSGATA.

Shortly after noon on Sunday a tragic incident occur- red at Ramsgate. A lady named Merriman, wife of Mr. Merriman, residing at 5, Canonburem-terrace, cut the throat of her daughter, aged three years, and then, after taking a quantity of belladonna and iodine, threw her- self from the drawing-room window. She was quickly removed to the Seamen's Hospital, where it was ascer- tained that her skull was fractured, her collar bone , bruised, and one leg broken. The effects of the poiso n and the injuries combined, caused the unfortunate lady's death, which took place at a quarter past four. It Is believed she was insane.

div.head: BERKSHIRE TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE BERKSHIRE TRAGEDY.

An inquest was held 4t Hurst, Berkshire, on Monday, ou the body of Herbert Bagent, aged 19, a gardener, in the service of Major-Goseral Beauchamp, of Hurst Lodge, who was murderer on Saturday last by Joseph Gazelle, a coachman in the same employ. On Friday afternoon deceased complained of prisoner's boy throwing at the fruit in the orchard. Prisoner, who was a violent- tempered man, said that he would do for him before long. On Saturday morning, when deceased was milk- ing the cows, prisoner struck him over the head with a. garden fork and then stuck the prongs into his brain, shattering the skull and causing instant death. A ver- dict of" Wilful murder" was returned against Joseph Gazelle, who was committed for trial.

div.head: MR. JOHN MORLEY. AT E.ENIEWORTH.
div.p: MR. JOHN MORLEY. AT E.ENIEWORTH.

Mr. John Morley, M.P., was the principal speaker at a demonstration of Warwickshire Liberals at Stoneleigh Park, the seat of LoM Leigh, on Monday, and said he was proud to standYMr. G. lidstona, even in the dark- est hour, for the'g,reat "cause he had taken up. The Tories, he maintained, had introduced the Free Educa- tion Bill not because they had any desire to do right, but because they feared the Liberals would bring it in and find favour with the country. Speaking of the necessity of reforms in the franchise, he said the voters' qualifying period of residence ought to be reduced to something like three or four months, and it was intoler- able and unfair that the political judgment and political wishes of a constituency should be falsified by troops of out-voters coming in to turn a real majority into a min- ority. nig Schoolmaster has not beet/ Humours of much abroad during the past twenty • Education. years; he has been hard at work amongst the youths and juveniles of the present generation; and the result is seen in a standard of education which is, so far as the masses are con- cerned, much higher than it has ever been before. It is the parents who are weak now in " book-learn- ing "as compared with their children. Many of them know it and admit it, and are at the same time determined that their offspring shall be better equipped for the battle of life than they themselves have been. It is in country places where ignorance. is even yet most dense—so dense that the prejudice against education is still strong. There is no lack. of School Boards--for the Education Department insists upon Boards being established where school accommodation is insufficent—but, unfortunately for the children, some of the members of the Boards are so ignorant and so bigoted that they do all they can to hinder rather than help the cause of education. A writer in the "Westminster Review," for August, states that there are 111 School Board areas in which the total population.. in each case does not exceed 1,000; in some the population Of the areas is less than 250, which. means a very stnaii icbooi often under the control of farmers who despise schooling. They are pre- sent for the most part, not to see that the code is administered, but to take care that not a penny is spent more than can be helped. In one case, a School Inspector made inquiry as to the dirty condition of the school floor. The teacher frankly stated that it had not been washed, to his know-- ledge, for sixteen years. The Inspector turned to the Chairman of the Board, a farmer, who in- stantly replied—and the reply was a crushing one in his opinion—that "the cleaning of the floor would necessitate an outlay of the ratepayers' money of six shillings !" Another chairman of a village School Board said—"Oive a-done wi'out eddycashun, and wat on airth does 'Odge's chil- durn want wi' huke-larrin'. Ull it lam nun to 'oe turtnuts any better?" The question, there is no denying, was a very pertinent one, assuming that the end and aim of Hedge's life is hoeing turnips. The chairman was doubtless well up on that sub- ject, and, like Tennyson's Lincolnshire; farmer, he could say:— "I reckons I 'ltnnot sa mooch to learn." But even he of the turnip turn of thought was put in the shade by a third chairman, who poured his contempt on "them book learnin men" by asking which of them "could take forty two-pennorth's like me and get safely 'otne ?" In view of such. samples of educationists, we cannot profess sur- prise that, in connection with the recent educa- tion Commission, it was reported that "the small rural boards are very reluctant to summon their neighbours for not sending their children to school, and that not unfrequently•members of the Board may be offenders against the law by employing children who should beat school." This indifference to:the progress of village scholars becomes the more serious now that steps are being taken to raise the age of half-timers in towns, and to keep them out of mills and workshops, even as half-timers, until eleven years of age has been reached. The same child living in the country might, if the local authorities thought fit, be sent at ten years of age to work full time at hedging, ditching, weeding, &c. Granted that the conditions as to health are different as between mill labour and farm labour, it must also be admitted that it is preposterous to regard it as a reasonable thing that children should finish their schooling at ten years of age. There:is something of course to be said for the farmers; they are under the pressure of high rents, &c.; but on the ether hand, if children were kept longer at school in the agricultural districts, there would be more work for adult labourers, who would be less fre- quently driven into towns to increase therein the struggle for existence. It might end in the Squire having to reduce rents, but worse things might happen, and do happen, than that. It must be pointed out, too, that where the School Board area is small, it is, proportionately, more costly to set up the machinery of a School Board and Board School. This leads to School Board rates of from is. to is. 6d. in the pound in rural districts as compared with something under 4d. in the pound in such places as Manchester and Liverpool. It is a matter for consideration whether, when the Liberals come into office, and expand the present narrow Education Bill it would not be desirable to enlarge School Board areas in rural districts. A system of grouping might be adopted which would simplify the machinery and equalise the cost; and, what is of no small importance, be the means of securing capable and intelligent men at the head of affairs. The humours of education will never be wholly absent; but the time is approaching when men who boast of their "forty two-penn'orth's " should preside over the bar parlour rather than the School Board.

It was unfortunate that the motion before the meeting went the length of requiring the Sanitary Committee to resign, for it failed to command the support of many members of the Council who are fully alive to the failure—the costly failure—of Longford Works. But it served, at any rate, as a basis for discussion ; and it resulted in such an exposure as has not been wit- messed for many a day. Outside the Sanitary Com- mittee, there does not seem to be a single member of the Town Council, who, on paying a visit to the works, has not been impressed with the glaring evidence of their deplorable condition. Indeed, some members of the Sanitary Committee have made similar admissions; and ono of them, Coun- cillor H. ROBERTS, frankly confessed that the management at Longford was "a disgrace to them." This is all, and more than all, that we have contended for; and it justifies to the full the demand which has been made, and which continues to be made, for a public inquiry, It is not sufficient to be told that this lamentable state of things is entirely owing to the late manager. Something of this kind was heard when Mr. Dinwiddie was made the scapegoat; And for some time afterwards the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee drew rosy pictures of the bene- fits to the ratepayers which would result from the increasing output. The Council wepe wheedled into throwing more thousands of good money “ter bad, and it is only a few months since Alderman 13!.71:- GESS asked for and obtained an advance of wage.s for the manager, on the ground that he was doing so well. And now he is discharged, and the state of things is admittedly disgraceful- The plant, which is in a foul and ruinous condition, is practi- cally at a standstill so far as the fprecluction of conOt.)lWfiff,;(?d., manure is QoUerned ; and two Conn- tri6rs who have paid recent visits to the works agree in stating that" the place is not fit for any- body to live or work in." And what is the remedy for this deplorable muddle? "Get a new manager" say the Sanit- ary Committee; but that has been done over and over again, and always with the same result. The ratepayers want to know how it is that the manager has gone wrong, and the plant has gone wrong, and the stock has gone wrong (to the tune of 200 tons) ; and all happened while the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee believed that all was going so well as to warrant an advance in salary ? What is wanted is not a repetition of a device of evil odour ; but a searching inquiry into the Longford Works and the Intercepting Depots —from top to bottom. We cannot go on poisoning the inhabitants, buying and wrecking costly plant, and wasting the ratepayers' money. It may be, as some of the Councillors think, that the present system never has done and never will do; or it may be that the system is right while the plant is at fault; or it may be that there would be a sensible improvement if alderman BURGESS Would take hi tL I_Yands off works which are evidently 'beyond him, and leave their supervision to a dis- tinct Committee selected by the Council for the purpose. But first of all, and above all, an inquiry should be instituted, if the representatives of the ratepayers are not to act as blind leaders of the blind. As to the Chairman of the anitary Committee saying that "the rates would have been 3d. in the £ more this year but for the money contributed by Longford works "—that would seem to have been regarded as a good joke, judging from the laughter with which it was received. But it is a joke the point of which we are unable to see; and, joke or no joke, it is untrue. In- deed, the very reverse is the truth, for any ratepayer who will take the trouble to turn to the Borough Treasurer's Report will see that the total deficit, or loss, on Longford Works for the past year is £2,132. Now, seeing that a penny in the 2 on the rates realises £567, any schoolboy will be equal to demonstrating that, instead of Longford Works having reduced the rates 3d. in the £, they have resulted in a loss which is equal to 31-d in the E. What would be thought of a foundry, a tannery, or candle works upon which over £20,000 had been expended, and which showed cash for goods sold during the year amount- ing to £1,530, while on the other hand the cost of the year's production was £3,038? Would it not be said that such a concern would soon be in the bankruptcy court? And so it would be with Long- ford Works, if the too patient ratepayers were not being bled year after year to keep it going. How much longer they mean to stand it we do not know; it is "a disgrace" to the Corporation at present; but if it be continued much longer un- der present conditions it will be a disgrace to the ratepayers.

We hold over, until our next issue, important details as to licensed houses in Runcorn and the neighbourhood.
- The Manchester Corporation stock for the Ship Canal Loan has gone off well. Judging from the applications, if double the amounthad been issued it would have been taken up.

There is still corn in Egypt; and there is water in the Canal—at the Easthanl end. Good use of it, too, was made on Bank Holiday by excursion- ists who tripped it—not on the light fantastic, but in special boats—with "Youth at the prow an pleasure at the helm." We shall have a chance yet 'of taking tickets to Timbuctoo.

Everybody by this has read the Queen's Speech; but, as the man said who had looked down the crater of Vesuvius, "There's nothing in it." Next year the Government will make a show of doing something, with an eye not to its accomplishment, but to the dissolution of Parliament. And the sooner it comes the better for the nation.

The run of bye-elections through the death of members" of Parliament has been extraordinary during the present Ministry. As soon as it is known that there will be a contest at Walsall through the death of Sir Charles Foster, the news comes of the death of Lord Dartmouth, causing a vacancy at Lewesham. The Liberals may be counted upon to keep the seat at Walsall; and there is a chance of at least reducing the Tory majority at Lewesham.

There has been a disposition to grumble amongst the hangers-on of royalty because the Emperor William has not left more than £5OO for the ser- vants *I Windsor Palace and Buckingham Palace. It is to his credit that he has not overdone it in the matter of humouring little people with great expectations. The money is his own, and yet it is not his own; he spends it as trustee for his people.

Southport is quite hurt—feels disgraced in fact —because a young man was drunk on the promen- ade,on Monday, and created a SCOAI9 by assaulting the police. Really, our sea-side neighbours are getting supersensitive. They should spend a month at Warrington, and promenade Butter- market-st., and other principal thoroughfares. They would get used to men of the drunk- and-disorderly type, who are ever ready to assault,the police. Like the poor, they are always with us.

These are brave words ; but, as his lordship has no seat to lose, it does not look so much like fighting .himself as egging on " the other fellow " to fight.

A large white bull-terrier bit a man in Blooms- bury so badly that he was laid up for five weeks. He sought compensation; but the case went against him because it was not proved that the dog had bitten anyone before. This is in accord with previous rulings; and, under it, a dog may worry a man, but not a sheep, for an exception is made in favour of stock. Verily a man may be of more value than many sparrows, but when it is a ease of dog-bites, he is not equal to a sheep.

Judge Gates in giving a decision, at Colne, on Tuesday, in a case brought forward by the Weavers' Association said stich associations served a good and useful purpose. if he had difficulties with Nvorkpeople, he should be glad .to deal with those who represented the men. It is noteworthy that Mr. Torn Mann, who has been addressing the chemical workers of this district, advocates similar views as to the advantage both, to rnplovers and employed, of having to deal in cases of dispute with people in authority.

It is the employer who desires to take some unfair advantage who sees the matter in another Fght. He prefers to dealwith his men individually, beating them down one by one. It is satisfactory however to see that in most of the great industries of the kingdom there are strong organisations on both sides. The result is conference after conference, when wages and other questions arise, and strikes are in this way frequently avoided. 15:o may he in the chemical trade,

P.S. Bradbury, of Aldershot fame, has escaped a conviction for perjury in the case of the girl arrested and said to be of loose character • but he has not escaped condemnation by Judge character; who at the Winchester Assizes, on Wednesday said—" The police had prepared an elaborate defence, and seemed to have scoured Aldershot for evidence, but it was evidence of an absolutely unreliable and untrustworthy character, and he entirely disbelieved it. Regarding the incidents attending the arrest, he believed the story of the women rather than the police version." This is severe censure, but, taking all the circumstances into account, it is deserved.

Prince Bismarck keeps popping up like a Jack- in-the-box—a foolish reminder that he is no longer a Jack-in-office. In a recent letter "the ex- Chancellor declares that the visit of the French Fleet to Cronstadt would not have taken place had he remained in power. It is the consequence of the three recent gross mistakes of German dip- lomacy, namely, the Empress Frederick'svisit to Paris, the renewal of the Triple Alliance, which was divulged by the Emperor William with such eagefness, and finally the German Emperor's noisy visit to London." If Prince Bismarck has really made these "random jottings," it would appear that he is deterrninod tc) let it be seen how little a big man can be.

The sentence of penal servitude for life which Mr. justice Grantham originally passed upon Mrs. Turner for screening her son after the murder of the girl at Horsforth, naturally evoked strong ex- pressions of disapproval on account of its severity. He has since reduced it to one of twelve months' imprisonment,doing this as a reward to the daugh- ter for her admirable conduct in the matter. But isn't this theatrical way of doing things calculated to introduce an element of uncertainty—to say nothing of its possible injustice? If the life sen- tence was too severe, and all are agreed upon that, how can it be said to have been just, in the first instance, to pronounco it And if it was just in the first instance, why reduce the sentence on one ' person hecause another person has done his duty? ' Mr. Justice Grantham has made an experiment which he would do well not to repeat.

Speaking at a Primrose League gathering, at Preston Brook, on Saturday, the lion. Alan de Tatton Egerton made some reference to Lord Salisbury's" twenty-years' of resolute government." He said "it was rather a curious coincidence that in exactly a quarter of that time, namely, five years, during which a firm Government had been carried on—they had Ireland in a state not alone of peace, but of prosperity." We don't see anything curious in five years as a quarter of twenty; but if the member for the Knutsford Division is on the look out for a curious coincidence he may find one in the fact that Lord Salisbury as to Ireland is where he was when he started. Ireland was at peace when he allowed the Crimes Act to lapse ; and, according to this latest authority, Ireland is at peace after five years' experience of a worse Crimes Act. Puzzle: Find the benefit of resolute government when it leaves you "as you were."

, ritygortg GAS COMi'ANY. The half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of this company was held at Runcorn Gas Works yesterday. Mr. F. Rigby J.P., the chairman of the directors, presided. A dividend up the rate of 10 per cent. per annum was declared, and the returning director, Mr. W. Whittaker, was re-elected. The retiring auditor, Mr.JamesPritchard, was re-appointed. The directorate having been reduced to five by the deaths of Messrs. R. B. Toft,R.Forester,and W. Gibson, it was resolved that in future the concern should be managed by five directors. Votes of thanks were accorded to the chairman, the manager, the secre- tary (Mr. J. R. Frith) and the directors.

MARRIAGE AT WIDNES. On Tuesday afternoon, at Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel, in the presence of a numerous congregation, Mr. John Barber, son of Mr. John Barber, Lacey-sreet, was united in the bonds of matrimony with Miss Isabella Hudson, niece of Mr. John Houghton, Rose Cottage, Albert-road. The bride was given away by Mr. Hough- ton, and her sister, Miss Annie Hudson, acted as brides- maid, and Mr. Arthur Barber was the best man. The Rev. G. S. Meek officiated. After breakfast at Rose Cottage the newly married couple proceeded to South- port, where they are spending the honeymoon. Lewri MOWERS.—Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warvngton. and at Earistown,—:advt.

FATAL PAILUTIN LAM? ACCIDENT AT WIDNES. A fatal lamp accident occurred at Widnes on Monday night. Mrs. Houseley, of 35, Witt-road, was coming downstairs carrying a lighted lamp when she caught her foot in her dress, stumbled, and struck the lamp against the wall, causing it to explode. Her dress was set on fire and she was terribly burned about the breast, arms and face. She was placed under the care of Dr. O'Neil, and after lingering in fearful agony, she died on Wed- nesday night. Her husband is left with the care of three small children. The inquest was held yesterday by Mr. Hus.tlapsl and a verdict of" Accidental death" was re- corded.

ODDFELLOWS DEMONSTRATION AT HALTON. On Bank Holiday, the members of the Earl of Chester's Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows, Man- chester Unity, Halton, assembled at their Lodge-room, Norton Arms, Halton, and according to custom marched in procession, headed by the Runcorn Volunteer Band, to the Royal Hotel, Runcorn, the headquarters of the William IV. Lodge. After staying here a short time, they re- turned to the Norton Armg, whae a first-class tea was served by the proprietor, Bro. Turley. At the haad of the procession was carried the new banner made of fine Italian silk. On one side was worked the emblem of the Order, and on the other a representation of a brother visiting. The banner has been provided by Bro. George Tutil, of London, at a cost of about 12,14. After tea, dancing was indulged in to the strains of the Volunteer Band.

ALLEGED UNLAWFUL WOUNDING AT WIDNES. Before Mr. Deacon at Widnes Police Court,on Monday Partrick Martin of Moss-st., was charged on remand with wounding John Kelly,of 15. Moss-road, on the 25th ult. Both men were employed at Messrs. Sullivan and Co.'s works and on the day named Kelly seeing a strap of a certain wheel, asked the prisoner what was the matter. The prisoner in reply, told him to mind his own business or he would make him. Kelly replied that he was not frightened and the prisoner then struck him on the head with an iron rake. A serious wound penetrat- ing to the bone was inflicted. The defence was that Kelly several times challenged the prisoner to fiqht and the lat- ter at length gave him a push causing him to fall over a barrow. It was denied that a blow was struck. The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial, bail being allowed.

WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGIIH. At the usual weekly meeting of this League held on Sunday under the presidency of Mr. P. Whelan, a reso- lution was passed congratulating Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien on being liberated from Balfour's clutches after six months of unjust and cruel imprisonment, and wel- coming the champims of the Irish cause back to public life at a time when a number of men were creating di- visions in the Irish ranks, and trying to perform what Cromwell and all other English invaders in Ireland failed to do, viz., to separate the shepherd from the flock. An earnest hope was expressed that Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien would be able to teach these evil doers that Irishmen at home and abroad will not allow them to destroy the only chance which Ireland has had during the past 91 years of gaining her freedom by-peaceful methods.

RAILWAY FATALITY NEAR ST. HELENS. Thomas Mounfield, of Thancont, an old servant of the London and North-Western Railway Company, was at work on the Ravenhead Branch of the St. Helens lines, on Wednesday, night, when he was crushed between the end of a wagon and a draw- bar hook. His condition appeared to be so serious that he was at once taken to the Providence Hos- pital, where he died on Thursday afternoon. J. Sc. W. DUTTON 8 SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.

Two WOMEN CONVICTED 354 TIMES. At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, Bridget Kildare, the notorious local character, made her 195th appearance. She pleaded guilty to a charge of drunkenness, and was fined 108. and costs.— Another female of considerable notoriety, named Elizabeth Tither, was also placed in the dock charged with drunkenness. She appeared for the 159th time, and was fined ss. and costs. The united convictions amounted to 354.
