INSURA N 3E. At the Foresters High Court, on Wednesday, Sir Albert Rollit, M.l read a letter from dui Post- master-General, stating that with the consent of the Treasury it was proposed to allow circulars to be sent by book post, whether attached or not to any other document that is admissible. This would ad- mit to bark-rate the statements of arrears sent out by friellenv 00Cieties which were formerly inadmis- sible. On Thue4aY2 Sir Ctuirles Dilke wos present, and spoke on the subject ot BuOtailllloon. He thought that in any change _in the poor laW it would be natural that the subject should be taken up district by district, and considered locally. They might consider among others the suggestion that part should he paid nationally and part locally, but that the local part should not come out of the poor rate.

A PUBLIC-HOUSE STRUCK BY LIGHTNING. During a heavy thunderstorm which passed over St. Helens on Tuesday afternoon, the York Hotel, Park-road, occupied by Mr. Joseph Gee, was struck by lightning. The chimney stack was damaged, and the electric current appeared to have descended the chimney, entered one of the bedrooms, stripped some of the paper from the walls, splintered the skirting boards, and passed along the gaspipe into the cellar.lmmediately afterwards it was found that the joists of the ceiling were in flames, and their extinction was only accomplished with difficulty. Portions of the gaspiping in the bedroom and cellar were melted by the lightning, and the meter was entirely disconnected. Fortunately no person sus- tained any iTijury. J. &W. 1)1/w0n's SUMMER SALE non on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.

SHOCKING FATALITY AT CITERDLEY. Yesterday afternoon week, at Cuerdley, a woman named Pye, wife of George Pye, a platelayer, re- siding on the canal bank, lost her life It appears there is no water tap in the deceased's house, and she had been accustomed for several years to ob- tain water for cleansing purposes from the engine I which conveys the waste from the British Alkali ' Works to the "tip," which is situated near deceased's home. When the engine driver saw Mrs. Pye com- ing, he stopped as usual to allow her to get the water. It seem, however, to accomplish this she had to go behind the engine, and consequently un- derneath the first wagon. This she must have at- tempted to do before the train had properly stopped, for her head was caught between the buders of the engine and the wagon, crushing it in a frightful manner, and causing Instantaneous death. Mr. Min- ton, manager, at the British Alkali Works, was on the engine at the time of the occurrence. PRUNtltit SAFETIES, Cash Or liire.—GARLAND, Warrington —Advt. , LIVERPOOL, ST. IIh'LENS, AND SOUTH LANCASHIRE
MILK ADULTERATION IN CHESHIRE.

Mr. Carter Bell, in his report to the Cheshire ICounty Council, mentions that 25 per cent. of the samples of milk he took in the last quarter were adulterated with water to the extent of from 5 to 20 per cent. In recommending a visitation of the farm by an inspector when an accusation is made against a milk dealer, Mr. Bell says that such a sys- tem has been carried out in Salford for many years, with such success that Salford has now the purest milk supply of any borough in the kingdom. J. & W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: RUNCORN MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.
div.p: RUNCORN MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.

The annual Sunday School services were held on Sun- day. In the morning the service was held in the Parish Church, and in the afternoon and evening in the Public Hall. The Rev. J. Fell, the chaplain to the Missions, was the preacher on each occasion, and the conzrega- tions were very large. Special hymns and anthems were sung under the conductorship of Mr. Price, Mr. Richard Shaw presiding at the harmonium. On Monday the scholars had their annual treat. About 400 were con- veyed in two boats along the Bridgewater Canal to Grapperikall, where they spent a happy day. Canon Greenall placed the Church schoolroom at the disposal of the excursionists, whose bodily wants were well at- tended to. Mr. R. A. Nayler threw open his grounds to the inspection of the young people, who much enjoyed this privilege. RUNCORN SONS GP TEMPERINCH.

At the fortnightly meeting of the Order on Saturday, Mr. Daniel Bisbrown read a paper on" Our National Drink Bill." Last year, he said, our people spent 139 i , millions in drink. This enormous sum would mean an average of £3 13s. for every man, woman and child in the country or for a family of live persons £lB ss. The total expenditure on drink for the year was 7i million in excess of last year. The income of our Christian churches for all purposes of maintainence and extension, including their benevolent institution, prob- ably did not exceed 18 millions yearly. This meant that people spent £1 in drink for every 2s. 6d. for Christ. It will be clearly seen that if this amount wasnot spent on drink it would be spent on other objects which would be for the comfort convenience and elevation of the people—crimes less, disease less, poverty, lunacy, land mortality less; and the moral status of the people would be raised.—There was a discussion in which the following officers and members took •part. Messrs. Thomas Cooke, Ed. Key, S. 31. Temperley, and Wm. Millinger. The paper was much appreciated thanks being accorded the essayist. Mr. Thos. Heesom occu- pied the chair. 'BT. MICHAEL'S CHANCEL, RUNCORN. Our readers and particularly those of them who hate given their help towards the completion of -St. Michael's Church must have wondered again and again what has occurred to prevent any progress from being made with the chancel. No one would be more surprised than the Vicar on coming home on the 26th of June to find that not a stone had been laid of the work for which a contract had been entered into in April, with a Liverpool firm of builders, Messrs. Nicholson'andiClarke, of Wellington-st. Messrs. Nicholson and Clarke undertook to complete the work before a fixed day in September, under a penalty for every week's delay, but up to the moment of the issue of this number (August 1), they have done nothing. The Building Committee have been using every endea- vour to put a better appearance upon their undertaking but up to the present they have been unable to effect anything. The necessary money is in th bank, or nearly all, the architect's working drawings made, the contract executed, and yet there is a standstill. We hone very soon to be able to announce that the Com- mittee has extricated itself from the disagreeable position it has been placed in, and that the work will really be begun if not by Messrs. Nicholson and Clarke at any tate by some other firm of contractors.—" Parish Church Magazine." J. W. DuTTos'S SUMAIvR SAL K now on. Sankey Street, Warringi (LB.—Advt.

div.head: ODDFELLOWS' ANNIVERSARY AT CULCHETH.
div.p: ODDFELLOWS' ANNIVERSARY AT CULCHETH.

The anniversary of the City of Refuge Lodge of the Royal Order of Oddfellows' Friendly Society was celebrated at the Old Noggin Inn, Culcheth, on Tuesday. The members met at the Lodge shortly after nine o'clock, and though the weather was very unfavourable, a procession was formed. Dinner was partaken of shortly after three o'clock. The band played an excellent selection of music on the route. The society is in a flourishing condition, and the arrangement was carried out by the Secretary, Mr. H. Jackson, in a praiseworthy manner.
PROPOSED NATIONAL FEDERATION OF LABOUR
UNIONS.

On Monday night a meeting of Labour Union delegates was held at Liverpool, to consider the advisability of forming a national federation of labour unions. Delegates attended representing nine unions, with a total membership of 67,000, and were from Liverpool, St. Helens, Sorthwich, Wins- ford, Durham, Bolfon, Newcastle-on-Tvne, &c. Mr. Samuel Yarwood, of the Northwich Saltworkers' Association, presided. The subject was discussed at considerable length, and there was only one society represented who preferred amalgamation instead of a federation. It was ultimately decided that a report of the meeting be issued to all labour societies, with shsrt papers on Amalgamation v. Federation. It WdS announced that the amalga- mation view would be written by Mr. Edward Hall, of the Tyneside and Newcastle Labourers' Union; and Mr. J. Chadwick, of the St. Helens and District Labour Union, would express the opinions of the Amalgamationists. Mr. J. Chadwick, of 37, Albion- street, Ist. Helens, was elected honorary secretary pro tem. 17. DuTTO2e2 SVMES UT,E now On, Sanl“..y Street, Warriugton. —Add.
RUNCORN SONS OF TE4PERANCE.

ANNUAL DEMONSTRATION. The members of the Runcorn branch of the Sons of Temperance held their annual demonstrations last week end and they were attended with much success. On Sunday afternoon a number of the members met in Devonshire Square, where a public meeting was held. An audience of much larger proportions than usual assembled and listened with interest to speeches delivered by Messrs. W. Jeffery, D. Smith, J. Moores, and S. M. Temperley. The pro- ceedings were conducted by Messrs. T. Cooke and E. Key. Afterwards the members walked in proces- sion to St. John's Presbyterian chapel, where the Rev. J. Pulford Williams, the pastor, delivered an eloquent sermon on the subject of " Christianity and its relation to temperance." He based his dis- course on the text " Do all things to the glory of God," The sacred edifice was well filled. The weathor was far from propitious for the more ! extensive demonstration of Bank holiday. Rain fell I heavily at the time when the proceedings should have . . . .
commenced, but with commenCiable ardo-ur the members
turned up in- large numbers,
When the procession filed
out of Devonshfie Square, at two o'clock; there were in the ranks 200 adults and 100 juveniles._ Leading the
way were the mounted marshal, Messrs. T. Heesoria and T. Lea, who were followed by Widnes Soap Works band, playing lively music. Next came the! beautiful banner of the Order, four cords of which were
held by four young ladies, Misses. Emily Randles, Stubbs, Mary Temperley, and Frances A. Stubbs. The silken cords were held by four young girls named Alice Cooke, Lizzie and May Leathwood, and Lizzie
Bisbrown. Next in order mirched the members, who were decorated with rosettes, the rear being brought up

1-3.3 the lifebot drawu on a luny kindly lent by Mr. F. Wiswall, engineer to the Ship Canal Company. The bog was manned by Messrs. W. Stubbs, G. H. Shingler. E. Higgins, and Samuel Stubbs. There were also on board" four boys named Frank Johnson, Earnest White, Thomas White. and Alfred Brown. The procession went through the principal thoroughfares is far as the crane in Halton-road, calls being made en route at the resid- ences of Dr. MacLennan and Dr. Robinson. The marshals Consisted of the committee, viz., 4ohn Jones, • T. Clarke, Wesley Cooke, James Johnson, John Taylor, Thomas Holt,S, M. Temperley,Wni: Cooke, W. Bisbrown, _ _
J. Bisbrown, John Hinilley,-and the secretaries, Messrs. T. Cooke and E. Key. After spending ashort time in a field off Irwell-lane, kindly lent by Mr. Hall, contractor,
_ an adjournment was made to -Bethesda Lecture Hall where a capital tea was provided,_ In the evening a
PUBLIC MEETING was held under the presidency of Mr. F. J. Norman, and

there was a good attendance. He was supported on the platform by the committee and the Rev. J. Pulford Williams, Mr. J. H. Musk (Manchester),and Mr. Mundin (Ship Canal Missionary.) Mr. E. key, secretary of the Cadet Section, pleaded the cause of the cadets. Children were admitted from
five to sixteen years and were then drafted into the Sons of Temperance, the admittance fee being paid for them. in Runcorn there were 105 cadets, and on the

authority of the editor of the "Sons of Temperance" this branch was preeminent in its financial aspect. There was no branch that stood so well financially. (Hear, hear.) He had personal experience, of the evils of drunkenness, and he urged upon the parents present to train up their children in the way of temperance. When we got temperance men and women then indeed would , the days of England be happy. The Chairman then announced that in connection with the Cadet Section, Mr. Heesom provided at his own expense two handsome prizes for those juvenile mem- bers who got most cadets during the session. During the past year John Daniel. Bisbrown was successful in win- ning the Ist prize and J. W. Raissden obtained the 2nd prize. The Chairman presented the prizes. He further announced that Master Bisbrown had won the 2nd prize for writing and the first prize for drawing the front elevation of a house in connection with examinations held by the Grand Division of the Order. Unfortu- nately the prizes had not yet arrived. Mr. T. Cook, the secretary, then read the annual report Two years, he said, had passed away since they had the pleasure of greeting one another and reporting on the work and progress of their Order, there having been abreakln their usual annual gathering last year. He therefore congratulated them on that happy re- assemblage and expressed the hope that this year's pro- ceedings wouldbe eminently profitable to the great cause of temperance and their Order. They might each take encouragement from and be stimulated by the success which had attended their efforts to continue on in their work of well-doing, and strive still more to be true to the noble principles of their Order, love, purity and fidelity. Much yet remained to be done. The principles of temperance were amongst the great progressive stps of the day, "a vast moralanachinery for the amelioration of human evils, and for the protection and advancement of human happiness. They were the shield of our homes, , the streength of our country, and the hope of the nation. Feeling therefore that their responsibility was great, let them by their ircreased zeal and devotion, show themselves equal to it. Their work was not only one of rescue from drink and its traffic, but also of teaching and encouraging habits of thrift. It was gratifying to be able to report the satisfantory increase of 1.574 members in the past year, making the total membership of the order in this country on December 31st last, 26,663. In the matter of cadets, while it could not be said that theincrease of 545 members for the past year was a large one, vet there was a bright side in con- nection with this work. It must not be forgotten that 7,559 juvenile members had been regularly trained and strengthened in the teetotal principles, and that in addi- tion there was cause to rejoice that 444 had been trans- ferred to the adult order. In the funds of tbeir Order they had a net gain in the year of £6,404, the total funds of the Society now being £97,736 12s. I.ld. During the year the Society had paid in sick claims alone £20,443 19s. 2c1.—£214 9s. 4d. of which was paid in sick claims in connection with the Runcorn Division. The Society had also paid in death claims during the year £3,739 10s. —£34 of which was paid for deaths in Runcorn DiVigol2. There was also given away to members in distress £319 14s. 8d„ The sickness rate was 8 days per member per annum, and the death rate 817 per thousand. The usual sick rate was 64 days and the death rate under 7 per 1,000. The difference was caused by influenza. There were now 270 members in tne Runcorn branch. (Ap- plause.) The Chairman, who on rising was loudly applauded, said he was constantly finding that opinions he had held years ago would not stand the test of fuller information, but he was thankful to say, that no matter how far he went into this temperance question,he had never yet,un- der any circumstances, or at any time, had to !make such an admission. (Applause.) All the information lie go!, , no matter from what source it came, only built up his teetotalism. (Applause.) Why he liked the teetotal cause was that it was real work—there was none of the faddist about it. If one-half the societies he was asked to join obtained what they were fighting for, he did not know how much better the world would be, but in the temperance societies they were brought face to face with the most awful influence for evil that existed to-dayaand it was worth wkile any man having a tussle with it— he would find a foeman worthy of his steel. He had re- cently gone pretty fully into the origin of the drink traffic, and the fact remained that drinking strong liquers was bred in the bone. Englishmen for a good many centuries had been drinking, and drinking, and unfortunately for many years they considered it a virtue to drink. He believed drinking was hereditary, and

that many of us had to suffer for the sins of our ancestors. Drink was a disease dipsomania, the doctors called it—and the great thing was to get their children never to touch drink ; and that grown up folks should not be induced to touch it; and then when they had attained this they hada great chance of putting this drinking custom right. (Applause.) He derived encour- agement from the fact that during the last decade several matters had attrafted the attention of politicians of in- fluence more than ever they did before ; and it was re- cognised that something heroic must be done to reduce the amount of wretchedness, misery and drunkenness, that existed amongst us. 'The remedy was easy—and it was merely not to touch drink. He wished every Tem- perance Society God speed. (Applause.) Alluding to the Sharp .v Wakefield case, the Chairman said he saw no reason why the law there expounded should not be put into effect, and the sooner the magistrates did so the better he should be pleased. The magistrates had now tremendous power in their hands, and the great work of the teetotal party was to peg away at the magistrates as hard as they possibly could, because from that direction alone at the present time redress of an im- portant character could be obtained. (Applause.) ' He was sorry that the question of national insurance had been introduced from a rather unpopular quarter' and that the friendly societies were inclined not to have much to do with it. He trusted that when the question I came before the Sons of Temperance they would give it mature and deliberate consideration because he was convinced that it was on right lines. The thrifty men had to look after the men who would not look after themselves, and he said hasten the day when the State would say to these men "We shall make you look after yourselves." (Applause.) Mr. F. H. Musk, of the U.K.A., Manchester, then de- livered a speech on temperance topics, illustrating and enforcing his remarks by numerous anecdotes. The Rev. J. Pulford Williams also spoke, dealing with the immorality of the drink traffic, remarking that we tolerated the publicans too much and made the drink traffic too respectable. In proposing a vote of thanks to the speakers, Mr. T. Lea expressed the pride lie felt in being the first representative of the Temperance party on the Board of Guardians—(Applause)—and he hoped they would be successful at the next Commissioners' elec- tion. (Applause.) Mr. D. Bisbrown seconded the motion, and said his motto had always been "Down with the liquor traffic and up with the people," and when Mr. Lea and he came forward at the Commissioners' election they would give no uncertain sound upon this particular matter. They had such confidence in the sentiments of the people and in public opinion that they were very confident of coming-off victorious. (Applause.) The meeting then concluded.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday. Mr. H. J. Grice presided, and there were present Messrs. P. Speakman C.C., J. Prit- chard, J. W. Lightburn, W. Mellor, R. Abel, E. Imison, E. W. Humphreys, F. Wiswall, J. Dobson, F. A. Lake (law clerk); E. Marshall (secretary) ; and M. Barker (surveyor). 11EALTH OF THE TO*N.

The Medical Officer (Dr. McDougall) reported the number of deaths during the past month as 25, a death-rate for the twelve months of 15 per I,ooo.—The Chairman remarked that this was extremely satis- factory.

HEALTH COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended among other things That Inspector S. J. Cooper be appointed an assistant inspector of common lodging-houses in place of Inspector Bowyer resigned.—The minutes were passed.
T HNICAL EDUCATION. IMPORTANT RESOLU-

TION. The Parliamentary Committee recommended that the Committee be empowered to employ professional assistance in the preparation of plans, Sze., in respect of the Technical Institute Scheme. That Messrs. Pritchard, Lightburn, Imison, Wiswall, and the Law Clerk, visit institutions for technical instruction at Staleybridge, Hyde, Stockport, Crewe, Manchester, and such other places, as they may think necessary. That Messrs. Pritchard, Grice, Taylor, Speakman' and Humphreys,be appointed a committee to approach and, if necessary, wait upon the overseers of the surrounding townships with regard to the application of the moneys allotted to their districts.—Mr. Pritchard moved the adoption of these minutes, and remarked that with the penny rate and contribution from the County Council the Board had about £4OO available for the purposes of technical educ- ation. It would also be within the recollection of the
members that they applied to the County Council for a building grant in aid of the technical institute which

the i3oard thought they would attempt to establish, and the Couneil,who still had a considerable sum unappropri- ated, wished for an outline of the proposed scheme. The Committee therefore wished to visit various institutions and to have professional assistance, so that they could give the details the Council asked for. A further sugges- tion had also emanated from the Technical Committee of

the Council—that Runcorn would be a very eligible centre for a certain district including Weston, Halton, Clifton, and other rural places. There would thus be a larger amount available for a technical institute in the benefits of which those townships could participate. Hence the appointment of a deputation to wait upon the overseers.—Mr. Lightburn seconded the motion, and suggestel that some other member should be put in his place on the Committee, as his existence on the Board might be cut short in a few weeks. (Laughter.)—Mr. Innson : We are all in the same boat.—Mr. Speakman, in supporting the recommendations, said he was a member of the County Technical Education Commit- tee. He took good care to be on that Committee so that the interests of Runcorn might be protected, and he felt sure that if Runcorn put forth a proper claim in a proper form such as he had already stated to the Committee of that Board and to the Committee of the County Council it would be recognised. There was money still in hand that would have to be dealt with, and the sooner Runcorti made their claim the better, and he urged the members not to relax their efforts but to place their scheme before the Committee at the earliest possible moment. (Hear, hear.)—The motion was carried.—The Parliamentary Committee also recommended that any deficiency incurred by the Runcorn School Board in connection with the Science and Art Classes to be held during the forthcoming win- ter be made good up to the extent of £75 for the finan- cial year. That application be made to the Department of Science and Art to sanction the teaching of modern languages, shorthand, bookkeeping and cookery at the aforesaid science and art classes such form of instruc- tion being required by the circumstances of the district. That Messrs. (rice, Wiswall and unison be appointed to re oresent the. Board under the Technical Instruction Act, 1838, on the School Board Science and Art Committee. Mr. Pritchard moved the adoption of the minutes and said the School Board, were merely taking up this ques- tion in a temporary way until the Commissioners had had time to mature its plans and provide an institute of its own- Where these classes would find a • home, and where scientific teaching would be given to a much fuller extent. We had not yet realised the im- portance of the technical instruction and the advantage • to be derived from it by the youth of the town. It was • admitted on all hands that if we were to maintain Qur industrial prosperity and hold our own with the nations of Europe our youth must take up these subjects.—Mr. Lightburn seconded the motion.—the Chairman said he was pleased to see every member of the Board was so earnest in his endeavours to obtain all the advantages ! possible for the town. Future generations would think , of them with gratitude and respect because of the action • they had taken on education.—The motion was carried unaninme,ly.

THE rituPOSED BRIDGE ACROSS THE MERSEY. The Parliamentary Committee recommended that a Sub- Comnaitteebe appointed, consititag of Messrs. Pritchard, Taylor., Wiswall, Fisher and Lightburn, for the purpose of conferring with the Widnes Authorities and conducting such negotiations as may be necessary for urging the respective County Councils to give favourable considera- tion to a scheme for constructing a Public Road Bridge across the Mersey between Runcorn and Widnes and to seek any powers that may be necessary te carry out such scheme; the Sub-Committee to report to the Parliament- ary Committee the result of such conferences and nego- tiations.—Mr. Pritchard moved the passing of this minute and said this question had arisen in consequence of a conversation a few of the Commissioners had had with a few members of the Widnes Local Board, who received the Commissioners with all courtesy. Since that meeting the Widnes members had taken an active interest in the project, and he believed they would heartily co-operate in its furtherance in the ;interests of the community they represented. The need of better communication between the inhabitants of Widnes and Runcorn had long been felt, and now that the populatio# of both towns were rapidly growing it was all the more necessary that better communication by roadway should be provided. It was a fact, that al- though the towns were only half a mile apart, and with- in yivv of each other, yet the severance, owing to the existing state of things was so complete, that they had nothing in common, and there was but scant business relationship existing between the two communities. This bridge would bring the inhabitants in close communica- tion, intercourse would arise, and trade would be fos- tered. They thought it was a question which ought to be taken up by the respective County Councils of the two counties. They were all thoroughly in favour of the project. The scheme was thoroughly feasible at a moderate cost. A plan had been recently prepared by Messrs. Fox, eminent engineers, which had been inform- ally shown to the Commissioners, who, while they did not commit themselves to anything, learned that .there was no difficulty in constructing a public road bridge between Runcorn and Widnes.—Mr.Lightburn seconded the resolution cordially. Re thought there was a feeling in some parts of Widnes against this scheme, on the ground that it would be to the advantage of of Runcorn at the expense of Widnes. That was a fallacy, and if those people would carry their argument to a logical conclusion they would move that the footbridge be des- troyed. " These objectors, however, were only a small section of the population.—The Chairman said this

. question affected the interests of both Lancashire and Cheshire. They all took a deep interest in the matter and he hoped they would all live to see it carried out successfully. On Tuesday, there was a deputation from the County Council to Runcorn with regard to the main road, and the idea was thrown out that this main road would be very important when it was connected with a public road bridge joining the two counties. The idea came upon one ef them by surprise and he said we should: have to wait some considerable time, but the hope was expressed that the County Council would be sympathe- tic with the Local authorities in the matter and take it up. There were several districts contiguous to Run- corn and Widnes represented on the County Councils. and when they saw the activity displayed by these ' towns they would see the advantage of taking the question up in the interests of the two counties. The bridge would bring South Lancashire and Widnes in connection with the Ship Canal, the advantage of which commercially would be very great. (Heart hear.) The Manchester Ship Canal was going to alter the features of this part of the country and there was no doubt that Runcorn had a great future before it. The motion was carried unanimously.
REMISSION OF A SIJR.CIZA- EGE.
The Finance Committee reported that the Local Govern- ment Board had received the surcharge of £lOO on Mr. Imison.
FLAGS V. COMPOSITION.

In accordance with the notice he had given Mr. Pritchard moved that resolution No. 1329 be amended by adding the words "except the part of Victoria-road as lies between Greenway-road and the north-eastern bound- ary of the Cemetery, which may be made with compos- ition. The resolution was carried. Both Mr. Lightburn and Mr. Humphreys gave notice of motion to rescind the resolution but withdrew them.
THE BOARD'S TRIP TO E&STHAM.
The Chairman moved a resolution acknowledging the courtesy with which the Board had been treated by the Ship Canal Company on the 22nd ult., on their trip from Latchford to Basthatn.
DUKES SICK CLUB.

A letter was read from Mr. T. Simister, secretary ,to the Dukes Sick Club asking for the time to be extended for the removal of three tenants from the cellar houses in Gilbert-st. On the motion of the Chairman the request was acceded to.

div.head: RAILWAY.
div.p: RAILWAY.

The half-yearly meeting of this Company was held on Wednesday at London-road Station, Mr. H. Seton- Karr, M.P., presiding. Mr. Edward Ross (secretary) submitted the Directors' report. of which the follow- ing is the substance : The Directors have pleasure in reporting that considerable progress has been made with the execution of the 'works since they were recommenced in the spring, and they are at present being proceeded with to their satisfaction. The company's land is being rapidly fenced in, and a steam navvy and other plant are employed upon the earth works. The bill promoted in the present session of Parliament by the company has received the Royal assent. This Act provides for the exten- sion of time for the compulsory acquisition of land for the purposes of the company's railways, and the alteration of the site of the station at Ashton-in- Makerfield. It so empowers the company to raise all or any part of the capital of the Act of 1586 in preference shares or stock, if so determined. The Sheffield compas,ny have obtained powers in their Various Powers Act of this session to subscribe a further sum of £20;000, in addition to £lOO,OOO already agreed to be subscribed.--On the motion of the Chairman seconded by Mr. Edward Chapman, the report was adopted. CHARITABLE BEWCESTS BY A ST. AELENS LA.DY By the will of the late Mrs. Ellen Middlehurst,. late of Shawhurst, Rainford, near St. Helens. pro- bate of which has just been granted to Miss Mary IShaw of Shawhurst, Mr. Thomas Shaw, of Lydiate, and Mr. Thomas Middiehurst of Feasley Cross. St. Helens, the executors named therein, the following charities benefit to the amounts named :—Rainford Catholic Church, £5O; Catholic Church, Lvidiate, £5O; Holy Cross Catholic Church. St. Helens, £5O ;St. Di arY's Catholic Church, Birchley, £25 • St. Mary's Lowe House Catholic Church, St. Helens, £25 ;' Sacred Heart Catholic Church, St. Helens, £25 • Catholic Orphan- age, Norwood, Surrey, £55; Catholic Blind Asylum, Liverpool, £25; Ecclesiastical Education Fund of theCathelic Diocese of Liverpool, £25; Catholic Poor School Committee of Lancashire, £25; Rome for the Little Sisters of the Poor, Liverpool, £25; and the Providence Free Hospital,St. Helens, £3OO. Deceased also gives her freehold properties in Rainford for the benefit as to one hall of the Rainford Catholic Church Expenses Fund, and as to the other half of the Rainford Catholic School for the purpose of educating free poor Catnolic children in the parish of Rainford. She also bequeaths pecuniary lega- cies to the servants in her employ at the time of her decease. J. '& W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt. THE COUNTY COUNCIL AND PRESCOT ROADS..

The monthly meeting of the members of the Prescot Highway Board, was held on Tuesday, Mr. H. R. d'A. Willis, J.P., presiding. There were also present Mr. W. L. M'Clure, J.P., Mr. J. Birchall, J.P., Mr. IL Tyrer, Mr. 3. Baker, and Messrs. Cross (clerk), and Mr. Goldsworth (surveyor.) A letter was read from the county council authorities refusing to adopt the Knowsley road as a main road until the board had put the same in good repair to the satisfaction of the county surveyor. The application to have the road leading from St. Helens to Farnworth Rail- way Station declared a main road was also re- fused. The road known as Wilderinere-lane, and that from Clock Face Inn to the Griffin Inn, Bold, were, however, taken over.—The Chairman pointed out that the county authorities had agreed to take over the road connecting Warrington with St. Helens, and the road connecting Widnes with St. Helens but they had refused to take over the roads at Farn- worth and Knowsley.—On the suggestion of the Sur- veyor,it was decided to ask the county surveyor whr• t repairs were required to the roads the County Coun- cil had declined to take over.—The Chairman, who is a member of the County Council, remarked that they were not to suppose that the county authori- ties had thrown over the Knowsley road alto- gether. The County Committee were now deal- ing with roads which lay between towns of 25,000 inhabitants, and the Knowsley road would have to stand over until the committee were authorised to deal with such roads.—Mr. Birchall suggested that if the footroad known as the Cockshoots, leading from the Warrington road to the Prescot Railway Station, was widened suffi- ciently for horses and conveyances it would be a great advantage to the district. It was decided to communicate with the Local Board upon the sub- ject.—The Surveyor reported that his expenditure upon the highways in the board's district during the past month had been £172 2s.

div.head: 1' RODSHAM.
div.p: 1' RODSHAM.

BANK HOLIDAY.—As usual on Bank Holiday, the visitors to the pleasure grounds on Overton Hills were very numerous, hailing from the towns and villages in the vicinity. The weather was far more favourable than was anticipated in the early morning. FEARFUL CHARGE AGAINST YOUTHS.—Before Mr. A. Thomas, at Frodsham Police Court on Tuesday, George Corker (17) and Joseph Clough (18), respectably con- nected youths, were charged with a commission of an unnatural offence in Gas Works-lane, on Sunday night. The prisoners were remanded until Friday. PASSING FOREIGN COIN.—At Frodsham Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. A. Thomas, Edward Lloyd, a labourer, from Wrexham, was charged with having on the 22nd July passed foreign coin at the White Lion public-house, Alvanley, and the Horse and Jockey, Helsby. On the day in question the prisoner called for a glass of ale at the White Lion, and in payment tendered a Dutch coin of the value of 10 centimes. It was of white metal and somewhat resembled a shilling, but was only of the value about a penny. Mr. Lord the prosecu tor refused to accept the coin, but after the prisoner's departure he found that he had previously taken one. Information was given to the police and the prisoner was apprehended by P.S. Doyle. It was then ascertained that the prisoner had attempted to pass one of the coins as a Lion shilling at the Horse and Jockey. The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. FUNERAL OF THE LATE Mn. damn ANDREWS.—On Mon- day afternoon the remains of one of the oldest inhabit- ants of Frodsham and neighbourhood were laid in their last resting place in the parish church-yard, Frodsham. Mr. Andrews was in his 91st year, having been born in r Septemlapr, 1800, and until quite recently had enjoyed remarkably good health. He was for many years senior overseer of the poor of the township of Frodsham, and on the formation of the Frodsham and Helsby Drainage Board was elected a member,which appointment he held up to the time of his death,the duties of the overseership having been relinquished a few years previously. In all matters connected with the parish he ever took a kindly interest. For more than forty years he interested him- self in Wesleyan Methodism • although not coming to the front, his attachment to the cause was most zealous, and he was held in great respect. A short memorial service was held in the Trinity Chapel, which was con- ducted by the Rev. P. Pizey, the circuit minister, when there was a large assembly of friends wishing to show their respect to the deceased's memory. The service at the Parish Church was gone through by the Rev. H. B. Blogg. M.A. vicar. The wreaths were numerous and very beautiful.

div.head: .LYMM.
div.p: .LYMM.

BAxHOLIDAN.--tymm was visited by large numbers of trippers on Monday. The weather, however, was not altogether favourable, as ram fell at intervals. DR. R. E. WiLmaisort.—At the Altrincham Board of Guardians, at Knutsferd, on Wednesday, Dr. R. E. Wil- liamson, of Lymm, resigned the appointment he held', under the Guardians as public vaccination officer for the- Lymm district, and his brother, Mr. H. M. L. William-- son, was appointed. SPEECK DAY AT TILE LYMM GRAMMAR SCIOOI.--The- annual speech day at the Lymm Grammar School, was held on Thursday. Ven. Archdeacon Gore was present to. distribute the prizes, and the Rev. G. W. Guest, rector of Lymm and chairman of the board of governors, pre- sided. There were also present Mr. P. Stubs, LP' : Dr Brabazon, J.P., Mr. J. T. Ridgway, Mr. C. Mclver governors ; Messrs. Ridyard, Cameron, Everton, Rohmer, Sec., &c., and a large company of ladies.—ln his report the Headmaster (Rev. J. Edwards Evans), said they had during the last 12 months made steady progress. In numbers they had again grown, and they had at present 32 boys, seven of whom were boarders. OPENING OF THE CONSERVATIVE CUM.—The new pre- mises of the Lymm Conservative Club were forma* opened on Wednesday evening by a banquet, at which the members entertained the Conservative candidate of the division, Mr. C. Disraeli. The chair was occupied by Mr. Peter Stubs, the chairman of the club. After dianer the Chairman proposed the usual loyal toasts, which were fully honoured.—Mr. J. Martin gave "Pros- perity to the Lymm Conservative Club," to which the Chairman responded.—Mr. E. Swanwick proposed "The Unionist cause," and coupled with it the names of Sir W. C. Brooks and Mr. C. Disraeli.—Mr. Coningsby Disraeli, ;mho was enthusiastically received, then gave • an address. Tte remainder of the evening was spent in harmony. CHARGES OF THEFT.—At Lvmm Police Court on Wed- nesday morning, before Mr. C. Lister and Dr. Brabazon, Wm. Mason and Wm. Nichols, Ship Canal labourers, living at Thelwall, were charged with having stolen a number et fowls the property of Elizabeth Houghton, farmer, Thelwall. Prisoners were suspected and appre- hended but the fowls were not found in their possession. They were discharged.—The same prisoners were nest charged with having stolen a watch and chain, valued at £B, from Thomas Miller, an engine-driver of Thelwall on the 25th July. It appeared that Miller and a friend came from Warrington by the last bus at night and after- wards fell asleep in a field off Thelwall-lane. When he awoke the watch and chain were gone. On the 29th July they were sold by the prisoners to a man named Kearsley, at the Dog and Dart Inn, Grappenhall, for £.l. In defence they said they found the articles in Thelwall-lane near the tannery. They were discharged. .

div.head: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LYMM LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held in the ^ Board offices, Lymm. on Thursday afternoon. Mr. H. Cameron (chairman) presided, and there were also pre- sent Messrs. Dutton, Brazendale, Whitelegg, Holt; C. J. Ridgway (law clerk), and W. Mallard (clerk) ; and Dr. Fox (medical officer). THE RECENT ILLNESS OF THE MEDICAL OFFICER.—TEE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.—The Chairman expressed the pleasure of the Board to see Dr. Fox recovered from his long and severe illness.—Dr. Fox thanked the chair- man for his kind expression. He had simply brought that day statistics for the second quarter of the year. They were very exceptional, as they had been through- out the country in consequence of that wretched disease . , influenza. In the second quarter there had been 3g deaths which was considerably more than generally oc- curred in the quarter, but when he told them that nearly • 50 per cent was due to influenza and chest affections, they would see that the larger number of deaths was not • due to any insanitary conditions. The exact per centage of deaths from chest complaints and influenza was 429. He was thankful to say the zymotic death-rate was again a cypher. There were some serious matters that ought to be reported on in the Board's district, and Ile trusted that, at the next meeting, he would he able to bring a report before them. GYMNASIUMS AND MUSEIIMS.—TIM Law Clerk stibmit- • ted the Act of Parliament which has been lately passed to empower public bodies like the Lymtn Lica' board to establish museums and gymnasiums. He thonetht a gymnasium might be of use to Lyintn, but he pointed out that they were limited to aid in. the £ rate, whieh - would realise about £4O a year. It was agread that each of the members of the Board should be, supplied with- copies of the Act. This was the principal business.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
ANOTHER THIEVISH JUVENILE ADVENTURER.

Walter Dumbell, aged 13, son of John Dumbell, tanner, of 67, Chorley-st., had to answer a charge on Saturday, before the Warrington magistrates, of stealing on the 29th Ult., from the house of his employer James Wilkin- son, ginger beer manufacturer, who lives at 157, Long- ford-st., and carries on business at 17 Rodney-st., the sum of 12 shillings.—The Chief Constable stated that the boy had been employed as an errand lad both at the shop and at the house. On the Wednesday night pri- soner left work between 8 and 9 o'clock, and handed ten shillings to his father, saying " I have been at Widnes And sold two boxes of ginger beer, and I have drawn this money for Mr. Wilkinson, but he has gone home. Take it till to morrow morning and save for we." On the Friday morning the father gave the lad the 125., and he went away, but the former being rather suspicious, saw Mr. Wilkinson and told him about what had occurred. It turned out that the boy had not gone back to his work, or seen his em- ployer, since leaving home ; and it was ascertained that he had gone to Southport. About midnight he was apprehended at home. He there told the police heMid not get the money for ginger beer at Widnes, but from a lad named Jones in Winwick-road. Afterwards he admitted that he did not know any boy of that name. At the police station he said he had not spent all the money, but 3s. 10d. of it was in a pit of water behind his father's house. 3s. 91c1. was found in that pit that morning. The balance he had spent at Southport in riding on the switchback railway, seeing some minstrels perform, and in ice cream, jujubes, &c.—The prisoner's father said the boy had given him trouble before by stealing money and leaving his work. His mother had been dead 3 years.—The lad was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment and 5 years' subsequent detention in a reformatory.

div.head: ROLLING IN THE MUD.
div.p: ROLLING IN THE MUD.

At the Borough Court, on Tuesday, a rough-looking young fellow, named Hart, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly, and with assaulting P.C. Clough, in Bridge-st., on the previous day. It appeared from the evidence that r.c. Clough was ejecting a man from a public-house, when Hart interfered in a violent manner. The officer and he struggled together for some time, and falling to the ground, rolled in the mud. A man named John Charles Cummins, gave evidence as to the moderation of the police officer, and the violence of the prisoner. The Chief Constable thanked this last witness for the assistance he had given, and said that on Bank Holiday it took the police all their time to keep order in the streets.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days, without the option of a fine. •
THEFTS FROM A BENEFACTOR.-A MONTH FOR STEALING 9D.

At the Magistrates' Court, on Wednesday, Annie Bond, wife of John Bond, army pensioner, of Warrington, was charged with stealing 9d. from the house of Albert Silvers, puddler, 3 Erwood-st. on the previous night. —The Chief Constable said the defendant did not live with her hus- band,and he did not want to know where she was,as she was such a source of annoyance to him. About half-past 11 on Tuesday night,Aug. -4th, the prisoner called at the complainant's house, and in consequence of the pitiable tale she told was allowed to remain there till morning. Mrs. Silvers then missed 6d. from her pocket, and, after suspecting her children, charged the prisoner, who ad- mitted the theft, and promised to pay the money back if the complainant would look over the matter. The pri- soner was allowed to stay notwithstanding the theft, and that on several occasions she came home drunk at night. On Wednesday morning, the sth inst., the complainant missed 3d. from her pocket. At night the prisoner came in drunk, and the complainant accused her of taking the 3d. She said "I am sorry for it: I won't do it again." Mr. Silvers acquainted Detective-Sergeant Monaghan who brought the prisoner to the police station at mid- night.—The prisoner was sent to jail for a month.
"A LUCKY TRAVELLER."

- - At the Warrington Magistrates' Court on Thursday, before Alderman Sutton (chairman), Alderman Greenall, Capt. Ridgway, Major Pickmere, and Mr. James Fair- dough, Robert Wilson was charged with offering in pledge at Mr. Morton's pawnshop, on Saturday night a watch supposed to have been stolen. Mr. Hunt said the prisoner was from Manchester, and had given his name at the pawnbroker's as John Wilson and at the station as Robert Wilson. He had asked for ss. on the watch at Mr. Morton's, and as his answers to Mr. Morton's manager were suspicious he gave the man into custody. At the police station he said he found the watch on the road from Manchester and made other unsatisfactory statements. He had also in hispossession a pearl-hafted knife which he also said he had found in the same road.— Mr. Morton's manager and P.S. Berry having given evi- dence, the prisoner adhered to his statements, as to find- ing the articles.—The Chairman: You must have been a very lucky traveller.—The prisoner: Yes, it was very extraordinarv.—Major Pickmere : Worth while travelling on that road.—The Chairman: Better go again.—The Chief Constable said he :should detain the watch.—The prisoner was fined 20s. and costs; in default seven days' hard labour.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
• WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Aldermen Burgess, Greenall, and Wright Councillors James Fairclough,and Voisey, and Mr. John Geddes.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Francis Lea, Ship Canal labourer. and Mary Garrity, in Wellington-st., at half- past twelve that morning, Robert Disdale and Thomas Carleton, in Bold-st., at 1 20 that morning, Thomas Cowley, in Friar's Green, on the 26th ult.. and Elizabeth Leyland, Green-st., on the 26th ult., ss. each.—Winifred Hall, married woman, charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bank-st., on the 27th ult., was dismissed. BAD LANGUAGE.—Mary Ann Reynolds, for this offence in Mill Yard, Fennell-st., on the 27th ult., was fined is. A CYCLIST AT FAULT.-11enry Mooney, of 24, Glaze- brook-st., was charged with riding his bicycle through Sankey-st., on the night of the 27th ult„ without using bell or whistle.—The constable who proved the case said he collided with a man in Market-gate. The defendant had a whistle in his pocket.—Moorley said his bell was being repaired .—The Chairman said he was sl near home that he might have walked the distance instead of putting the public in jeopardy by not having his bell. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb) and Alderman Sutton. DRUNK AND DisoßnEßLT.—Henry Palmer, labourer, a native of Woolwich, drunk and disorderly in Fennell-se., on Saturday night, and John Garvin lodging-house keeper, Ship-yard, drunk and disorderly in that yard the same night, were fined ss. each.—James Green, an Irish labourer, drunk and disorderly in Brown-st. the same night, 10s.—Wm. Farrell, of Manchester. drunk and dis- orderly in Orford-st.,at 2.30 a.m. on Sunday also charged under a warrant with being drunk and disorderly on April 16th last, was discharged. DRUNK.—Patrick Dempsey, charged with being drank drunk in Mersey-st. on Sunday night, was dismissed. TITESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley (in the chair), Mr. E. M. Crosfield, and Alderman Wright. DEUNKENNESS.—MichaeI Maloney, drunk and dis- orderly, in Bridge-st., on the previous night, 55.; Jno. Tully, drunk and disorderly, in Horsemarket-st., on the previous night, ss. and Costs; Nicholas Loughlin and Edward Parry, drunk and disorderly. on Friars-green, the previous night, ss. each; Mary Rylands, drunk in Arpley-road, on the previous night, 55.; Martin Cal- laghan, drunk and disorderly, in Bank-st., that morning, ss.

AN UNLICENSED LODGING HOUSE.—Edward Walsh was charged with having kept a lodging-house in Percival's- fold, without its having been registered. Inspector Church said that when he visited the house there were six persons in it, including four lodgers, although there was only one living room and no through ventilation. Inspector Norman said the defendant had 'kept similar lodging-houses in other parts of the town, and seemed to set the Sanitary Committee at defiance. The house in Percival's-fold would, he thought, be scheduled as unfit for human habitation, and houses of that sort were cer- tainly not fit to keep lodgers in.—The Chairman: Simply nurseries for disease, I suppose P—lnspector Norman: That is just it.—A fine of 10s. and costs, in all 175., was imposed. AN UNNEUZZLED Dm—Joseph Kirkham was sum- moned for having allowed his dog to be at large un- muzzled on the 14th July, in Catherine-st. It was stated that the dog belonged to Kirkham's son, and the sum- mons was withdrawn.

ScHoot, CASES.—For neglecting to send their children regularly to school, the following parents were fined : Eliza Banner, Pierpoint-st., fined 55.; Thomas Brace- girdle, Edward-st. ; John Gorton Latchford, 55.;. Frank Lee, Froghall-lane, ss. ; John Mackie, Warburton-st., 55.; Joseph Owen, Oliver-st.' 55.; Richard Ridgway,Bewsey- road, 10s. (two cases) ; Thomas Rowlands, Leonard-st., 55.; and Joseph Wilcock, Greenall-st., ss.—These were the first school cases which had been heard since the. holidays. Mr. Riley prosecuted on behalf of the School Attendance Committee of the Corporation.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman 11-o Imes (chairman), Aid. Chandley, and Mr. J. Geddes.

NON-MAINTENANCE OF CHILDREN.—John -Leach, tailor, was charged by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Board of Guardians, with leaving four children chlrgeable to the Union. He had given himself up at Stockport, when drunk.—The defendant said he had given himself up be- cause he could not rest; as he had suffered so much remorse. The death of his wife had upset him and driven him to drink. His sister lived in Folly-lane, and her husband would be bound for him, if necessary, and he (the defendant) would pay by instalments what was due.—The case was adjourned till Friday, to allow the defendant's brother-in-law to be bound over for him, and the Bench offered to release him on bail amounting to 110.

DRUNK AND DISORDBRLY:—Martin Bliley was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C.'s Harrington, Turner, and Clough, on. the previous night. The detendant was drunk and using very bad language, when Harrington several times requested him to go away, and he refused. Some of his friends took him away, but he broke loose and used bad language again to Harrington. He took him into custody, and he be- came very rough. Constables Clough and Turner came to his assistance, and the prisoner broke the whistle of one of the officers, and they all three had a severe struggle with him. The defendant said P.C. Harrington struck him, and when he saw him going away quietly struck him again, and took him into custody, then drove him to be rough by twisting his wrists with the hand- cuffs. The defendant was fined ss. and costs for being drun k and disorderly, and 20s, and costs for the assaults. —James Banner, for being drunk and disorderly on Tuesday night, in Bridge-st., and assaulting P.C. Mea- cock, who bad to get the assistance of a young man to take him into custody, was lined ss. and costs in each case.—lsabella Banner, wife of the previous prisoner, charged with being drunk and disorderly in his company, on Tuesday night, and who had a child with her at the time, was discharged. DRUNK AND INDECENT.—Elizabeth Evans, drunk and indecent in Arpley-road, about midnight,on the 4th inst., was fined ss.

FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton, and Mr White. NON-MAINTENANCE OF CHILDREN.--JOhll Leach, was charged on remand with leaving his four children charge- able to the Union.—Mr. Shearer said the defendant's friends had agreed to pay the amount due; and asked the bench to adjourn the case a week to.allow him an oppor- tunity to take the children out of the Workhouse.—Alder- man Sutton adopted this course. WOMEN'S SQUABRLES.—Sarah Jarvis, wife of a Cor- poration labourer, and Margaret Kelly,both of Antrobus- st., charged each other with assault in the Ist inst. Kelly said she was in the room which she rented in Jarvis' house, and Jarvis came to her and asked for her rent, threatening to knock it out of her if she did not pay it, and hit her with a plate and a cup. Her husband pulled her out, and gave her. a " crack " in the face, and she screamed murder and struck complainant with the poker. Her husband put her out of the door and she said she would make complainant drink her blood, and knocked the door to pieces in trying to get in.— Jarvis said she asked Kelly for 4s. 6d., and she refused to pay. She told her to go, and she hit her, and used very bad language, and dashed a tin of water over her.Witne,ss put her out, and she smashed the door with a bucket. Lewis Jarvis corroborated his wife, and said Kelly was drunk.—Both women were bound over to keep the peace for six months, and or- dered to pay 3s. 6d. costs .—Mary Collins was charged with assaulting Margaret Cain, on Saturday last. The case was dismissed. The complainant caused some amusement by entering the box and stating that she wanted her case in which she had been summoned to be heard, but she was informed that there had been no sum- mons issued. Cain voluntarily entered the defeadant's box, and the case was heard, but dismissed. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Emma Howard, 41st ap- pearance, drunk and disorderly in Howard-st., the pre- vious night. Mr. Hunt said the conduct of the prisoner had for some time past been most disgraceful. She car- ried on with men in the open day.—She was sent to gaol for a month.—Bodelia Knockton and Mary France were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horsemar- ket-st., on Thursday afternoon, and Knockfon was also charged with using indecent language in Bank-st., on Wednesday. Knockton,who now made her 51st appear- ance, was sent to jail for a month for being drunk and disorderly, and for 14- days. for using bad language. France, who made her 18th appearance, was sent for a month's hard labour, and as she left the Court exclaimed to the constable who proved the case :—" Yes, I will month you, when I come out." She also observed that the magistrates might give them a quart before they went.

NON-FULFILMENT or SERVICE. —Annie Mahoney was charged by Ellen Oakes, fustian cutter, with refusing to perform her contract as her employee, And she claimed 12s. compensation.—She was ordered to pay 45., at the rate of is. a week and the costs.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. John Crosfield (chairman) and John White. FIGHTING.—Jane Smith and, Ruth Ashford, charged with fighting with each other on Saturday night, at Sankey Bridges, were ordered to pay costs. No LAMP ON HIS MACHINE.—Wm. Riddle was charged with riding a bicycle on the night of the 15th inst., at Great Sankey, without having his lamp lit. He was fined is. and costs,
ASLEEP ON HIS LURRY.-Arthur HougUtoß, for being asleep while in charge of his lurry in , Liverpool-road, Great Sankey, on the 10th ult., was :fined 2s. 6d. and costs. _
DRUNK.—Maria Simpson, drunk on :the highway at Sankey Bridges, on the 11th ult., was fined 103. and costs. _ _ . .

DISORDERLY CoN-Ducr.—Frederick Simpson' husband of the previous prisoner, was charged with being dis- orderly on Saturday night at Sankey Bridges. He struck his wife several times in the street. He was mulcted in the costs.

CARGES OF CRUELTY TO HOESES.—James Bilshaw and Ernest Simm, a boy, were charged with cruelty to a horse by working it while in an unfit state, on the 12th ult., at Southworth-with-Croft. He had been using the animal while suffering from a large wound, to draw a waggonette which was loaded with passengers. On be- ing prevented by a constable from using the animal further that day he had paid 10s. for the passengers to go home by other means. In consideration of this cir- cumstance, Bilshaw was only fined ss. and costs, and Sims, driver, was dismissed.—James Green was sum- moned for a like offence on Sunday afternoon, at the same place. His case was adjourned, on his application, till next Sessions, that he might bring a veterinary sur- geon as a witness. CHARGE OF THEET.—NO PROSECUTOR.—Benjamin Dig- num stood charged with stealing a hammer and a knife value 103., property of John Mann, of Haydock, but as the prosecutor had disappeared from the district, the case could not be proceeded with, and the prisoner was removed in custody.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. H. Wade Deacon.

BEGGING.—James McCann, of no fixed abode, was charged with begging. He said he had come from Ire- land to obtain work, but had been unsuccessful. Mr. Deacon pointed out that it was illegal to beg, and after advising him to again try and obtain work, discharged him.

DISORDERLY CONDUCT.—WiIIiam Mansell, of Warring- ton-road, a signalman employed by the Sheffield and Midland Railway Company, was found guilty of dis- orderly behaviour, and was fined 20s. including costs.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. A. Earle and Lieutenant- Colonel Gaskell. MISCELLANEOUS.—For drunkenness a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Mary Fyldes, Wm. Cousins, Margaret O'Neil, Nora Redmond, Austin Beesley, Ann Walsh, Harriett Cassidy, and Bridget Rigby. On charges of creating breaches of the peace, Margaret Brown, Sarah Barlow, and James Verdin were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months.— Thomas Conroy was fined 2s. 6d. and coats for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled. AssAuurs.—William Schumann of Bent-st.,was charged with assaulting R. Grant, a School BGard Attendance Officer. The Board had had great difficulty in getting the defendant's children to school and thadefendant had been fined 20 times in consequence. On the 28th ult. defendant met Grant in the street,and,without provoca- tion, struck him a violent blow on the head and threw him to the ground. Mr. Danby, the clerk, asked that an example should be made, and a fine of £l, and costs 16s. 6d., was imposed.—Thomag Brown, Walmsley-st., was charged with assaulting a boy named Frank Bradey. WARRINGTON 'V. BOLTON.—The first match of this an- nual fixture took place at Arpley, on Saturday, before a large attendance. The match was voted as almost a cer- taiuty for the homesters, but the uncertainty which is attached to the summer pastime was never more clearly demonstrated, for Bolton batting first put together 78— a not altogether formidable score—but Warrington, when they took up the detente, failed ingloriously, and a little over an hour sufficed for the whole side being dismissed for 52 runs. To explain the defeat is indeed puzzling, and -must be added to the many mysteries which occur during a season's campaign. Starting the batting, Bolton commenced with Stanley and Staton to the deliveries of Smith and Bell. Only two runs had been signalled when Bell dismissed Stanley in his second over, whilst with an additional couple, Podmore brought off a fine catch which settled Staten. Walker and Ellis played steadily for a time, but one of Smith's expresses was placed in the safe hands of Lee at slip, and the board read 16-3-7. With the two Bolton professionals associated, Ellis and Bolton, some short runs were scored, and the total was carried t 025, when Ellis played too late at one from Smith, the retiring batsman having made nine. Rushton adopted the same tactics as Ellis, and after several short runs had been added, Smith caught the new batsman napping, and making a pre- tence to bowl, Rushton stepped over the crease, and the bails were removed. Sutcliffe, who was speedily recog- nised as the International footballer, at once made mat- ters lively, and runs coming at a rapid pace Captain Adam relieved Bell. Bennett was well taken by Proud, whilst Williams was bowled with a trimmer. Pod- more effected a capital shy which accounted for Bashall, and Shepherd being bowled three runs later, the total read 57-9-2. With Whittle joining Sutcliffe, runs came at a rapid pace, especially from Smith, but when the total had reaohed 78, Whittle drove one from Bell which struck Sutcliffe hard in the uecit,and

CRICKET.

The Lancashire Eleven, says the "'Manchester Guar- dian," came very creditably, under Mr. Crosfield's leadership, out of the return match, with Yorkshire. The batting of the home side was good throughout, and the bowling remarkably so. It was a feather even in Wat- son's cap to beat George Ulyett so thoroughly as he did with a ball that broke across the wicket ; and the early loss of that formidable batsman, followed immediately by the downfall of Hall and Wardall, was a misfortune from which Yorkshire never recovered. Peel was dis- tinctly the hero of the match on the Yorkshire side. He bowled for an hour on Friday, and fielded splendidly at cover-point, and then kept up his wicket against all the assaults of the Lancashire bowlers until theeall of time. It was in stopping an exceedingly k hard hit from him that Mold hurt his right wrist so 'severely that he was not be able to play in the Essex match.

On Saturday also, when all the others except Wain- wright failed, Peel hit with great resolution, and we were glad to see that his fine performance was applauded as warmly by opponents as by his own side. On the Lancashire side, Briggs distinguished himself greatly. We have rarely seen him bowl with more com- mand of the ball either in "spin" or in. puzzling varia- tions of pace and pitch, whilst his fielding of his own bowling, and also at cover-point was of the highest pos- sible class. The Lancashire fielding-was very good, es- pecialty "in the countryrand Mr. Crosfield, Sugg, and Yates came in for special acknowledgment.

We said of,Mr. Crosfield long agethat he was worth playing for his fielding if he never got a run. Since that was written Mr. Crosfield has come back to his old form as to run-getting and fields as well as ever. Hunter kept wicket magnificently for the visitors, and the side fielded in a manner which enhances, the value of the victory over them, but they were a. beaten team after the first half-hour in their first innings. This is the second occasion on which Mr. Crosfield has captained the team in a first-class match. At Beckenham, last year he led them against Kent, and Lancashire won with great case.

div.head: M IS CELLA NE OUS.
div.p: M IS CELLA NE OUS.

On Monday the eighth annual race for the quarter- mile salt water championship of the world, came off at Southsea, under the laws of the Amateur Swimming Association, the event being the, chief item at the fifteenth annual bank holiday festival of the,Portsmouth Swimming Club. The course- .consisted of eight laps beeweett the clubs two stages. The weather proved un- fortunate, a high south-west wind causing. the sea to be very rough, and rain fell during the contest. All six who had entered put in an armarance, and a fairly good start was effected by Mr. H. H. Oliver,. the official starter, though Walter Brickett, captain of the Unity Swimming Club, .was the last at the dive. From the commencement there was but little doubt as to the result, as W. Evans, captain of the Swan Swimming Club, Man- chester,at once took a decided lead. He swam very powerfully with his left overhand stroke, and won easily in 7min. 15sec. He was theholder of the thirty guinea silver challenge cup, and as it has to be won three times consecutively to entitle to ownership, it will be his should he be again fortunate next year. At the end of the second lap Evans was leading by four yards, while W. J. Stratton (captain Zenhyr S.C.) was• second, and Andrew Dale (captain S.h..London &C.) third. At the half distance Dale was second to Evans,. Stratton third, Brickett fourth, A. E. Angell (Portsmouth, S.C.) fifth, and H. Aust (Unity S.C.) last. The result was Evans one, Stratton two (7min. 37sec,), Brickett third (7min. 4912-sec.) The second wins the gold medal and the third the silver medal. Dale was fourth, haila, yard behind Brickett.

While cyclists belonging to London and the home counties are disporting themselves aecording to annual custom at their camp among the Surrey hills, their brethren of the wheel in the Nerth.Country are haying a similarly pleasant time at Harrogate. The North of England Cyclists' Meet is now an institution fifteen years old, so That it can claim a seniority of no-less than eight years over that organized by the. Southern Counties Cycling Clubs, which is this year held near Dorking. At Harrogate no fewer than 400 riders took part in the grand march past, and when it is added that of the Cyclists' Touring Club, which • numbers something like 25,000 adherents, only 12 members were in the proces- sion some slight suggestion is afforded of the enormous number of wheelmen which this country can boast at the 'present day.

The English football team in South Africa, on Thurs- day, played a combined frfteen of King Williamstown and East London, the attendance:being the largest, and the weather, as on former occasions,. all that could be desired. It was hoped that with, the support of the East London men the local team .wouldbe able to give a better account of themselves, than on Tuesday, but although the colonials played a plucky game the result was never in doubt from the start, the visitors. winning the match bffive goals and one try to nil.

ATHIBMIC: The promoters of the Warrington: Football Club Sports had a rather unpleasant. experience of the uncertainties of Bank Holiday weather in, this pert of the country. On Monday morning the climatic conditions were so bad as to hold out little hope that the sports could be brought offwith anything like success;: but, fortunately, the un- expected sometimes happens, and it did in this case, the critical part of the afternoon being on the wholo pretty favourable, and as a consequence there was a fair aver- age gathering of spectators.

Though it could not besaid that tke meeting was very extensively patronised by athletes of the first rank, on the whole there was .a capital list of entries, and as the handicapping was wonderfully close in many cases there were some =Ring finishes. The playing members race is always a lively event, and on Monday, as usual, there was no end of interest centred in it, and when Webster. —getting into those prodigious strides of his which so often excite enthusiasm on the football field—won" in a..,1 canter," as the phrasegoes, there was some tall cheering* The win was clearly a popular one.

There is generally a crop of lively episodes in the shape of" spills, in bicycle races and there was just a suffi- cient share of these on Monday, though it is pleasant to record that none of the riders were seriously the worse for their tumbles,whatever might besaid of the machines. In the two miles handicap both Molyneux and Broad- head ,gave. samples of well-judged riding and the way in which.the latter ran into second, place was a treat to see_

Credit should certainly be given, to the Committee and others who had the organising and carrying out, of the sports in their hands, for everything seemed to run smoothly, and the whole affairpassed off in a satisfactory fashion.

SEARCHING INQUIRY. An ingnest was held on Saturday morning by Mr.W.T.Husband, deputy eoroner,at the White Hail, Inta,•Sankey-st., touching the death of Mr. Wm:. Lawless,.aged 49 years-, fishmonger and poulterer,. Corporation-stwon the SOth ult. Mr. Fowler, solici- tor,. appeared towatch the case on behalf of the re-- ' latives, and MI. Stowers attended on behalf of the Itnperial Union? Accident Assurance Co., London, in Which .Co. the deceased was insured fot .£l,ooot Thomas- Lawless, son of the deceased, -said, he lived with his father. He saw him on Sunday morn- ing the 19th ult., about lib o'clock, after he was brought home. Mr. Welding, oneof the witnesses;. said the deceased: had met with an accident in. Liverpool-road; and:witness had better call in a dos. tor as -he was very ill. Witness saw that he was ill. He complained of pains in his-head and back, and, said • he-had had aoaccident,. but did not say what sort of an. accident.. Witness sent for Dr. Spinke that mcrning, directly they, got the deceased to bed. • Witness was cut when the doctor came. His father was not so seriously ill as- to make witness stop:at home. He did not anticipate death. The deceased seemed a trifle better next day. He did not go to business as. usual, but went across the market to the White Hart Inn.. He was knocking about at home and outside as usual on Tuesday,but ' did not attend to business. He- complained about fearfulpainsin his -head, all the time from the time of his being brought in,. He did not tell him what had caused the pains. Witness-never heard anything more about. the accident until a gentleman asked him how his father was,and told himm. The deceased told witness on Sunday that he had hurt his head. On Wednesday he said his head felt very bad, and kept on complaining. Dr.. Spigks, called and saw him every day. He remarked that deceased ought , not to have been out on certain.day& Witness did not tell his father-that. Oh Tuesday by the doctor's advice, the deceased had a dtive with him and wit- ness's uncle. Peter Lawless.. On coming back he looked a trifle better. Next day,. witness went to Liverpool on business, and did not see deceased till about 1 o'clock when he was unconscious. Dr. Spinks was still attending him, He died at 12.5 p.m. on Thursday,the,3oth ult.. He-nine insured in the Imperial Union Accident Assurance Co., for £l,ooo.—By Mr. FoWler :. The •deceased died at his brother's, at the Corporatiou Inn,—By the Coroner: Witness's uncle told him that the deceased stayed there the previous night on account of the noise at home of people getting up, and. the. like.—By Dr. Stowers: There was, no other • reason known to witness for his doing so.—By the Coroner: Wit- ness occupied the same bedroomas the deceased at home, and had done so ever, since the death of the latter's wife, four months ago.—By Dr. Stowers: The deceased did not care to sleep inthe same room as his wife died in.—By the Jiiry :: Witness ,saw his father every day after the accident. He was a lot duller after it. The noise of the children an- noyed him, but did not before; Witness did not know what was ailing him. He had cause to think he was rather strange.. He never looked to see if there were any bruises. The- deceased was not able after the fall to look after the business. Wit- ness did it for him.

Benjamin Welding said he met MI% Lawless on Sunday the 19th ult, at 20 minutes to 10,Land walked with him through Penketh. When they got to the other side of Sankey Chapel he had a very heavy fall on the back of his head. Witness thought his umbrella geUing between his legs caused his fall. He was perfectly sober. Mr. Lea and witness raised him up, and, told the driver of a passing carriage to send a cab, .which he did. The fall stunned the deceased 'tremendously. .but he. was able to walk without assistance after he got over, the blow. A cab came up and they put him in. He said he felt very sick, and they called at the Bowling Green, and he vomited in the yard. Mr. Dutton, gave hies a drink of lime water, and witness brought him borne. He seemed a little better then, but very dull from, the stun. Wit- ness told Thomas Lawless to .send for a doctor as his father was dangerously hurt.—By Dr. Stowers: The de- ceased was sober, and showed /19, evidence of having taken alcohol that morning. Witness, afterwards ad- mitted to Dr. Stowers that he • did run to the Chapel House public-house andget the deceased some brandy and wet his lips with: it.—By a jpryma,n : Witness thought the deceased rather. screened his ailing. That would account for the son.not =liming: he was as bad as he really was. Thomas Lea, of Sankey Bridges, said be overtook Mr. Lawless and Mr. Dutton on the highway., and stopped to talk to them. The deceased's umbrella got betwixt his legs, and befell on to the back of his head. He lay un- conscious about ten minutes. Witness had known him for 40 years, and he looked as well that morning as he ever saw him. He was's, sober man gAnerally, and had no drink in witness's Rresence that morning; and he never saw him out of the way with drink. Joseph Massey, 12, Powys-st. Bank Quay, deposed to overtaking the deceased and M;:. Lea walking together, and to walking with them, about 200 yards. Witness further deposed to baing brought back after leaving them, and finding thetdeceased on his back unconscious, and that he had a bleeding cut on the back of his head. Peter I Jawless, the deceased', brother, landlord of the. Corporation Inn, deposed to the deceased dying at his house, wad to his having been attended by Dr. Spinks,- witness did not then., know what for. Dr. Spinas told him his brother would die„ but gave him no impression as to wl mat he would die.of. The deceased complained of pains in the head.—By the jury: Previous to the an cident the deceased was in good health, but after his wife's t leath was a little too low-spirited. The deceased came i nto his house on. Tuesday . between 12 and 11 p.m., a .nd complained of feeling very poorly, and had some r tort wine warm. Witness advised him to go home,. but he preferred to stay at the inn because he could be quiete r there.

- Dr. C. N. Spinks was- then examined. Hesaid he fired attetu led the deceased, after the accident, on 'Sunday the- 19th; about 1 p.m. He told him he had had a fall at Sank ey. He examined his head and found no markk or wow id on it. He had just heard for the first time about his having a cut on the head. It must have been a very small one. "He found that deceased was suffering from concussion of the brain,and prescribed accordingly.. He 'atte nded him night and morning daily until he died. He could not keep him in bed. As his case began to load( very serious, Dr. White was, at witness's request, caned in for a consultation, Death was caused by con- cussion of the brain followed by effusion, the result pro- bably of a fall.—By Dr. Stowers : He discovered nothing incompatible with death from natural causes. Wfthess never saw the deceasedworse for drink. He was reported to have been addicted to drink.—Dr. Stowers: De you think iais possible his habits in that respect may have altered.- since the death of his wife ?—Dr. Spinks It generally is so. but Ineversaw him drunk in my. life.— By the Coroner : Witness, had treated him for inebriety ' some five years ago, Ile-gave him some medicine four or five days before the accident, but it was not quite the same. Witness noticed no sign of intemperance on the Standay morning in.decessed. The Coroner then addressed the jury. He said the en- , quiry had lasted a deal longer than he thought was ' necassary, bua he was-aiprious to get to the bottom of the matter. The evidence undoubtedly showed that the deceased had had a falk but one witness said he saw a cubon deceased's head and the doctor said hedid not see one. It was these things that made one suspicioas of the case. The deceased's. son gave his evidence in rather a peculiar way. Perhaps it was unintentional,, but he said when the lather-get home Mr. Welding mentioned the word aceident„and his father mentioned the word accident ; and there was it appeared to him (the Coroner) too.much, stress laid on the word .accident. The deceased was, insured and this and one or two other things, had ,made-hirn determined to. get to. the bottom of this matter. The doctor, was, he thought,too anxious in his evitienceto. connect the death ,with the fall, and he (the eoroner).had pulled him up. What he meant to say was that death wascaused by some blow, or concus--1 sion of the brain, It was practically proved that thei deceased did have a fall. Dr. Stowers .requested him to 'tell the jury, as. be always did in. sucla cases, that they had nothing to do with questions of compensation, and: the InsuraaceCompany were tint in the slightest degree- bound by their verdict, although,of course the enquiry wouldno doubt aid them in coming to a decision. Dr. Stowers also-desired him to tell the jury that there had beenno.poot mortela examination, He (the Coroner) had) not thought this necessary. If the jury wished; of course they. could have one. The-jury, after about seven minutes' private delibera- tion,,returned a verdict that the deceased died trAmn the effects ca fall on Sunday the 19th ult.

div.head: FAMINE, IN INDIA.
div.p: FAMINE, IN INDIA.
PEOPLE VYING OF STARVATION.

Nfannes, THIIRSDA34.—The hopes hitherto entertained that famine would be averted in the districts of Chingle- put and North Arca have now been almost abandoned. The heat there is unprecedented, and rains have been insufficient to save the crops. The state of things in Wandiwash, Maderpank, and Calastry, in particular, is very distressing.. Several authenticated instances are already reported of deaths from starvation among vill- agers, who, in. some places, are reduced to eating aloes. Cattle are dying in large numbers for want of food anti water, although the forest reserves have been throwni open, for grazing.
