div.head: RAINFORD ATHLETIC FESTIVAL
div.p: RAINFORD ATHLETIC FESTIVAL

the 14th annual festival under the ausnices of I the Rainford Athletic Society took place in a field lent for the occasion by Mrs. J. Birchall, at Rain- ford, near St. Helens, on Tuesday afternoon. Un- fortunately rain fell in heavy showers, and con- siderably interfered with the comfort of both competitors and spectators. :Notwithstanding the inclemency of the weather, about 3,000 petsons assembled to witness the contests. Prizes to the value of .f.. 52 were offered and a very strong entry was received. The officials were as fullows : Judges Messrs. E. Sephton, B. Smith, J. Pilkington, and o:Whalley ; handicapper and timekeeper, Mr. R. P. Ellis; referee, Mr. T. Moncrieff ; starter, Mr. P. Boardman; secretary, Mr. John Ball; treasurer, Mr. B. Smith ; and assistant secretary, Mr. A.Rigby. Results- -300 YARDS BOYS' RACE.-1, J. Cowley (421 yards) ;2, J. Dutton (30) ; 3, J. Hayes (52i.) MILE BICYCLE RACE (Local.)-1, J. A protest was laid against Kennedy, the allegation being that he was an American professional. The point will be decided by the committee of the Amateur Athletic Association, and the prizes withheld. Only the three placed men completed the distance, and the race was won easily by Swift. Time, 7mins. 56sec5. OPEN 100 YARDS MAIDEN RACE.-1, F. Bailey, Liver- pool (10 yards start) ; 2, R. div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.

ANNU.L ATHLETIC FESTIVAL. The seventy annual athletic festival of the Warrington Football Club was held in the football field, Wilderspool Causeway, on Monday afternoon. The weather was most unpropitious during the morning, rain falling heavily, and et the time for the commencement of the sports it was still descending,although there were alterna- tions of sunshine which were cheering to the hearts ' of those who desired the, success ot the festival. Notwithstanding the uncertainty of the elementary conditions, there were soon after the sports com- menggd between 2,500 and 3,000 persons present. It was ansidered by some that probably the rain of the morning had really conduced to this result, because a large number had been deterred by it from taking trips abroad, and then as the weather improved they made up their minds to go to the sports. As the afternoon advanced, the heavens cleared, and the chief part of the proceedings passed off under the brightest atmospheric aspects. The entries were about as numerous as usual, and the merit of the various competitions was fully up to the standard of former years. In consequence of the rain the ground was not in quite such a favourable condition as could have been desired, and an unusual number of falls was the result. The betting men mustered in force outside the ring, and near the entrance end of the field, a most animated spectacle was presented partaking strongly of the obiracteristics of similar scenes to be witnessed at horse races. By the kind permission of the officers the band of the Ist Volunteer Battalion (P.W.V.) South Lancashire Regiment, was in attendance, and enhanced the pleasureableness of the occasionyvith the performance of various choice military and other airs. The officials were as follows :—Clerk of the'course, Mr. T. Pemberton; starter, Mr. James Walsh ; judges, Messrs. W. Tinsley, W. Pierpoint, J. Evans, and H. Ashton; committee, Messrs. C. It. Adamson, W. Dillon, W. Ilewitt, J. W. Evans, W. Speakman, T. Bowers, W. Antrobus,lT. Smith, T. Barnes, sen., T. Barnes, jun., George Smith. John Holmes, T. Davies. T. Lally, and John Boyle ; handicapper and referee, Mr. T. Sutton, representa- tive of the " Athletic News " ; hon. treasurer, Mr. T. Pemberton ; lion, secretary, Mr. J. E. Warren. The following were the events :- 220 YARDS' PLAYING MEMBERS' RACE.—lst prize, cruet stand • 2nd, kettle and stand; 3rd, beer jug ; 4th, flask. Ist heat 1„ H. Webster ; 2, F. Heesomi 2nd heat: 1, J. T. Massey ;2, J. Holmes. 3rd heat: 1, W. Antrobus ; a, Fair. Turner. Final: 1, H. Webster; 2, ; J. T. Massey ;3, F. Heesom 4, W. Antrobus. This event excited probably more interest than any other in the course of the afternoon. A number of well-known local fostballers, each of whom had his particular following, took part, and the excitement towards the .closewas great. div.head: SENTENCE bF DEATH.
div.p: SENTENCE bF DEATH.

At the Winchester Assizes, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Cave, Edward Henry Fawcett was tried for the wilful murder of his wife at Port,sea, on the 4th April last. The parties were married 18 years ago, when pri- soner was a stoker in the Navy. Four children were born, but three died, the survivor being only four years of age. When living at Greenwich the parties quarrel- led, and the prisoner was bound over to keep the peace. They then separated, Mrs. Fawcett going to Portsea with her child. Prisoner went there and shot her with a revolver. Prisoner admitted the crime, and was sen- tenced to death.

div.head: TWO PERSONS BURNED TO DEATH IN
div.p: TWO PERSONS BURNED TO DEATH IN
LONDON.

A fire, resulting in the loss of two lives, occurred at a quarter to three o'clock on Saturday morning at 107, Upper North-st., Poplar, on the premises.of Mr. B. Bigg, oil and colourman. For a time the ground floor was like a furnace,and the inflammable materials contained in the place were burning with the greatest strength. In the the course of half-an-hour, however, the fire was sub- dued and effectually prevented from spreading to the adjoining premises, and directly the place had sufficiently cooled, the firemen entered and found the terribly charred remains of the occupant, Mr. Benjamin Bigg. Proceed- ceeding to the wreck of another room, the fireman found the dead of Miss Bigg, who had evidently died from suffocation.

div.head: SWISS REPUBLIC.
div.p: THE SWISS REPUBLIC.
600 YEARS OLD.

The Berne celebration of the sixth centenary of the establishment of the Swiss Confederation was ushered in at -five o'clock on Saturday morning by a salvo of artillery, and an hour later the various bands, massed in the chief square of the town, performed the Swiss National Anthem. At half-past eight low mass was cele- brated in the Church of St. Martin, and a brief address on the event of the day was delivered in presence of the delegates from the various cantons and cities 'there assembled. The chief event of the day was the grand historical procession, which started from the Town Hall at one o'clock for the Place de Fête, and comprised various picturesque groups in costumes illustrative of the social and industrial life of Switzerland from the 12th to the 18th centuries. At six o'clock a grand banquet was given to the can- tonal delegates, and in the evening the town and en- virons Ns, ere beautifully illuminated, while there were displays of fireworks and bonfires on the surrounding. heights. Those present at the festivities included the Swiss Ministers in Paris and Rome, the Charge d'Affaires in London, and the whole of the diplomatic body in Berne.

div.head: RAILWAY PORTER CRUSHED TO
div.p: A RAILWAY PORTER CRUSHED TO
DEATH AT WARRINGTON.

On Tuesday morning, Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy- coroner, held an inquest at the 'White Hart Inn, Sankey-St., as to the cause of the death of William Buckley, aged 24 years,who was killed, on Saturday afternoon, in the warehouse at the Central Hallway Station. Mr. F. Simpson, railway police superin- tendent, represented the C.L.C. The first witness called, was Peter Buckley, of Longford-st., who said the deceased was his son,and hao been employed on the Cheshire Lines as a goods porter for about four months. He was slightly deaf in one ear. Samuel Storey, 160, Orford-lane, said he was a warehouse- man. On Saturday afternoon deceased was sheeting up a wagon, he being at the top corner and witness at the bottom corner. Both had their backs to the engines. Witness heard a top lot of wagons clanging, , and on lifting: a heavy screen looked round and saw deceased being crlished between buffers. He could not say whose fault it was. There were distinct orders not to go between buffers. Witness did not hear any warning that the train was backing down. Peter Knight, a foreman shunter, said he was on duty at 4.15 p.m. on Saturday afternoon. The pilot engine whistled twice, and then backed down to- wards the wagon. Witness looked but did not see any. one, as deceased must have been on the other side. There were no instructions to look at both sides of the wagons. In reply to the jury, witness said the usual whistles and shouts were given. John Wood, inspector, said he was at the warehouse and saw the previous witness standing at the door and shout. He had warned the deceased and other men not to go between the buffers; bz, had, in fact, gone so far as to discharge several men who had disobeyed his instructions. The Coroner suggested that a bell might be provided to warn people in shunting. He also mentioned that he should have to leave by an early train to attend an inquest at Cuerdley. After some conversation it was decided to adjourn the inquest for a week. The Coroner intimated that he would consider the advisability of fining two men who had been called for the jury but had no attended.

div.head: LIVERPOOL MURDER
div.p: THE LIVERPOOL MURDER

At the Liverpool Assizes on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Smith, the trial of John Conway, the delegate of the Sailors' and Firemen's Union, for the murder of the boy Nicholas Martin at the premises in Stanhope-st.' used as branch offices of the Union, was resumed and concluded. Mr. Hopwood, Q.C., briefly summed up for the prosecution, and Mr. Segar addressed the jury for the defence, contending that the evidence, purely cir- cumstantial, failed to amount to proof that the prisoner had committed the murder. In summing-up, his Lord- ship said he felt sure, from the evidence, the jury would see without doubt that a wicked murder had been com- mitted. While they had every wish that the murderer should be detected, they must be careful as to who they found guilty of the crime. No motive had been assigned for the crime, but if the evidence led them to the con- clusion without doubt that the prisoner committed the 'murder it was not necessary that they should fathom the motive. The prisoner had previously borne a good character, and hadserved his country in the Army, and should there be any ds;)ubt as to the prosecution having made out a case, it was their duty to acquit him. Before the jury retired to consider the verdict, the Clerk of Assize read a statement which had been prepared by the prisoner, and in this he asserted his innocence, and repeated the story of having met a foreign sailor who requested him to bay the bag and other articles for him; that as the sailor did not call for them, he took a cab and drove to the pier-head and delivered over the bag and its contents to a sailor, who gave him a sovereign for his trouble. The prisoner also gave an account of his move- ments between the Saturday and Tuesday, with a view of showing that he could not have committed the mur- der. Aster an absence of about 25 minutes, the jury returned with a verdict of guilty, and the judge then, Eater putting on the black cap, pronounced sentence of death in the usual manner.

John Conway has written to Mr. Nicholson, district secretary of the Sailors' and Firemen's Union, earnestly requesting the promotion of a petition for a reprieve. Conway earnestly declares his innocence. Thursday, the 20th inst., has been fixed for his execution.
THE MURDER OF A GIRL AT LEEDS,
TRIAL OF THE SON.

The trial of Turner for themurder of a little girl at Horsforth was brought to a conclusion at Leeds Assizes on Saturday evening. Mrs. Turner, the mother of the prisoner, was again called and examined by the Judge with the view of eliciting some further disclosures with regard to the horrible crime. Mr. Mellor made such defence as was possible on the theory that Turner was not the real criminal but had got into trouble by shel- tering the man who committed the crime. The Jury found the prisoner guilty, and Mr. Justice Grantham, in sentencing him to death, said that if he had been dis- covered by the people of Horsforth they would have lynched him. Had Those people seen the body of the poor child, "not all the power of the law or the police could ever have prevented them from tearing him limb from limb." At the close of the sentence the people in the gallery applauded loudly, and in the street the learned Judge was cheered vociferously by a great crowd.

div.head: MRS. TURNER'S SENTENCE REDUCED
div.p: MRS. TURNER'S SENTENCE REDUCED

At the Leeds Assizes, on Monday, Mr. Justice Grant- ham intimated that he had given orders to have Mrs. Turner's sentence reduced from penal servitude for life to one of 12 months' imprisonment. The Judge address- ing Mr. and Mrs. Joy and Mrs. Cotterill said :—I postponed until to-day the announcement to you of the reward I intended for you, and that reward is the hope of the res- toration to you in a comparatively short period of time of the mother and friend whose conduct had necessitated at the time the passing upon her of such a severe sentence. Although sentences of penal servitude for life are rarely carried out if subsequent good conduct justifies any re- mission, yet her age made it unlikely that she would oe restored to you, or that any possible remission would be of much service to her. What better reward could I therefore give you for your goo sl conduct than that of that life which had practically t 6 be taken from you ? I 4have much pleasure, Mrs. Joy, in telling you that I have given orders to have your mother's sentence reduced to one of 12 months' imprisdnment.—This announcement was received with evident gratitude by those to whom it was specially addressed and with much satisfaction by all in court.
The morning of Tuesday, the 18th inst., has been fixed for the execution of -Turner, the Horsforth mur- derer.

div.head: THEFT OF TOOLS.
div.p: THEFT OF TOOLS.

On Monday morning at the Newton Town Irall before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie and T. D. Grimke-, Drayton, Benjamin Digman of no fixed address,was brought up on a charge of stealing a slater's ham- mer and knife, on Saturday afternoon, the property of George Man. It appeared from the evidence of P.C. Cameron, that Mann met the prisoner in St. Helens, and they journeyed together by train to Haydock, the former with the intention of going to Bolton and the latter to Leigh. They both lay down on the siae of Evans's private line from Haydock to Earlestown, and Mann fell asleep, having the bag con- taining the tools by his side. When he awoke, the pri- soner had gone, and the bag also was missing. Mann gave information to tho police. and P.C. Cameron pro- ceeded to Earlestown station where he saw the prisoner !taking a ticket for Leigh, and the bag was then in his possession. Cameron arrested him and took him to the poiice station where he charged him with stealing the . toOlz, but he made no reply. The owner of the tools aid Act appear to prosecute, and prisoner was remanded •.to the. Petty Sessions at Warrington on Wednesday.

div.head: ROBERT FOULKES.
div.p: ROBERT FOULKES.
MI?. W. S. CAINE AND RELIGIOUS WORK.

Sir,—" Churches are mere places of Business." Mr. W. S. Caine, the eccentric but honest politician, a Bap- tist, but not a bigot, has been spending some of his leisure in examining various kinds of religious work in London. And- this in what he learnt :—" Many large Nonconformist Churches' are mere places of business for the purpose of securing an income to the minister. Hardly any of them are doing any aggressive work. They are absorbed in their own little affairs, and doing nothing to fight the devil all over London." Tnis des- cription of pewed chapels is an exact description of pewed churches. These are carried on principally to secure an income for the minister, and, as the late Arch- bishop of York, Dr. Maguee, once said: "They are conducted on commercial principles:" As they are monopolised by the tenants, "aggressive work" is im- possible, and their ministrations being principally for themselves and their narrow circle, they do little to con- tend against" the world, the flesh and the devil." Mr. Caine certainly adds that the Church is doing more than any other body for the poor and the sinful, but this, we contend, is mainly accomplished by her free and open places of worship.—Yours, &c., MONTHLY PAPER. THE BOROUGH ACCOUNTS : LONGFORD MANURE WORKS.

Sir,—A few facts now and then gleaned from the Borough Accounts recently issued, may not be without interest to some of your readers who have not an oppor- tunity of making tkemselves acquainted with the Trea- surer's statements. CANDIDATES FOR RELIEVING OFFICERSHIP. Sir,—Permit me to explain through your paper, for the information of, and in fairness to, all candidates for the vacant office of relieving officer, that, although prohibited from a personal canvass of the Guardians, each candidate is at liberty, if he desires, to send by post to each Guardian a printed copy of his application and testimonials, in addition to the one to be sent to me. —Yours, &c., J. C. SI7TTON. Warrington, August Stlir 1891,

div.head: ESTABLISHED CHURCH.
div.p: THE ESTABLISHED CHURCH.

Sir,—The Marquis of Salisbury in his recent speech at the banquet at St. James Hall said; "In Wales and Scotland we must fight with our utmost vigour to main- tain the Established Church of the country. But unless I am deceived, over the whole of England the Established Church,has,during the last five years,gained considerably in power and removed to a longer distance the epoch when her existence will be the object of sustained attack." I differ from his lordship, and consider the ep!scopal appointments he has made to be one of the chief causes which will hurry on disestablishment. Take Chester, Dr. Jayne in sound theology appears alto- gether at sea; read his statement at confirmation abOut bringing the gift of the Holy Spirit; his objection to the Scriptural Evening Communion; his sympathy with Bishop King; his elevating the teaching of the Prayer Book above the Bible; his sympathy for young students from the Ritualistic School at Leeds; and his unwillingness to carry out his ordination vow, "to be ready to banish and drive away all false doctrine and erroneous teaching." Archbishop Maclagan, Dr. Gott and others are all more or less Romanizers. Then the Bishop of London with his veto, a power over any complaint of the laity which would not be tolerated in any other Christian commu- nity. July 27th, 1891.
APPALLING RAILWAY DIS- ASTER IN AMERICA.
COLLISION BETWEEN A LUGGAGE AND A PASSENGER TRAIN. '
TWELVE LIVES LOSS AND NINETEEN PERSONS INJURED.

NEW YORK, THIIRSDAY.—Another terrible railway acci- dent, resulting in the loss of twelve 4ives, occurred this morning near Savannah, State of New York,on the Lake Shore line. The morning was foggy in the vicinity of the disaster, and a flagman was told off to hand- signal the traffic,especially to keep back the west-bound night passenger train. He had set the signals against the passenger train, which, however, passed them. On the track right ahead there was a heavy goods train, which had previously broken apart, owing to a coupling iron snapping. The men in charge of the goods train were coupling up again after the mishap when the pass- enger train dashed into the trucks with terrific force and appalling results. The impact of the collision may be estimated from the fact that twelve goods trucks and several passenger cars were smashed and piled up into almost one great heap. The passenger locomotive turned over, and the embers from its furnaces soon set the wreckage on fire. The cries of the injured passengers buried beneath the wreckage were from the first most distressing, but they became louder and more agonising when the smell of the burning woodwork and the crack- ling of the flames notified them of this additional horror of fire. Fortunately, there was plenty of help at hand, as the passengers in the rear cars had escaped with only a shaking, and they soon set to work to rescue their more unfortunate fellow-travellers. It was soon dis- covered that not a soul remained alive in the smoking car next to the engine and tender of the passenger train and attention was concentrated upon the injured people in the other wrecked carriages. The absorb- ing intent was to extricate all the living creatures be-fore the flames could reach them, and this, thanks to the pluck and tenacity of passengers and rail- way employees alike, was happily accomplish:.d. Mcst of the bodies also were recovered before they had been much burned. Of the twelve killed, one was the fireman on the passenger locomotive,and the remain- ing eleven were all Italians, who were in the first smok- ing car. Eleven Italians and eight Americans were ex- tricated, seriously injured, from the next two wrecked cars. The wounds were roughly attended to on the spot, and they were then sent on to Syracuse for skilled treat- ment.

Meanwhile, the flames had spread so fiercely that the attempts to extinguish them were abandoned. The fire burnt itself out. All the passenger cars, except the three rear sleepers, were entirely destroyed by fire, and no fewer that twelve goods trucks were demolished. The unfortunate Italians were all working-men, on their way to a job in connection with the tunnel now in course of construction near Niagaira Falls.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
HOLIDAY VISITORS TO EASTHAM.

There was an enormous holiday traffic on the Man- chester Ship Canal, on Monday. Notwithstanding the broken weather many thousands of excursionists visited the Eastham and Ellesmere Port section, and took ad- vantage of the presence of two steamers to have a sail along that finished part of the undertaking. The steamers plying on the canal were the Knight of the Cross, and the St. Mawe's Castle, and on each trip they were crowded to their utmost capacity. Everything passed off without the slightest hitch. Mr. Marshall Stevens was on the spot during the day.

div.head: NEW DIRECTORS
div.p: NEW DIRECTORS

The Special Comn:-littee-Cit-h-e-eo-in-Oration re the Man- chester Ship Canal have resolved to recommend the Mayor, Aldermen Sir John Harwooi, Walton Smith, and Chesters Thompson, and Councillor Southern for nomin- ation by the City Council as representatives of the Cor- poration on the Ship Canal directorate.

div.head: FRIENDLY SOCIETY AGENTS ON THE CANAL.
div.p: FRIENDLY SOCIETY AGENTS ON THE CANAL.

On Thursday about 200 members belonging to the Agents and Collectors' Union of the Royal Liver Friendly Society visited the Ship Canal, on the occasion of their annual outing. They proceeded in different detachments on the St. Mawes Castle to Ellesmere Port and back, after which they partook of a sumptuous repast at the Eastham Hotel. A special boat was chartered to bring the excursionists back to Liverpool, which they reached shottly after eleven, all highly gratified with their day in the country. The members present were from all parts of the United Kingdom.

div.head: VISIT OF THE IVIA.NCHESTER COAPORATION.
div.p: VISIT OF THE IVIA.NCHESTER COAPORATION.

On Thursday the Manchester Corporation made their first official visit to the Manchester Ship Canal, of which they are now practically part owners. The party num- bered between 50 and 100, and included a large number of the directorate of the Canal Company and chief offi- cials. The visitors arrived in Liverpool during the fore- noon from Manchester, and embarked at the Landing- stage on board the Earl of Ellesmere, which plies regu- larly between Liverpool and Ellesmere Port. Among the chief personages present were the Mayor of Manchester and Sir Joseph Lee, deputy chairman of the Canal Com- pany. The Earl of Ellesmere steamed straight into the canal locks, without calling at Eastarn, the tide at the time being sufficiently high to admit of a passage through the narrow sandstone channel leading into .the canal. The party landed at Ellesmere Port, where a saloon carriage was in waiting on the contractors' line. In this they were conveyed by the Eastham huts to the main line of the London and North-Western system; thence on to the Canal Company's siding, and back by the usual detour to the contractors' main lines. The Ince section was then examined in some detail the scene of the recent catastrophe and the progress of the works being pointed out. The official visit was afterwards pro- longed to thesubsequent sections seriatins to the ter- mination of the canal at Salford. ACCIDENT TO A LABOURER.

On Saturday night a Ship Canal labourer Climbed over the fencing of the canal at Thelwall, and tumbled down into the cutting.. He was at once conveyed to the hos- pital, where his injuries were attended to. They were, however, found to be se slight that the man was dis- charged from the hospital next day.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
RANK HOLIDAY.

Bank Holiday was observed at Penketh in a very quiet manner. The new cabinet and tanning works were open as usual, as well as most of the shops in the village. A con.srderable number of the male sex journeyed to Warrington to see the sports in con- nection with the Football Club. About 945 in the evening a storm of great violence passed over the village, lasting several hours. On Tuesday morning the low-lying parts of the roads were flooded to a considerable depth. FOUNDATION STONE LAYING.

On Monday afternoon, the re-laying of the foun- dation stone of the Wesleyan Chapel took place. Owing to the unfavourable state of the weather, there was only a small number of the congregation present. Prior to laying the stone, a short service, conducted by the Rev. John Gunnell, was held in the school-room. Mr. R. Garnett gave a brief his- tory of the advance of Wesleyanisn2 in Penketh, and referred to the old chapel which was built at the corner of Stock'-lane in 1818. After a time the congregation became too large for this chapel, and the present chapel was built in 1861 from plans prepared by the late Mr. Wm. Winn, architect. It was enlarged in 187 D; and the additional accommo- dation then provided has sufficed up to the present time, but it had now become necessary to again enlarge it. Mr. R. Cook and the Rev. John Gunnell then addressed the meeting. As the weather was now found to have cleared up somewhat, everyone proceeded to the chapel, where the foundation stone was successfully laid by Mr. R. Garnett. WEDDING PRESENT AT SANKEY BRIDGES.

An interesting ceremony was performed last Saturday evening at the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel. Mr. Thomas Brough, who has recently been married, was presented with a beautiful marble timepiece, in recognition of his long ser- vices as organist to the chapel. The proceedings commenced at six o'clock, when about 75 persons sat down to tea in the schoolroom. They after- wards adjourned to the chapel, where a public meeting was held, Mr. Summersgill acting as chair- man. The meeting being opened, Mr.. Richardson sang "Comfort ye," from the " Meesiah " very effectually. Mr. Summersgill then congratulated Mr. Brough on his marriage, and made a very humorous speech on clocks. The Rev. H. Waterworth also spoke. Mr. Summersgill then called upon Mr. Blythe to make the present- ation. Mr. Blythe, in presenting the timepiece,said that since Mr. Brough had been the organist the singing had greatly improved. He hoped that he would have a long and happy married life. Mr. T. Brouga, in reply, said he was only too willing to do what be could for the chapel. He thanked them with all his heart for the beautiful present they had given him. After this a solo by Miss Brough, "The Better Land," and by Mr. Richardson,_ " There is a green hill, far away," were sung, and addresses were delivered by Messrs. Summerfield, Entwistle, Corradine, George, C.George, Woolley, and Lawton. A vote of thanks to Mr. Summersgill, Mr. Richard- son, and Miss Brough brought the meeting to a close.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDA.Y, AUGUST 8, 1891.
CHEMICAL WORKERS DEMONSTRATION AT WIDNES. SPEECH OF MR. TOM MANN.

There was a labour demonstration of some magni- tude took 'place at Widnes, on Saturday, in con- nection with the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union of Great Britain and Ireland, a public meeting being held in ,he Drill Hall, after the mem- bers of the union, carrying Their banner, and headed by band, had paraded the prin- ipal streets. At the meet-

•;ng the chair was occupied by Mr. r. - ._iresident of the union, who was accompanied by Mr. Tom Mann, of the London Dockers Union and a member of the Labour Com- mission, and by Mr. T. Healey, president of the Widnes branch of the organisation. The Chairman, referring to the threatened re- duction of wages in the chemical yards of St.Helens, said that the union was desirous of approaching the question in a moderate, reasonable, and conciliatory spirit. He knew what a strike and the attendant suffering meant, and a strike was the very last thing he would think of resorting to. But if one was to take place at all, it must not be a strike in any particular yards affected, but it must be a strike all along the line. (Cheers.) If the reduction had been attempted twelve months ago in any of the yards they could easily have fought the matter single-handed, but now, if the works in St. Helens were stopped, the certainty was that the chemical syndicate would look to Widnes for increased pro- duction to meet the demands made upon them. Thus they would suffer in St. Helens, without seriously affecting those whom they were figh ting—the chem- cal and copper masters. It would not be, however, i until all negotiations had failed, and they were driven to it, that they would take up the matter in a vigorous fashion. The responsibility for the threatened reduction really rested with the men who held aloof from the union,for up to last Christ- mas, when a majority of the men were :combined, there were no thoughts of a reduction. The proposal was only made now that the men were weaker. (Cheers.)

Mr. Tom Mann, who held the attention of the meeting tor an hour and a half, made a speech on the labour prob- lem. Having spoken of reports that had reached him o.c. the hard conditions under which the chemical workers laboured, he said that he had made it his business to in- quire into the accuracy or otherwise of the reports. He found that the men had to work under conditions that were very brutalising, that tendei to take a great deal of their manhood out of them, and, in his opinion, the amount of wages they received was really insufficient, considering the serious nature of their employment. i These engaged n chemical works were employed at labour than which there was nothing more poisonous or more trying, and when he learned that the newly-formed syndicate had determined upon reducing wages, he thought that now it would be seen whether there was any real unionism in the men or not. He did not personally object to combinations of the masters, as he would rather deal with an organised body than a harum-scarum lot of employers, who could not be pinned down to any definite line of action. They must always remember that the real fighting out of the industrial problem that was now agitating the world must be done intellectually and not physically, and that it was the duty of them all to try and settle all difficulties by discussion and negotia- tion, and not by strike or lock-out. (Cheers.) It was necessary for him to emphasise that, in order that they should not be under the impression that he was there to advocate a strike. He had come to dissuade them from doing anything rash,to ask them to be careful ,and if thej- could possibly help it, not to allow the employers to draw them out. Above all things they must avoid a cessation of labour. He feared that, according to the intention of the syndicate, there would, if it was carried out, boa reduction equal to one-third of the wages of the men, although the selling price of the manufactured article had gone up considerably during the time the present rate of wages had been paid. It seemed utterly preposterous that any syndicate should act in the manner reported. They were living in a country were trades unionism was net a new thing. As a result of clearheadedness in the first place and dogged pertinacity following it up the men of Lancashire had succeeded in wresting from the employers reductions of working hours, increased pay, better conditions of work, and had been able to meet their employers' officials with their own officials. They had driven the masters to organise , also, and now, as in the case of the textile trade of ' Lancashire, they were able to settle disputes by arbitra- tion in an amicable manner. He was not there to beg of any man to join the union, but he would ask them had they observed the great labour movement that had been rolling along for years past, This labour war would not last for ever. Either one party or the other would come right side up, and it would be the fault of the labour party if they were not found right side up. His trades unionism thought it possible, by sound policy, to ultim- ately completely banish poverty from the land. (Cheers.) He believed that there was no necessity to have any man, woman, or child in this country short of the ordinary requisites of human existence. He believed that it was possible with an effectve industrial organisation to have a state of society where there should be work for all, and overwork for none—(cheers)--where the workers would recognise that wealth did not consist of money, which was only a means of exchange, but in food, clothing, furnitzue, houseroom, and other commodities. He argued that with proper organisation it was possible to ' have enough for all,and traced the present state of things to the sectional organisations of industry, which net only fought against the workers, but against their own class, competing with each other instead of combining. The parliamentary institutions of this country should tie controlled by the wealth producers, and not by capitalists, who legislated in their own interests instead of in the interests of the worker. The same was true with regard to municipal institu- tions. Let them away with politics, A plague on both political parties who each in turn gulled the labouring class. At one time the Tories enjoyed the good things of the world ; at another the Liberals en- joyed those good things ; but the chemical workers were always at the grindstone, enjoying nothing but—bleach- ing powder. (Cheers.) If they were to work out their salvation they must give up the tweedledurn and twee- dledee of Liberal's and Tories, and reckon them as "six of one and half-a-dozen of the other. 'They must recog- nise none but these who were prepared to try and un- derstand the labour movement, and work • for the possi- bility of every human creature having sufficient of the necessaries of life, and having leisure enough to enable them to live lives worthy of men and women. Widnes, it was expected, would soon be incorpmated. He ex- horted them not to allow the capitalists to monopolise the seats on the New Town Council. (Cheers. Votes of thanks brought the proceedings to a close. MEETING ON SUNDAY AT ST. HELENS.

Under the auspices of the Chemical and Copper Workers Union of Great Britain and Ireland a demonstration was held at St. Helens on Sunday afternoon. About three o'clock a procession was formed at the British, Lion, Raven-st., and, headed by the banner of the union and the Rbughdales Brass Band, the members proceeded through the principal streets of the town and reached the Town Hall shortly after 3.30. At the meeting Mr. P. J. King, president of the union, occupied the chair, and was supported by Mr. Tom Mann, president of the Dockers' Union of London, and a member of the Royal Commission on Labour, Councillor J. P. Mearns. Me. H. L. Riley, and others.—Councillor J. P. Mearns moved the following resolution :—" That we, the chemical and copper workers of St. Helens and district resolVe to strengthen the hands of the union by becoming and remaining faithful members and so assisting in opposing the unjust demands of the employers and generally to benefit the union.—Mr. H. L. Riley seconded it, and Mr. Tom Mann supported it in a speech similar to that de- livered by him at Widnes on Saturday and a report of which appears elsewhere. The customary votes of thanks closed the proceedings.
THE NEW CHURCH FOR SUTTON.
FOUNDATION STONE LAYING.

On Tuesday afternoon Miss Pilkington, daughter of Mr. William Pilkington. J.P., D.L., of Roby, laid the foundation stone of a new church, to be dedi- cated to "All Saints," in the parish of St. Nicholas, Sutton, St. Helens. Mr. William Pilkington is the lord of the manor, and his generous disposition has been manifested by a gift of the site, which adjoins the National Schools in Ellarnsbridge-road, supplemented with a donation of £l,OOO. The ceremony was an- nounced to be performed by Mrs. Pilkington, but in her regrettable absence through indisposition Miss Pilkington formally laid the stone. Nothwithstand- ing the very heavy rain immediately preceding the interesting event, there was a very large attendance of the parishioners and friends. The new edifice is being erected at a cost of about £6,800, and towards this amount the sum of £4,560 has bee' raised. The chief contributors have been Mr. William Pilkington, the site and £l,OOO ; Mrs. Whyatt (Bold Hall,) £6OO ; Mr. William Blinkhorn J.P., £500; the shareholders of the London and Manchester Plate Glass Company, whose works are in the parish £300; and Mrs. Hughes (Sherdley Hall), Mr. A. Sinclair, J.P. Mr. F. Pemberton, and King's College, Cambridge, £lOO each. The plans have been prepared by Messrs. Paley, Austen, and Paley, of Lancaster, and the contract for the work has been let to Mr. S. Webster, builder, Bootle. The style of. architecture is that known as tne perpendicular, with flowing tracery. Accommodation will, be provided for 800 worshippers.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RITNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The contributions to the Curates' Fund, of Run- corn Parish Church, have shown such an increase dining the past year, that the Vicar feels "justified in making the second curate's stipend rather larger in amount, so that Mr. Seeley will in future receive £l4O instead of £120." The local subscriptions to the curates' fund amount to £l3l ss. 6d., and the largest items are :—Sir Richard Brooke, £25; Lady Brooke, £5 ; Major Orred, £25; Christ Church, £24 12s. 6d. ; Messrs. Greenall and Co., £10; Mr. Charles Wing, £5 ; Mr. Whittaker, £4 ; Mr. Gregory, Li Is. ; Miss Lowe, .£1 is.; Mr. Sutton, £1 is. ; Mr: H. White, Li Is.; Mr. Jordan, £l.

In this month's Runcorn Parish Magazine the Rev. Canon Wood, thus refers to Free Education :—The gravest questions are before our school managers and we may well pray God to guide their actions, aright when no less a matter than the future edu- cation of the children of this town is at stake. In our next number we shall be able to announce what will be done when the first September arrives—in the meantime allow m.e to point out that what the ' Education Bill of the present Government proposes is not to make Education free in the sense of paying for it entirely out of the taxes, but to give the man- agers ten shillings out of taxes annually for every unit of average attendance in the schools. Now ten shillings annually is not (equivalent to more than 21d. a week it to so much. The Church collections and private subscriptions cannot therefore be dis- pensed with, nor can some payments by the parent, unless the schools are sold to the School Board which would mean that the local rates would be most seriously augmented, and the difficulty of giving religious teaching greatly increased. It will probably be found a cheaper land better thing for the town for those who can afford a small school fee to pay it cheerfully and for those who cannot to accept the offer at free places which the School Board will most likely decide to make them."

In connection with the above I have heard a penny fee will probably be charged throughout all departments of the Parish Schools and that the Wec,leyans will have a graduated scale of one penny, twopence and threepence. The Catholic School will be made free and without a doubt so will the Board Schools. In regard to the conclusion of the vicar's letter, I may remark that the Board Schools are now quite full and there will be no free places to offer unless the School Board decides to build another snool. The vicar is evidently of opinion that the Church schools will not be able to retain the present large number of scholars at the Parish School and provision will have to be made for those who decide to have free education. I am told that of the thousand scholars who attend the Parish Day School not more than 350 attend the Sunday School, so it is fair to assume the parents of the remaining 650 are not interested in religious education as taught by the Church of England. It will be a ' serious question if this large number deserts in fav- our of free and unsectarian education.

If the value of property is any sign of the pros- perity of a town, Runcorn must be very prosperous at the present time. The other day Mr. T. Clegg, a local auctioneer, offered amongst other lots three shops for sale in Bridge-st., and they realised no less a sum than £2,950, Mr. Buck, chemist, bidding up to £1,400 in order to retain the building he occupies. The sum realised for five lots sold amounted to a total of £3,650. It would be inter- esting if it could be ascertained to what extent the Ship Canal had influenced tl'e price of property with- in the past two years. Rents were certainly never so high.

The forthcoming election of members to the Runcorn Board of Commissioners promises to be of a very lively and interesting character. Ott the present occasion six members retire and their names are Messrs, Jas. Pritchard, J. W. Lightburn, W. Mellor, E. Iraison, J. Dobson, and W. R. Wass. It is not only probable but practically certain that these gentlemen will seek re-election, but whether they will run in harness or each like Hal of the Wynd fight for his own hand is not certain.

Elated at their success in the Guardians election, tha temperance party are bringing forward Mr. T. Lee and Mr. D. Bisbrown, and it would appear that their idea is to oust the two retiring gentlemen who are closely identified with the liquor traffic.. Both Mr. Lea and Mr. Bisbrown are well known and ar- dent teetotallers and at the meeting of the Sons of Temperance on Monday, Mr. Norman related an in- cident which is worthy of repetition.

Sometime ago Mr. Bisbrown was lett by will a licensed house in one of the main thoroughfares of Runcorn, and as such it was worth a considerable amount of money. A life-long teetotaller, and a person whose motto is "Down with the liquor traffic, and up with the people," Mr. Bisbrown acted up to his principles and allowed the license to lapse, and the building is no longer a place for dis- pensing what many consider "distilled damnation." A sacrifice of this kind, proves the sincerity of a man's convictions;

Besides the temperance candidates, Mr. S. Yar- wood may perhaps again put on his armour and enter the lists. Mr. 1. Roberts, draper, Church-st., has a grievance in regard to sanitary matters, and it is said will seek the suffrages of the ratepayers in order that he may purify the fountain head, while a widely known manufacturer of mineral waters in Mr. Isaac Stubbs is also spoken of as one desiring to serve his fellows in the local legislature. A month. may, however, reveal much, and affairs on September 3rd may wear a different aspect.

Many of the readers of this column will regret that Mr. J. Weston, the agent for the Runcorn Sec- tion of the Ship Canal, is severing his connection with the Company and will shortly leave the town. It is no exaggeration to say that Mr. Weston has been in charge of two sections where the most difficult and arduous work had to be carricd out. At Weston (No. 3) he had to deal with the Weaver estuary, and he leaves behind him there two monuments of his constructive skill and engineer- ing capacity in the Marsh Lock, and the Weaver sluices. While he has had charge of the Runcorn (No. 4) section great progress has been made and the construction of the Widnes and Bridgewater Locks have been advanced to a stage when their completion cannot be far distant, the chief difficul- ties having been surmounted. His successor is Mr. E. D. Jones of the Ince section.

Mr. Thomas Snape' C.C.,.0f Widnes, is concluding his campaign in the Heyward Division with vigour and success. All sections of the party are rallying to his support, recognizing in him not only a true and tried public man, but a Lancashire man of the best type and one well fitted for -parliamentary work.

div.head: BY AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT,
div.p: BY AN EARLESTOWN CORRESPONDENT,

The two female officers who for the past six months have had charge of the Salvation Army here, have been transferred to another district, and the author of the scandal which was diligently cir- culawd, respecting one of them, remains undis- coverEd. Two more earnest Christians I think could rot be found,and the painstaking efforts they made to further the cause, were worthy of every credit. To circulate statements iwhich were highly detri- rigkntal to their character, is most unwarrant- able.

Last week the Salvation Army had a very lively time, and, from all accounts, secured some goonl results. The Indian Durbar was quite a new thing here, and comments of a varied nature were made respecting the affair. I thought it was a little far-fetched, but, as the members of the order say, it was the means of bringing together a num- ber of people who otherwise would have taken,no, interest in the proceedings, and, what is better still, they secured one convert. Then again there was the farewell meeting on the Wednesday night. No fault could be found with this, but nine o'clock is quite late enough to discourse discordant music in the street, and if the Salvationists will take the hint, they will not display their musical abilities after that hour. Half-past ten 18 unreasonable.

Again I am asked to grumble about the betting nuisance. Betting is an ?ccupation which does not interest me one whit,but it appears other people are not so indifferent. Some are interested in it one way and some another,but when small crowds con- gzegate about your place of business, it is time to show in which way your sympathies go. In Liver- pool and Manchester we frequently hear of betting raids; and such a thing as book-making in the streets would rot be tolerated. Here, however,in an easy- going place like Earlestown, it can be carried on with impunity. When it ig carried on in such a manner as to cause annoyance to tradespeople, the police shollid take severe measures, and moil the nuisance.

div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Mr. Spurgeon still continues to improve. Lord Salisbury left London yesterday for Dieppe. The Duke of Cleveland passed a more :comfortable night, but was very feeble yesterday. CMCKE T. Sussex beat Gloucester by 55 runs; Kent all out, fel.owed:on ; Somerset beat Yorkshire by six wickets. THE FRENCH FLEET. The Northern Fleet weighed anchor at Dover yestez day morning, and steamed down Channel for Portsmouth, to await the arrival of the French Fleet. THE LATE EARL DARTMOUTH. The late Eart Dartmouth's remains were yesterday re- moved from London to Patshull, near 'Wolverhampton, where tbey were interred yesterday afternoon. MR.. O'BRIEN'S DISPUTED BANKRUPTCY. Mr. Chance has lodged a notice that Mr. W. O'Brien will dispute the validity of the order adjudicating him a bankrupt issued at the instance of Lord Salisbury. The debt and the act of bankruptcy will also be disputed. CHARGE AGAINST LADY DE LA ZOUCH. At Marlborough-st. Police Court, yesterday afternoon, Lady De La Zouch was charged, on a summons, with being drunk in Hyde Park on the 25th ult. For the de- fence it was contended that her ladyship was dazed,hav- ing been thrown by her pony. The magistrates said it was evident a mistake had been made, and dismissed the case.
A WHITECFIAPEL MYSTERY. .SUSPECTED ATTEMPT AT SUICIDE.

The Exchange Agency states that tiie,-I;;Ece—strongly suspect that the latest Whiteehapel mystery is a case of attempted suicide. The old woman named Wolfe was found on Thursday about midnight in Dellow-street, Shadwell, suffering from wounds in her throat, and a razor was besides her. She was removed to the Lon- don Hospital, where her injuries were attended to. Sub- sequently she alleged that she had been attacked and wounded by a man, whom she described, who had induced her to enter the court with him. The ina,is- trate at the Thames Police Court was sent for to take her depositions, and the Scotland Yards authorities were communicated with. The woman has become uncon- scious and it is feared that her wounds will prove fatal.

div.head: HOLY COAT OF TREVES.
div.p: THE HOLY COAT OF TREVES.

TRB YES, FRIDAX.—The actual exposition of the Holy Coat of Treves to the veneration of pilgrims will not begin until the 20th inst. Yesterday the so-called ele- vation of the Coat, that is, the removal of the relic by the bishop from the shrine in which it is preserved, took place.

div.head: MINISTER'S SON AND HIS
div.p: A MINISTER'S SON AND HIS

APPRENTICESHIP TO STONEMASONS. At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, Arthur Mordan, aged 22, was sued by Messrs. Williams and Clay, stonemasons,for recovery of 10s. compensation for damage sustained through leaving their employ on July 31st.. Mr. Browne appeared for the defendant.—Mr. Clay stated that. the defen- dant, on the manner in which he did his work be- ing complained of, put on his coat and went away. He put in the indentures of apprenticeship of the defendant up to the year 1892. In reply to Mr-Browne, he said he did not know the defendant was over 21 years of age, Mr. Williams had never taken up a mallet to hit the defeadant, got hold of him, or threatened to shoot him. Witness paid him.l,3s..a week.—Mr. Browne: He is not an apprentice now. He is over 21.—Witness said the defendant had never arranged with him that the in- dentures should not be enforced after he was 21.—Mr. Williams gave evidence that on the day in question the defendant was spoiling his work, and he took hold of the chisel and pulled it away from him. He thought it a very great shame that it should be said he offered to strike the defendant with a mallet. Ho never took hold of him.—Mr. Browns: Did you ever threaten to shoot him ?—Witness: Well, it might be a figure of speech. I should never think of anything of the sort. It is most ridiculeus.—Mr. Browne contended that as the inden- tures specified an increase of wages from ald. to 3fd. an hour on the defendant reaching 21 years of age, the complainants must have known his age, and that being over 21, he was no longer an apprentice ; also that there was no proof that notice to the defendant was necessary, and that the defendant, left because he was in .fearof, violence from the complain- ant. His client's fellow employes dare not come as witnesses for fear of their employers. In the course of his remarks Mr. Williams interrupted and Mr. Browne desired him to sit down, but he refused to do so and re- entered the complainant's box remarking that if Mr. Browse carried on that way something would come out of the matter.—The defendant gave evidence corroborat- ing his solicitor's statement,and said Mr. Williams would have struck him with the- mallet if he had not taken up a hammer to defend himself. He had left because of Mr. Williams's constant cursing and swearing and viblent temper. It was now his intention, though not' at first, to withdraw from the contract. The firm, had retused to let him go on payment of a sum of money. He was so afraid of Mr. Williams's violence that he could not stay. He had threatened him imnumerable times. There was not a man in the shop who could not confirm what ha said.—ln the course of his evidence Mr. Clay remarked: Why don't you tell him the truth at once that you want to go to be a parson. The Bench considered the defendant had a legal right to break the contract,, but that there had not been sufficient- notice by the defendant and mulcted him 2s. costs..

Whilst working in Stoke Tunnel, near Grantham, on the Groat Northern Railway, on Thursday morning, a bricklayer's labourer named Henry Cross, Aged 45 years, was knocked down by a goods train and killed. He was .terribly mutilated. The Queen's Bench, on Thursday, granted the applic- ation of tht3 Local Government Board, for a rule nisi for a mandamus directing the Guardians of aettering Union to*appcint a vaccination officer, the- post having been vacant since September. NEWTON VOLUNTEER: IN. CAMP.

On Saturday about 110 members of F Company (Newton), of the 6c V.8.K.L.R., left Newton for the purpose of goihg under canvaeat. Ramsey, with the regiment. The Company mustered at the orderly room, and marched to the station where they took the 10 o'clock train to Liverpool. They were under the command of Captain MtCoropodale. and were- accompanied by Col. Wood)andSergeant-Instructor Parkes. On arrival at Liverpool they joined the main body of the regiment,,and journeyed to Ram, sey by the isle of Man steam packet Companyls boat Snaefell. They hada very pleasant passage to the Island, and on aarival• at Ramsey they were greeted by large crowds of people who lined the pier.. After disemba3king the regiment marahed to the camp, which was pitched at Milntown, headed by the band, which was in charge of bandmaster Burke, some lively music being discoursed on the way. On Sunday morning the regiment turned out to church parade, the service being, conducted by the Rev. Dr. Barclay, chaplain of the corps, and in the afternoon the band played a selection of sacred music, which was much en-toyed by a large gathering of people. On Tuesday the Bishop held garden party, to whioh the o 'tame d the regimeht I were invited.

THE NATIONAL TELEPHONE CO. LIMITED. TELEPHONE PATENTS. OTICE.—As it has recently been publicly stated in several quarters that the Telephone Patents held by the National Telephone Company expire on the 30t14 July next, the Directors deem it their duty to give public notice that this statement is only true with regard to the first of Edi- son's Transmitter Patents, and that the various forms of carbon transmitter in common use in this country (the Blake, the Hunnings, the Crossley, etc.) are covered by later patents which do not expire until the latter part of 1892 and the beginning of 1893. The Directors desire to warn the public that the manufac- ture sale and use of these instruments, and of instruments constructed in colourable imitation thereof, will conanue to be an infringement of the Company's Patent Rights. By order of the Board. ALBERT ANNS, Secretary. Oxford Court, Canon-street, London. B.C. 30th June, 1891.

Carr (Sankey-st.)., Thomas Lewis (Waterloo-road), Andrew McCann (Pleasant-st.),and Wm. Glynn(Nelson- st.), pleaded guilty to stealing a quantity of provisions from the shop of Mr. Carney, grocer, Waterloo-road, on the 29th July. George Carr who had been in a reform- story for 5 years was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour, and the others were sent to gaol for 10 days afterwards to be detained five yearsin a reformatory. POACHING.—Frank Grimes and Joseph Hughes, of St. Helens, were charged with trespassing on land in the oc- cupation of Mr. W. Jones. Moore, rA Bold, in pursuit of game, on the 29th July. The prisoners were each sen- tenced to a month's hard labour. They had attacked the gamekeeper and constable with stones.

lam not at all a good hand at begging, but I have been asked to call the attention of the ratepayers to the fact that the schools which are approaching completion in Market-st.,are a long way from being paid for.
